en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
*Sāsanavaṃsappadīpikā*:
The Buddha, the best of bipeds, is the destroyer of darkness.
Having slain the lotus-born Kaja and awakened to enlightenment,
he stands firmly established upon the mountain-peak of the Path in the void;
may he protect me for a long time with constant happiness, forever and ever.
Requested by bhikkhus who had come from various distant regions, even from the island of Siṃhala, he [constructed] a dwelling.
It is indeed illuminated by the lamp of the lineage of the teachers (Sāsanavaṃsappadīpikā), just as it was by those of old.
The methods for reciting in detail and the analytical determinations have been composed;
furthermore, they belong to the Maramma tradition.
Simply by the fact of their having been composed,
it conveys the meaning very well even to those dwelling on other islands.
Therefore, indeed, having compared it with the various texts,
I shall compose this work in the original language.
"Let the virtuous examine this. Herein, this is the outline:
1. The Path of the Narrative of the History of the Dispensation as it Reached Nine Stages.
2. The narrative account of the history of the Dispensation in the Island of Siṃhala;
3. The narrative account of the history of the Dispensation in Suvaṇṇabhūmi; 4.
The narrative account of the history of the Dispensation in the Yona country.
5. The section on the history of the dispensation in the kingdom of Vanavāsi;
6. The section on the history of the dispensation in the kingdom of Aparanta; 7.
The section on the history of the dispensation in the kingdoms of Kaśmīra and Gandhāra.
8. The Path of Discourse on the History of the Saṅgha in the Mahiṃsaka Province;
9. The Path of Discourse on the History of the Saṅgha in the Great Province (Mahāraṭṭha);
10. The Path of Discourse on the History of the Saṅgha in the Cīna Province.
1. The Section on the History of the Dispensation Appearing in Nine Stages. 1.
In this regard, the section on the history of the dispensation appearing in nine stages should be understood as follows.
For our Blessed One, the Sammasambuddha, for the sake of the welfare of those to be trained, disregarding the happiness within his own grasp, [proceeded from] the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara...
At his feet, having adorned himself with a *mañjūsaka* flower called the "Exposition," he—
disregarding his own weariness through many births over four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, and having fulfilled the thirty perfections—
passed away from his existence as Vessantara and experienced the celestial bliss in the Tusita heaven.
Then, being urged by the devas, he took rebirth on the full moon day of the month of Āsāḷha,
on a Thursday, in the womb of Queen Māyā— who belonged to the unadulterated lineage of King Asaṃbhinnattha—
of the great King Suddhodana, whose royal line was likewise unadulterated; and from that time until the month of Vesākha, due to his incomparable nature...
Having been born on a Friday during the full moon, and having attained the prosperity of kingship at the age of sixteen,
after twenty-nine years had passed, he beheld the four omens shown by the devas at the time of departing from the auspicious park;
having become filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he made the Great Renunciation and, on the bank of the river named Anomā, [encountered] a bee...
Having shaved off his hair, which was like gold in color, and having clothed himself in the saffron robes of Devadatta,
he ate the milk-rice given by the merchant’s daughter named Sujātā on the bank of the river named Neranjarā at dawn on the full moon day of the month of Vesākha,
using forty-nine mouthfuls; this was according to the natural law of previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Having lowered his golden bowl into the river and approached the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), he sat upon the invincible throne (Aparājitapallaṅka).

Beginning from the beginningless cycle of existence, he severed the heads of the hundreds of enemies that are the mental defilements (kilesa)—which had followed him like a shadow—with the fourfold army of the Path (magga).
Having attained the sovereignty of the Great Dharma King over the three worlds, [he reigned] for forty-five years.

Having spread the net of his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) over various places for the sake of various beings, and having displayed the knowledge of his teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*), he taught the Dhamma and established the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

Having established it, at a time when the lifespan was eighty years, after shining forth like a mass of flames that has finished its burning, he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu*). Death.
Indeed, this Dhamma has no inherent nature of discerning that "this is to be cherished exceedingly in the three worlds," "this is to be revered exceedingly," or "this is to be feared exceedingly.
It proceeds taking even the Blessed One himself—the Supreme Person of the three worlds—as its object;
how much less, then, us? Oh, how wonderful is the nature of conditioned phenomena! And on this point, there are these verses:
This law of death indeed belongs to one who is shameless and lacks moral dread,
even as he takes away the highest pinnacle of the three worlds.
He went even further than that toward others.
Like a thief who is a butcher of cows,
he set out only to kill.
Just as one who has obtained an ox in this world finds its utility to be only that much,
so too is it with the King of Death.
He does not recognize the virtue of those who are kind here;
for he has set out only to kill.
When the Blessed One had been completely extinguished for seven days, the Venerable Mahākassapa,
traveling from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with one thousand three hundred and fifty bhikkhus, heard on the way that the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had passed away.
Seeing the bhikkhus weeping and not yet free from sorrow, he [saw] a man named Subhadda who had gone forth in old age.
A bhikkhu speaks thus: “Friends, do not lament; there is no one here for whom you should grieve.
Previously we were oppressed by a wandering ascetic who said, ‘Do this; this is permitted for you; do not do that;
this is not permitted for you,’ just like a slave to a debt-collector. But now we...”
"Whatever we desire, that we are able to do; but whatever we do not desire, that we are able to avoid.
Having heard this, [he thought]: "If such a hostile person exists, the teaching of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, will quickly disappear.
Now, while a body resembling a mass of gold still exists, it has been produced through suffering..."

"A great danger has arisen for the Dispensation; thinking that such a person, having obtained such a companion, might cause his own progress to decline rather than increase, he was overcome with mental distress.
Having attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*), he thought:
'I shall have this monk clothed here and now in white garments, scatter ashes over his body, and cast him out.'"
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera: "Now, while the body of the ascetic Gotama still exists, the assembly is engaged in dispute; people will speak ill of this.
Having subsequently stilled this thought and forgiven them, even as he was attaining final Nibbāna, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, [remained] by that...
Reflecting that "the Dhamma taught by him still exists; and for the sake of firmly establishing the Dhamma taught by him, when it is being recited in chorus,
the Dispensation will not disappear through such individuals but will surely endure for a long time," and recollecting the spiritual assistance rendered to the Blessed One—
such as the gift of the sandalwood robe from the riverbank— he [proceeded] after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One...
In the third month, on the fifth day after the full moon of the month of Āsāḷha, at Rājagaha in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, relying upon the king named Ajātasattu,
he held the First Council together with five hundred Arahants over seven months.
At that time, having completely removed one hundred and forty-eight years of the Kaliyuga, the Dispensation became equal in duration to the Kaliyuga.

Having done so, he established it. Now, when Ajātasattu had attained the kingship for eight years, at that time in the kingdom of Marumba, in the city of Taṅkosaṅgata, a king named Jambudīpadhaja had attained the kingship for more than five years.
And in this First Council, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Upāli, the Venerable Ānanda, and the Venerable...
Anuruddha and others, numbering five hundred great elders, recited the scriptures first and thus supported the Dispensation.
Thus, the wicked words of the evil renunciant Subhadda became a cause for the support of the Dispensation.
This evil renunciant named Subhadda was a barber by caste and a resident of the city of Ātumā. When he—
When the Blessed One was traveling to the city of Ātumā, Attana’s two sons had their hair and beards trimmed by a barber;
they then prepared rice gruel with the rice, oil, and other provisions they had obtained and offered it to the Buddha together with the Saṅgha. However, the Blessed One did not accept it;
he asked the reason for it, rebuked them, and [declared] the offense of *dukkaṭa* for undertaking what is unallowable.
He also prescribed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for a monk who had previously been a barber for shaving. For that reason,
having conceived a grudge and desiring to destroy the Dispensation, he spoke such wicked words as if he were vomiting out a red-hot iron ball that he had swallowed.
King Ajātasattu favored them, saying, "Let the Wheel of Dhamma be yours; I shall set in motion the Wheel of Authority. Let them sing together with full freedom.
Thus, it should be understood that this was the first instance of royal patronage for the Dispensation.
Furthermore, the lineages of the heads of the five hundred Arahants, such as Mahākassapa and others, became manifold and beyond counting. As for what occurs here...
What follows hereafter should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Those great elders, having recited the scriptures, attained final Nibbāna. And in this regard, there are these verses:
"And those elders who possessed supernormal powers..."
Having held the First Council and having upheld the Dispensation,
they fell victim to death.
Although psychic powers exist,
yet having abandoned them,
they have attained nibbāna, brought death under their control.
Having reached us, they are like birds with clipped wings. What talk can there be for us?
But as for our capturing them—
"There is no essence in death;
thus should the wise man bear it in mind.
This is the summary of the account of the first council.
Thereafter, for another hundred years, their succession of disciples maintained the teaching and came [to us].
Then, as the days and nights passed in due course, one hundred years after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Vajjiputta monks from Vesālī declared at Vesālī:
"The practice of the salt-in-a-horn is permissible; the practice of the two-finger-breadth is permissible; the practice of the interval between villages is permissible."

"The practice of staying together in a residence is permissible; the practice of subsequent consent is permissible; the practice of customary behavior is permissible; the practice of churning [milk] is permissible;

it is permissible to drink fermented grain-liquor; it is permissible to have a sitting mat without a border; it is permissible to accept gold and silver"—these ten points they proclaimed as allowable.
Of them, King Kālāsoka, the son of Susunāga, was a partisan.
Now at that time, the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta, while wandering on tour among the Vajjis, heard that the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī were reportedly proclaiming ten points in Vesālī.
He thought, "This is not fitting, that I should [allow] a failure of the teaching of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers..."
Having heard this, he thought, "I shall remain unconcerned; having restrained those who speak contrary to the Dhamma, I will illuminate the Dhamma," and so he proceeded toward Vesālī.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāyasa arrived at the Vālukārāma in Vesālī with seven hundred Arahants, including Revata and Sabbakāmī, intending to hold a communal recitation (saṅgīti). And the monks of the Vajjiputta clan...
With hostile intent, they approached King Kālāsoka and reported: "Great King, we have been dwelling here in this Great Forest Monastery, guarding the Perfumed Chamber.
Now, Great King, other monks who speak contrary to the Dhamma have arrived, desiring to plunder and destroy us.
And King Kālāsoka, for the purpose of preventing the incoming monks from entering—
"Stop him! he sent to his ministers. But as the ministers went to stop him, through the supernatural power of the deities, they did not see the monks.
On that very same day, during the night, King Kālāsoka saw a dream in which he appeared to fall into the Lohakumbhī hell.
His sister, the elder nun named Nandā, was traveling through the air and preaching the Dhamma.
Having restrained the Mahātheras and demonstrated the great faultiness of supporting monks who speak contrary to the Dhamma,
he gave counsel for the sake of upholding the Dispensation.
King Kālāsoka, having attained a sense of spiritual urgency, apologized to the Venerable Mahāyasa Thera and the others, and like King Ajātasattu, he provided support for the communal recitation.
The Elder Mahāyasa and others, relying on King Kālāsoka, refuted the unrighteous points proclaimed by the Vajjiputta monks at the Vālukārāma; after eight months, they held the Second Council.
At that time, ten years had passed since the coronation of King Kālāsoka—the son of King Susunāga—in the city of Pāṭaliputta in the Middle Country.
However, in the kingdom of Para, in the city of Sirikhettanagara, [there was] one named Dvattagoṅka...
One year had passed prior to the king’s consecration, while the teaching of the Victor (Jina) had lasted for one hundred years.

At this Second Council, seven hundred great elders, numbering approximately seven hundred—headed by the highly renowned Revata and Sabbakāmī—convened the second council and upheld the second dispensation.
Among them was the Venerable Elder Mahāyasa, who was praised by the Blessed One with five of the "foremost" (*etadagga*) epithets, just as the Elder Ānanda had been.

He became a co-resident disciple (*saddhivihārika*). The illumination of the unrighteous points (*adhammavatthu*) by the Vajjiputtaka monks was indeed the cause for the Second Council (*dutiya-saṅgīti*).

Furthermore, King Kālāsoka, although previously a companion of the monks who spoke what is not Dhamma, subsequently became a companion of the monks who speak according to the Dhamma and rendered them assistance.
Therefore, it should be understood that the king was the one who upheld the Second Dispensation (*sāsana*).

At the Second Council, however, the lineage of disciples of the seven hundred great elders, headed by the great elders Mahāyasa Thera and Revata Sabbakāmī, became manifold, exceeding the path of calculation.
Whatever remains to be said hereafter should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Those great elders, having recited the Dhamma for the second time, passed away into Parinibbāna. And on this point there are these verses:
And those wise elders,
having held the Second Council and having upheld the Teaching, [passed away].
They have fallen under the sway of Death.
Even those elders who possessed supernormal powers eventually came under the power of Death.
"How indeed have we been liberated,
and how shall we be liberated from what remains?"—
this is the summary of the account of the second council.
Thereafter, for two hundred and thirty-eight years, the teaching of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
remained untroubled and free from corruption. When those two hundred and thirty-eight years had elapsed, during the reign of the king named Siridhammāsoka in the city of Pāṭaliputta,
[the people], having gained faith in the Buddha’s teaching through the novice Nigrodha, provided material requisites and honor to the Saṅgha of monks.
There was a great multitude. At that time, about sixty thousand members of other sects (titthiyas), out of regard for gain and honor, though they had not actually gone forth, acted as if they had;
they participated in the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other formal acts, just like cranes in the midst of swans, or wild calves among cattle, or donkeys in the midst of thoroughbred horses.
At that time, the community of bhikkhus, reflecting that the assembly was now impure, did not perform the Uposatha.
Having become a source of corruption within the Dispensation, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies were suspended for seven years.
King Siridhammasoka, having heard of this, sent a minister with the command: "Settle this legal dispute and cause the Uposatha to be performed."
And the friend, being himself deluded because he was unable to ask the king what he should do when the monks were unwilling to perform the Uposatha,
stirred things up with the words of another who was deluded, saying, "Great King, if the Saṅgha of monks does not perform the Uposatha,
it intends to destroy the Saṅgha of monks"— thus, being himself deluded, he repeated the words of one who was deluded.
Having heard this, he went to the monastery and caused the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to break their observance of the Uposatha.
When the king heard of this, he became filled with dread, thinking, "This fool has committed such a cruel deed even without my command;
will I be released from this evil karma, or not? Thus, being seized by fear, [he sent for] the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa at the Ganges.
Having brought him back from the opposite side, he questioned the Elder regarding that matter.

The Elder replied, "By means of the *Dīpakatittira Jātaka*, I shall liberate him from evil karma through his lack of sentience. For seven days, he instructed King Siridhammāsoka in the debate against the sectarians;
having weighed the arguments in debate, he caused sixty thousand sectarians to leave the fold of the Dispensation.
At that time, however, he observed the Uposatha. In accordance with the method prescribed by the Blessed One, he expounded the *Kathāvatthu* in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
And at the Asokārāma, approximately one thousand great elders recited the texts over the course of nine months.
At that time, in the Middle Country, after King Aśoka the Glorious had attained sovereignty over the city of Pāṭaliputta, eighteen years had passed.
In the kingdom of Marammarāṭṭha, however, after King Ramboṅka had attained sovereignty over the city of Sirikhettanagara, twelve years passed. And during this Third Council,
the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa, having gone to the Brahma-world with the Great Elders who were the members of the Second Council,
requested the Great Brahmā named Tissa to support the Dispensation according to the established procedure.
Having passed away from there, he was reborn here in the womb of a brahmin woman named Moggalīyā.
Out of regard for gain and honor, he established a monastery for sixty thousand non-Buddhist ascetics;
because the assembly was impure due to his admission of them into rituals such as the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, the failure to perform the Uposatha for seven years occurred within the Dispensation.

The very reason for this was the upholding [of the Dispensation]. After the great elders, headed by Mahāmoggaliputtatissa, Majjhantika, and Mahāreva, had held the Third Council, they upheld the Dispensation for the third time.
And King Siridhammāsoka, having observed the arguments of the heretics, [acted] by means of expelling the heretics from the Dispensation and other measures.
The King should be understood as the upholder of the Dispensation.
There were many lineages of disciples descending from the great elders Mahāmoggaliputtatissa, Majjhantika, Mahāreva, and others, numbering about a thousand and exceeding the path of calculation.
Whatever remains to be said regarding this should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Those great elders...
Having recited the Third [Council], they attained final Nibbāna. And regarding this, there are these verses:
"Those elders who possessed great psychic power, having recited the Teaching,"
They have gone under the sway of Death,
like the sun into the womb of clouds;
just as these [beings] go, so do they pass away.
In the same way, we too shall go;
for who indeed can escape from death?
Beings have death as their ultimate destination.
Therefore, a wise person,
for the very purpose of realizing that very same deathless Nibbāna,
[should apply themselves].
"One should perform merit at all times.
This is the summary of the account of the Third Council.
Thereafter, having investigated where the teaching of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, would be firmly established, [they determined it].

The Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa, seeing that the teaching of the Conqueror was about to be firmly established in border regions, dispatched great elders individually to establish the teaching of the Conqueror in nine locations.
Specifically, he sent the Elder Mahāmahinda to the island of Sīhaḷa, saying: "Go to this island and establish the teaching there."
He sent the Elder Soṇa and the Elder Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi; the Elder Mahārakkhita to the Yona country;
the Elder Rakkhita to the Vanavāsī kingdom; the Elder Yonaka-Dhammarakkhita to the Aparanta kingdom;
the Elder Majjhantika to the kingdoms of Kaśmīra and Gandhāra; the Elder Mahārevata to the Mahimsaka region; and the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita...
[Mahinda sent] Mahāraṭṭha, Majjhimatthera, and Cīnaraṭṭha. And there he dispatched them together with a Saṅgha sufficient for the higher ordination (*upasampadā*).
Those great elders went separately and established the Dispensation in various places.
Having established it in those various locations, [the land] shone with the radiance of the monks’ saffron robes, surpassing the clouds, mist, dust, and Rāhu.
Like the moon when it has emerged from the clouds, the teaching of the Victor was established without hindrance.
Among those nine locations, the one named Suvaṇṇabhūmi is now simply the city of Sudhamma.

If one asks how this is known, it is through inference from the route or inference from the location. How is it known through inference from the route? It is said that from here [one reaches] Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
It is seven hundred yojanas; a ship does not travel by a single wind, but travels in seven days and nights.

Now, at one time, even while traveling in this manner for seven days, the ship did not pass over the back of the whirlpool-fish in the river—as stated in the Aṭṭhakathā regarding the measurement of the path from the island of Siṃhala to Suvaṇṇabhūmi—[this was] before the time of Sukhumma.
This corresponds to the distance of the path traveled to the island of Siṃhala.
It is said that from Sudhamma to the island of Siṃhala there are seven hundred yojanas; when the wind blows directly, a wind-ship reaches it in seven days and nights.
This is understood by inference from such a route.
How is it known by inference from the circumstances? It is said that Suvaṇṇabhūmi is situated near the great ocean and is a great port frequented by merchants from various foreign kingdoms.
For this very reason, Mahājanaka Kumāra and others came to Suvaṇṇabhūmi by ship from the city of Campā and other places for the purpose of trade. Sudhammapura, too—
Now it remains right near the great ocean. Thus it is understood from its location.
Others, however, say that Suvaṇṇabhūmi is indeed the Haribhuñja kingdom, because of the abundance of gold there. Still others say it is the Siyam kingdom itself. All of this must be investigated.
Others say that Aparanta is a separate kingdom altogether; yet others say that Aparanta is indeed the Sunāparanta kingdom.

They say this; and that is indeed appropriate. If one asks why "Aparanta" is understood to be specifically the Sunāparanta country, it is because it is mentioned by two names in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

For in the commentary on the *Upari-paṇṇāsa* and in the commentary on the *Saḷāyatana-saṃyutta*, the masters of the commentaries state that the Elder Koṇḍañña of the Sunāparanta country attained the status of being foremost among those who receive voting tickets (*salākādāna*).

This was said by connecting "Suna" with "Aparanta-raṭṭha. However, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, that same country is mentioned without the word "Suna. Here, the word "Suna" is a synonym for "son.
King Mandhātu’s eldest son, having summoned the inhabitants of the four continents, [addressed] them individually...
He assigned separate dwelling places for them. Among those, the region for the inhabitants of the Northern Island was called the kingdom of Kuru;

that for the inhabitants of the Eastern Island was called the kingdom of Vedeha; and that for the inhabitants of the Western Island was called Aparanta. Because they were born in the western island, they are referred to by the term "Sunas.
For even though they were born there, their sons are called either "Jātā" or "Sunā," just as the Vajjiputtakas [are named after their birthplace].
"Bhikkhu": It should be understood that this very term is designated by means of the word "nose" (*sunasa*) either according to their desire for conduct or according to the elegance of their speech.
That which is called the "Yona country" is simply the dwelling place of the Yavana people, which is referred to as *yaṅgaṅgha*.
The place called the city of Sirikhetta was the district known as Vanavāsī. However, some say that Vanavāsī was merely a kingdom and not the location of the city of Sirikhetta; that is not correct.
For it is precisely the location of the city of Sirikhetta that is named the district of Vanavāsī. If one asks why this is known, it is because of our king’s brother-king.
In the city of Sirikhetta, at a time when it was concealed by thickets, he recovered an ancient bronze Buddha image that had been submerged within a mound of earth;
on its pedestal, an ancient inscription is seen stating, "This is for the purpose of worship by the forest-dwellers and the inhabitants of Raṭṭha," and from this it is understood.
The country named Kasmīragandhāra consists of the kingdom of Kasmīra and the kingdom of Gandhāra. These two kingdoms exist as a single contiguous unit;
for that very reason, he sent the Elder Majjha to both kingdoms. However, because it is a common noun (*janapada*), it takes the neuter singular form.
At that time, however, because it was a territory established under the command of a single king, it is expressed in the singular number.
They say that this is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
The region called Mahiṃsakamaṇḍala is the Andhaka country, which is referred to as the Yakkhapura country.

The "Great Country" (*Mahāraṭṭha*) is the Mahānagara country; for nowadays people indeed refer to it as the Mahānagara country by joining the word "great" (*mahā*) with the term "city" (*nagara*). Some teachers also call it the Siam country (*Siāmaraṭṭha*).
"Cīnaratta" refers to the country of Cīna, which stands as one continuous region connected to the Himālaya mountains.
This constitutes the establishment of the Sāsana in nine separate locations.
Now, the account of the succession of Elders from the beginning must be told. For, of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha...
Saddhivihārika was the Elder Upāli; his disciple was the Elder Dāsaka; his disciple was the Elder Soṇaka;

his disciples were the Elders Siggava and Candavajjī; and their disciple was the Elder Moggaliputtatissa—these five great elders were the originators of the lineage of teachers (ācariyaparamparā) in the history of the Dispensation. For [the lineages] that constitute their succession of disciples...
The succession of teachers shall not be interrupted until the end of time.
Furthermore, by means of the lineage of preceptors, only modest monks (*lajjibhikkhū*) should be admitted and taught, and not shameless monks (*alajjibhikkhū*).

For even though shameless monks may be highly learned, being driven by greed for gain and honor from the world, they destroy the fabric of the Dhamma and incite great danger upon the noble Dispensation. This is called the work of protecting the Dispensation.

For this is indeed the domain of those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*), not of those who lack it. Therefore, the ancient Elders (theras), without disregarding the thought, "Who indeed will protect the Dispensation in the future?", uttered these words three times:
"In the future, those who possess a sense of shame will protect the Dispensation; those who possess a sense of shame will protect it;
those who possess a sense of shame will protect it. Thus, even in the Middle Country, there are individuals who lack a sense of shame.
It should be understood that there were many [such monks].

For more than a hundred years after the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the Blessed One, the Vajjiputta monks, following the same method previously described, proclaimed points contrary to the Dhamma;
they consulted with those evil monks who had been excluded at the time of the First Council.
Having sought out companions, they held a recitation like the Great Elders did during the Great Council (*mahāsaṅgīti*).

Having done so, they became separate groups. "Alas! This is a laughable matter, just as an old jackal, conceiving pride through his mere resemblance to a four-footed animal, imagines himself to be a lion and lets out a lion’s roar like a lion. They [corrupted] the true word (*pāvacana*).
Not knowing things as they truly are, they proclaimed the meaning to be "as it truly is" based merely on the shadow of the words.

They even removed certain portions of the scriptures, and that [alteration] occurred only within their own faction, not within the faction of those who speak according to the Dhamma. Having subverted the Dhamma and Vinaya, they acted solely according to their own whims.
This, however, was a single faction of those who speak what is not Dhamma, known as the Mahāsaṅgīti.
After that, when some time had passed, they split from one another due to mutual disputes;
thus, two groups emerged: one called the Gokulika and another called the Ekavyāvahārika.
Subsequently, from within the Gokulika group itself, they split again due to mutual differences, resulting in two further groups: one called the Bahussutika and another called the Paññattivāda.
Furthermore, from among those very same groups, one group named the Cetiyavādins split off.
After a long time had passed since then, two groups split from the Dhammavādins:
one group named the Mahīṃsāsakas who entered a dissimilar faction, and another named the Vajjiputtakas. Subsequently, from the Vajjiputtaka group itself...
Having split from one another, four schools emerged: the group called Dhammuttariya, the group called Bhaddayānika, the group called Channāgārika, and the group called Samutiya.

Furthermore, having split from one another from within the Mahīṃsāsaka school, five schools emerged: the group called Sabbatthivāda, the group called Dhammaguttika, the group called Kassapiya, the group called Saṅkantika, and the group called Suttavāda.

Thus, among the Great Elders who were reciting the Second Council in the Middle Country, seventeen groups of those who spoke what was not Dhamma (adhammavādī) split off from the group of Elders who spoke the Dhamma (dhammavādī).

And those groups of those who spoke what was not Dhamma became an endless succession within the lineage of Elders in the Dispensation. For they were of no benefit to the Dispensation, nor to the lineage of Elders.
Once they have entered, it is impossible to seize them, just as a crane cannot seize [fish] among a flock of swans, just as a wild ox cannot seize [cattle] among a herd of cows,
and just as a counterfeit coin cannot seize [value] among a collection of gold. Furthermore,

the lineage of elders descending from the Elder Mahākassapa should be understood according to the method set forth in the Parivāra-khandhaka and in the *Samantapāsādikā* commentary, beginning with "Upāli and Dāsaka," and so forth.

By inferring the pure conduct and other qualities of the Elder Upāli and the others, it can be known that the conduct and other qualities of those elders were pure as far back as the time of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa; just as, by inferring the rains from the clouds upstream on a river,
one can perceive the abundance of water in the river downstream— this is what is called the method of inference based on a cause (*kāraṇānumāna*).

However, as long as there were the Elder Moggaliputtatissa and others, it was possible to know that the Elder Upāli possessed pure conduct and so forth by inferring the pure conduct and other qualities of those elders;
just as, for example, having seen smoke above and inferred from it,
one can know that fire exists— this is what is called inference from the effect (phalānumāna).
However, by inferring the pure conduct and other qualities of the Elder Upāli at the beginning and the Elder Moggaliputtatissa at the end,
it is possible to know that the conduct of the elders in between— such as Dāsaka, Soṇa, and Siggava— was likewise pure; just as, for example,
having seen the tracks of deer on the near side and the far side of a stone slab, one infers [the same tracks] in the middle.
"It can be known that there is a footprint of the path [of the Dhamma] hidden in the middle"—this is called the method of the deer's footprint.
Thus, by means of these three methods, it should be understood that this group of elders (theravāda-gaṇa) speaks according to the Dhamma and is modest and virtuous.
This same method should be applied to what follows as well. And the succession of elders, up until its recording in books, is found in the Parivāra-khandhaka and in the Samantapāsādikā.
Thereafter, Mahinda, Iṭṭhiya, and the others are to be understood according to the method described [above].
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Account of the History of the Dispensation up to the Ninth Stage," in the *Sāsanavaṃsa*.
2. The Chapter on the History of the Dispensation in the Island of Siṃhala.
Now, the opportunity has arrived to speak of the history of the Dispensation in the Island of Siṃhala; therefore, I shall relate it.
For the Island of Siṃhala, being the place where the Dispensation was established, is like the interior of a shrine (cetiyagabbha). The Perfectly Enlightened One...
It is said that even during his lifetime, he went to the island of Siṃhala three times.

The first time, having gone alone for the purpose of subduing the *yakkhas*, and having subdued them, he thought, "After I have attained final nibbāna, the Dispensation will be established on the island of Siṃhala," and thus he summoned the island three times to provide protection for the Tambapaṇṇi island. The second time, [he went] for the sake of his maternal uncle and nephew...
The Nāgarāja went alone for the purpose of taming them, and having tamed them, he departed. On his third journey,
accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, he went to the site of the Mahācetiya, the site of the Thūpārāma-cetiya,
the site where the Mahābodhi was established, the site of the Mahiyaṅgaṇa-cetiya, the site of the Mudiṅgaṇa-cetiya, the site of the Dīghavāpi-cetiya, and the site of the Kalyāṇiya-cetiya.
And having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), he sat down.
At that time, however, the Dispensation remained submerged for some time.

Later, sent by the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa—who had been firmly established in the lineage of elders as previously described—the Elder Mahinda [arrived] when thirty-five years had passed since the Wheel of the Conqueror.
When two hundred and thirty-five years had elapsed since the Wheel of the Conqueror, in the second month of Kattika, he went to the island of Siṃhala together with these elders:

Dutiya-Kattiya, Iṭṭiya, Uttiya, Sambula, and Bhaddasāla. At that same time, in the second month of Kattika, when two hundred and thirty-five years had passed, the elders Soṇa, Uttara, and others [set out] for the purpose of establishing the Dispensation within their respective [domains].
Having taken up their respective responsibilities, they went to their various destinations.

However, after waiting for seven months, when two hundred and thirty-six years had elapsed since the Wheel of the Conqueror, the Elder Mahinda departed for the island of Sri Lanka on the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha in order to establish the Sāsana there. For that very reason—
Among those nine locations, he went to the island of Sīhaḷa on the two hundred and thirty-sixth [day].
However, the other eight locations he visited on exactly the two hundred and thirty-fifth [day]; thus they should be recorded separately.
But why did the Elder Mahāmahinda wait for seven months before going to the island of Sīhaḷa last of all?
In the island of Siṃhala, there was a king named Muṭasīva who was weakened by old age and unable to uphold the Dispensation;
however, his son, the prince named Devānaṃpiyatissa, being young, would be capable of upholding the Dispensation.
Let him first receive the kingdom from his mother in the city of Vedissa on Mount Vijita.

It should be understood that after waiting for seven months out of consideration, thinking, "I shall see my kinsmen first," the Elder Mahinda departed for the island of Siṃhala on the very second year and thirty-sixth day [of the dispensation] of the Victor’s wheel.
And the Elder Mahinda was accompanied by the four elders beginning with Iṭṭiya, by his nephew the novice Sumanas, and by Bhaṇḍuka.
Together with these two hundred and thirty-six wheels of the Conqueror (Jinacakkas), on the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha,
like golden swans ascending into the sky in the month of Jeṭṭha, they rose into the air and alighted upon the peak of Mount Missaka in the eastern direction of Anurādhapura.
On the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha, people in the island of Laṅkā celebrated a festival because the lunar mansion was Jeṭṭhā-Mūla.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Vinayaṭīkā* named *Sāratthadīpanī*: "On the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha, the lunar mansion is either Jeṭṭhā or Mūla.
And therein, the full moon mansion is [discussed] according to the method of investigating the full moon mansion among the royal ministers.
It should be understood that it was said thus.

King Devānampiya Tissa, having ordered his ministers to proclaim a festival called the "Constellation Festival," departed from the city accompanied by a retinue of forty thousand men and proceeded toward Mount Missakapabbata.
Pāyāsi desired to go hunting. Then, a certain deity dwelling on that mountain, having enticed the king with the form of a deer and summoned him, brought him face-to-face with the Elder.
Seeing the king approaching, the Elder made a resolution, thinking, "Let the king see me alone, and not the others," and then [he transformed himself].
"Tissa, come here! he said. Upon hearing this, the king thought: "In this entire island, there is not a single human being capable of addressing me by the name 'Tissa.
Yet this man, wearing tattered garments and clad in a soiled saffron robe, addresses me by my name. Who could this be? Is he a human or a non-human? The Elder replied:
"O Great King, we are recluses, disciples of the Dhamma King;
out of compassion for you alone, we have come here from Jambudīpa.
At that time, King Devānampiyatissa had been consecrated with the royal inauguration sent by King Aśoka for one month.
For on the full moon day of Visākha, they performed his consecration.

And he, recollecting the recent report of the propagation of the Dispensation—which he had heard shortly before concerning the Dhamma-presents sent by King Asoka and which was connected with the virtues of the Triple Gem—upon hearing those words of the Elder, "Great King, we are recluses, disciples of the Dhamma-King," thought, "Have the Noble Ones indeed arrived? and at that very moment...
Having laid aside his weapons, he sat down to one side, engaging in friendly conversation. As it is said:
"Having laid aside his weapons, he sat down to one side;
having sat down, the king exchanged greetings, which were full of meaningful purpose."
While he was still engaged in friendly conversation, those forty thousand men also arrived and surrounded him.
Then the Elder pointed out the other six men as well. When the king saw them, he asked, "When did these come?
"Along with me, Great King," he replied. "But now, there are other such ascetics in Jambudīpa as well."
There are, O Great King, even now in Jambudīpa those who are like lamps in the darkness, fanned by the wind of the seers;
in that land there are many disciples of the Buddha— possessors of the threefold knowledge, masters of psychic power, skilled in reading the minds of others, and Arahants whose taints are exhausted.
"Venerable sir, by what means have you come? "Neither by water, Great King, nor by land," he replied. The king understood that they had come through the air.
Desiring to test whether the king possessed self-control regarding his bodily excretions, the Elder asked a question concerning a nearby mango tree.
“What is the name of this tree, Great King? “It is called an *amba* tree, venerable sir.
“But, Great King, apart from this *amba*, is there any other *amba* tree or not? “There are many other *amba* trees as well, venerable sir.
“Setting aside this *amba* and those *amba* trees, Great King, are there indeed any other trees? “There are, venerable sir; however,”
"Not mango trees. "Aside from other mangoes and non-mangoes, is there any other tree?
"This very one, venerable sir, is a mango tree. "Excellent, great king; you are wise.
"Great king, do you have any kinsmen? "Yes, venerable sir, many people. "Setting those aside, are there any who are not kinsmen?"
“There is, Great King. “Venerable sir, those who are strangers are more numerous than those who are kinsmen.
“Setting aside your kinsmen and your strangers, is there anyone else, Great King? “It is I myself, venerable sir. “Excellent, Great King!
That which is called ‘self’ is neither a kinsman nor a stranger to oneself.”
Then the wise elder, thinking that the king would be able to understand the Dhamma, preached the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta (The Short Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint).
At the conclusion of the discourse, the king, together with forty thousand living beings, was established in the three refuges.
Beyond this, whatever remains to be said should be understood according to the method set forth in the Samantapāsādikā and other such works.
Thus, in the island of Sri Lanka, the succession of disciples who came from down to support the Sāsana beginning with Thera Mahinda became numerous, exceeding the path of calculation.
How so? Thera Ariṭṭha was the disciple of Thera Mahāmahinda; his disciple was Tissa-datta;
his disciple was Kāḷasumana; his disciple was Dīgha; his disciple was Dīghasumana.
His disciple was Kāḷasumana; his disciple was Nāga; his disciple was Buddharakkhita; his disciple was Tissa; his disciple was Reva;
his disciple was Sumana; his disciple was Cūḷanāga; his disciple was Dhammapāli;
his disciple was Khema; his disciple was Upālissa; his disciple was Phussadeva; his disciple...
Sumana; his disciple was Mahāpaduma; his disciple was Mahāsīva; his disciple was Upāli; his disciple was Mahānāga;
his disciple was Abhaya; his disciple was Tissa; his disciple was Sumana;
his disciple was Cūḷābhaya; his disciple was Tissa; his disciple was Cūḷadeva; his disciple was Sīva. This [lineage] continues thus...
The fourth council, known as that which was committed to writing, should be understood as the lineage of elders (*thera-paramparā*).

For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It should be understood that [the Dhamma] has been brought down by a succession of teachers (*ācariya-paramparā*) consisting of their very pupils (*antevāsika-paramparā*), continuing until the present day.
Thus, it should be understood that the succession of teachers, which constitutes the succession of their pupils, has come down through the Dispensation until the present time, becoming well-known.
In the Dispensation, those who are called "bearers of the Vinaya" (vinayadharā) must be endowed with the three characteristics.

For three characteristics are to be desired in a bearer of the Vinaya. What are these three? His Sutta is well-learned, well-recited, and well-determined according to the rules and the phrasing—this is the first characteristic.
Furthermore, he stands firm in the Vinaya and is unshakable—this is the second characteristic. He knows the meaning of the rules and is skilled in their exposition—this is the third characteristic.
"This is the second. Furthermore, his lineage of teachers is well-learned, well-attended to, and well-retained"—this is the third.
In this context, "his lineage of teachers is well-learned" means that his succession of elders and his succession of lineages have been properly grasped.
"Well-attended to" means properly attended to; it is known as soon as it is brought to mind.
It becomes like a lamp for that [purpose].
"Well-ascertained" means thoroughly ascertained; it has been ascertained through the sequence of what precedes and follows, and by way of both the meaning and the reason.
Having abandoned one's own opinion, one speaks according to the purity of the teacher, thinking: "My teacher [studied] in the presence of such-and-such a teacher."

He learned it; "from such-and-such"—thus, having brought forward the entire lineage of teachers as a constituent part of the Thera-vāda, he establishes the sequence by concluding that it reached as far as the Elder Upāli, who learned it in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having brought it down even from there, [he continues]:
the Elder Upāli learned it in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Elder Dāsaka [learned it] from his own preceptor, the Elder Upāli.
The Elder Soṇaka [recited] his own preceptor, the Elder Dōsaka; the Elder Siggava, his own preceptor, the Elder Soṇaka;

and the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa, his own preceptors, the Elders Siggava and Caṇḍavajjī—thus having brought forward the entire lineage of teachers as a constituent part of the Theravāda, he [recited] his own preceptor.
Having reached [the next person], he establishes it. For when thus received, the lineage of teachers is well-received.

However, one who is unable to do so should master two or three recitations. For it is proper to know, according to the very last method, how both the teacher and the teacher’s teacher spoke the text and its interrogation.
As for the lineage of elders mentioned above, it extends from the time of the Blessed One’s lifetime until the time of its being committed to books.
They maintained the Tipiṭaka by oral recitation alone; they did not commit it to writing in books so as to preserve it in its entirety.
Thus the Great Theras upheld the Dispensation by performing difficult tasks. Herein is an illustrative story:
it is said that in the island of Ceylon, due to the fear of Caṇḍātissa, the people were thrown into turmoil, the rain did not fall, and there was the fear of famine.
At that time, Akka, the lord of the gods, arrived and said: "Venerable sirs, you will not be able to maintain the Piṭaka.
Therefore, board a ship and go to Jambudīpa. If the ship should prove insufficient, cross over by means of wood or bamboo;
we shall protect you for the sake of your safety. Thus he spoke.
Then about sixty monks went to the seashore and thought again: "We shall not go to Jambudīpa;
we will dwell right here and preserve the Tipiṭaka. Subsequently, the ship turned back from the landing place and went to the Malaya district in a part of the Sihaḷa island.
There they sustained themselves on roots, fruits, and the like, and engaged in recitation.
Being excessively oppressed by the fear of drought, and unable even to do this, they placed their chests upon the sandy surface,
set head against head, and without uttering a word, performed [the recitation] mentally alone. Thus, for twelve years,
they protected the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries and supported the Dispensation.

When twelve years had passed, however, that danger subsided; seven hundred monks who were previously traveling to Jambudīpa arrived and entered the Maṇḍalārāma monastery in the Rāma district of the island of Sīhaḷa.
Those sixty or so monks also went to that very monastery, consulted with one another, and engaged in recitation.
Then they harmonize with one another and do not conflict; they blend together like the waters of the Yamunā with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Thus it should be understood that the Great Elders performed difficult tasks by preserving the Three Piṭakas through oral recitation alone.
That they preserved the scriptures without missing even a single word—that too was indeed a difficult task.
It is said that in the island of Siṃhala, the son of a householder named Punabbasu,
the Elder Tissa, having mastered the Buddha’s word, came to this Jambudīpa; there, having mastered the Buddha’s word in the presence of the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita,
as he was departing, he felt a doubt arise at the very spot where he boarded the ship, even though he had traveled a path of a hundred yojanas.
Returning to his teacher’s presence, he encountered a householder along the way and answered his question.
The man, having gained faith, gave him a cloth worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. He too brought it and presented it to the teacher.
The Elder had it pounded and made a border for his sitting mat. "For what purpose? [the householder asked]. "For the sake of the future [rebirth]," [he replied].
It was for the sake of favoring the people. It seems he thought thus: "By reflecting upon the path we have traveled, future fellow-celibates will consider that their own practice must be fulfilled.
Having resolved his doubts in the presence of the Teacher, the Elder Tissa also returned to his own place on the island of Siṃhala. In this way, even a single word of the scriptures...
It should be understood that even the mere retention [of the teachings] without becoming disenchanted is indeed a difficult task (*dukkarakamma*).

Furthermore, they protect that which is for the most part not yet mastered by means of learning, retention, and so forth, for the sake of its non-disappearance and non-forgetfulness; that too is indeed a difficult task.
It is said that during a great calamity in the island of Sri Lanka, the *Mahāniddesa* was mastered by only a single monk. Then, for the Elder Tissa of the Four Nikāyas...
The preceptor, the Elder Mahātipiṭaka, said to the Elder Mahārakkhita: "Friend Mahārakkhita, learn the *Mahāniddesa* from such-and-such a person.
[He replied: "Venerable sir, I will not learn it from that wicked Kirāta woman. [The preceptor said: "Learn it, friend;
I shall sit beside you. [He replied: "Very well, venerable sir; I shall learn it while you are sitting there. Having made this agreement, for a day and night—
While he was studying [the Mahāniddesa] continuously, on the day of its conclusion, he saw a woman on a lower couch and said: "Venerable sir, I have heard this before;
had I known it would be like this, I would not have studied the Dhamma in such a person's presence.
Nevertheless, many great elders (mahātheras) learned it from him and established the Mahāniddesa. Thus, for the most part...
It should be understood that even the preservation— by means of learning, memorization, and so forth— of that which they do not make proficient,
for the sake of its non-disappearance and non-confusion, is indeed a difficult task. Thus,
from the time of the Blessed One’s own lifetime onwards, for a long period, there has been a succession of great elders as previously described.
They maintained the scriptures (pariyatti) by oral recitation alone. Oh, how great was the abundance of mindfulness, wisdom, and concentration possessed by those ancient Great Elders!

Indeed, it was because of this that they were able to maintain them through oral recitation alone. The maintenance of the scriptures by the ancient elders through oral recitation alone amounted to four hundred and ninety-five [discourses].
According to the method set forth in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, the *Sāratthasaṅgaha*, and other works, when four hundred and fifty-six years had elapsed since the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One,
King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi— son of King Saddhātissa, the eighteenth monarch of the island of Tambapaṇṇi—
ascended the throne; and when he had been king for six years, beings were yet to come who would be deficient in mindfulness, wisdom, and concentration.
Having reflected that they would not be able to preserve [the teachings] by means of oral recitation,
those five hundred great elders who had arrived in succession— having been previously mentioned— relied upon King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi and, in a certain part of the island of Tambapaṇḍī,
in the Malaya district at Ālokaleṇa, committed the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) to writing.

And it should be understood that, when compared with the previously mentioned councils, this is indeed known as the Fourth Council. For it is stated in the *Vinaya-ṭīkā* named *Sāratthadīpanī*: "The council of committing [the texts] to writing is similar to the Fourth Council.

Furthermore, at that same time, King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi reigned in the island of Ceylon, and a king named Kukkuṭasīsa reigned in the city of Sirikhetta in the kingdom of Burma. During the reign of the king who was leading [his people] toward the City of the Immortals (Amarapura), by the monks of the island of Ceylon here...
Regarding the account of the transmission of the letters, it is recorded that they were committed to writing when four hundred and thirty-three years had elapsed.
For it is stated therein: "The period measuring four hundred and thirty-three years.
This [account] extends as far as the time they were committed to writing on the island of Siṃhala.
The establishment of the Dispensation.

Furthermore, in Jambudvīpa and Sihaḷadvīpa, the bhikkhus split into separate factions according to their groups, just as the river flowing out from Lake Anotatta splits into the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and so forth. Therein, in Jambudvīpa...
We shall discuss the schism of the *gaṇas* further below.
However, the schism of the *gaṇas* on the island of Siṃhala should be understood as follows. How so?
For on the island of Siṃhala, when one hundred and eighteen years plus two months had elapsed since the time the Dispensation was established, King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi caused [the Mahāvihāra] to be built...
At the Abhayagiri Monastery, a group split off from the community of Mahāvihāravāsins by distorting both the text and the meaning of the Parivāra-khaṇḍaka;
this group was known as the Abhayagirivāsigaṇa, and it was also called the Dhammarucigaṇa.
When two hundred and forty-two years had passed since the schism of the Abhayagirivāsigaṇa, [during the reign of] Mahāsena...

In the Jetavana Monastery built by King [Mahinda], the monks, having formulated the texts of both the *Visaṅgapāṭha* erroneously, became a separate group apart from the community residing at Abhayagiri; that was known as the Jetavana-vāsigaṇa, and its other name was the Sāgaliyagaṇa.
From the time this Jetavana-vāsigaṇa split, three hundred and fifty-one years [passed].
Furthermore, the monks residing at Upāri-Kurunda and those residing at Kolamba, relying upon King Dāṭhāpatisīha by name,
having composed [their own version] through a distorted interpretation of the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*,

the *Parivāra*, and the *Khandhaka* texts, and having separately formed two groups, they weighed and scrutinized the supreme authority of the residents of the Mahāvihāra; thus [they established] the name "Mahāvihāra."

Having taken [the side of the king], one group split off. Thus, in the island of Siṃhala, four groups split off together with the Mahāvihāravāsin group, which was the lineage of the Elder Mahāmahinda and his successors.
Among them, only the Mahāvihāravāsin group was a proponent of the Dhamma (dhammavādin), while the others were proponents of what is not the Dhamma (adhammavādin). They...

And because of the statement that "the three groups of those who speak against the Dhamma (adhammavādino) abandoned the true meaning and acted without regard for the Dhamma by means of what was not the true meaning," it follows that in the island of Sri Lanka,
those three shameless groups who spoke against the Dhamma wandered about without observing the training rules concerning the "perfectly round" [robe] and the "well-covered" [robe].
From that time onwards, among certain monks in the Dispensation, there arose various kinds of [divergent practices].
It should be understood that [the monks] were seen wearing lower robes (*nivāsana*),
upper robes (*pārupana*), and so forth. From the time the groups of those who spoke what was not the Dhamma (*adhammavādi*) split, more than five hundred and twenty-seven years later,
King Sirisaṅghabodhi took the side of the Mahāvihāra group against the three groups of those who spoke what was not the Dhamma.
Having suppressed [the opposition], he upheld the teaching of the Jina.
That King Sirisaṅghabodhi experienced the prosperity of sovereignty at the same time as our King Anuruddha in the city of Ariṇḍama in the kingdom of Maramma.
Subsequently, during the reign of King Vohārakatissa in the island of Siṃhala, together with a minister named Kapila...
Having recited [the scriptures], he suppressed the faction of those who spoke what is not the Dhamma by relying on the monks residing at the Mahāvihāra, and thus upheld the Conqueror’s dispensation.

Thereafter, during the time of the king named Goṭṭhābhaya, he ordained monks from across the sea who resided at Abhayagiri and purified the dispensation by relying on the monks residing at the Mahāvihāra.
Even after that, during the time of the king named Mahāsena, who was the son of King Goṭṭhābhaya, [he did the same for] those residing at Abhayagiri...

Among the monks, a certain monk named Saṅghamitta, having conspired with King Mahāsena to destroy the Mahāvihāra monastery—the dwelling place of the Arahants such as the Elder Mahāmahinda—began his efforts.
At that time, there were no monks residing in the Mahāvihāra for nine years. Oh, how great was the supernatural power of those Great Elders!
Shameless monks destroyed the dwelling places [of the virtuous], just as crows destroy the nesting place of golden swans.
Among the monks residing at Jetavana, there was a monk named Tissa who, having conspired with that very king, sought to abolish the boundary (sīmā) of the Mahāvihāra.
However, because they lacked integrity, the act of abolishing the boundary did not succeed.
"Ah! How truly extraordinary is the evil deed of those who are immoral!
Just as a lowly branch-deer might tear apart a costly garment of Kāsī cloth, even so has the person who causes the schism become exceedingly far removed from the object to be split.
And on this matter, there are these verses:
Just as a wicked branch-demon, though himself of little value,
with great effort tears apart the fine Kāsī cloth— expensive, woven, and finely spun—
so too does the wicked speaker of what is contrary to the Dhamma [tear apart] the beautiful assembly of those who speak according to the Dhamma.
"With great effort he broke it asunder—oh, how wonderful this is!
Those who were to be broken by him remained far, at a great distance from the breakers;
from the very earth to the peak of existence—it is a wonder that beings do not understand their own karma!"
Thus, because of the power of the groups that speak what is contrary to the Dhamma, the group that speaks according to the Dhamma declines.

Just as golden swans are unable to maintain their natural course due to the wind from the wings of vultures, even so the speaker of the Dhamma declines because of the power of those who speak what is contrary to the Dhamma.
Like a golden deer dwelling in a tiger forest, he seeks his food according to his own inclination.
He did not obtain the opportunity to practice the Dhamma.
More than four hundred and seventy-two thousand years after the establishment of the Sasana on the island of Sri Lanka,
and more than seven hundred and eighty thousand years after the Parinibbāna of the Sammasambuddha—
A king named Mahārāja reigned as ruler.

That king, relying upon him, the monks dwelling in the Mahāvihāra—headed by the Elder Kassapa of Ñadumbaragiri—cleansed the stains from the Dispensation, just as a money-changer cleanses impurities from gold.
Having expelled those who spoke what was not the Dhamma from the community of the Mahāvihāra dwellers, they purified it. And that great king...
It should be understood that in our country of Burma, in the city of Arimaddana, one named Narapaticañcu-sūna exercised sovereignty as a contemporary of the king.
Subsequently, relying upon King Vijayabāhu and King Parakkamabāhu, those residing at the Mahāvihāra...

The monks made the dispensation pure; having expelled all those who spoke what was not Dhamma, the community of Mahāvihāravāsins alone remained established, like the moon freed from the impurities of clouds and other defilements.
Although King Sirisaṅghabodhi, King Vohārikatissa, and King Goṭṭhābhaya also purified the dispensation, [the lineage of the Mahāvihāravāsins alone endured].
Because the groups of those who spoke unrighteously had not been entirely eradicated, the Dispensation was not yet completely pure.

It was only during the time of these very kings—King Sirisaṅghabodhi, the great King Vijayabāhu, and King Parakkamabāhu—that the Dispensation became completely pure through the total destruction of all those who spoke unrighteously. At that time, however:
One who speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not even able to rise from his seat, just as Kosiya [could not] at dawn.
Later, however, after a long time had passed, due to the fear of those of wrong view and of different birth, the Sasana receded in the island of Laṅkā;
because not even a quorum of monks was to be found, during the reign of King Mahāvijayabāhu—
In his time, he brought the Saṅgha from the land of Rāmañña and established the Sasana.
After that, during the reign of the king named Vimaladhammasūriya, he brought the Saṅgha from the kingdom of Rakkhāpura and established the Sasana.
And after that, during the reign of the king named Vimala, he likewise brought the Saṅgha from that very same place.
He established the Dispensation. Subsequently, during the time of the king named Kittisirirājasīha, he brought the Saṅgha from the kingdom of Siam and acted in the same manner.
This is the account of the decline of the Dispensation on the island of Siṃhala.
Subsequently, when eight hundred and ninety years had elapsed since the teaching of the Jina, during the reign of the king named Buddhadasa, a certain elder preacher of the Dhamma—
having translated and compiled the remainder of the Suttanta Piṭaka, excluding the Vinaya Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—
established it in the Sinhalese language. The reason for this is stated in the Cūḷavaṃsa.
It is said that King Buddhadāsa had about eighty sons, who were addressed by the very names of the eighty great disciples.
Among those sons, a prince named Upatissa, who was addressed by the name of the Elder Sāriputta,
reigned for forty-two years after his father had passed away.
After that, his younger brother, the prince named Mahānāma, reigned for twenty-two years. During the reign of that king,
when nine hundred and thirty-three years had elapsed since the Jina’s Wheel [of Dhamma], and at the time when sixty-six kings had completed their rule over the island of Sīhaḷa,
the Elder named Buddhaghosa went to the island of Sīhaḷa and [translated] the commentaries written in the Sīhaḷa language.
It was written after being translated into the Māgadhī language.
Furthermore, that King Mahānāma reigned at the same time as the king named Savilāññikrovi in the city of Siripaccaya in our country of Burma (Marammaraṭṭha).
In the *Parittaniddāna*, however, [it is said to have been under] the king named Brūmavi?thī.
It is stated that he reigned at the same time [as the Buddha];

however, that is indeed not tenable. For in the island of Siṃhala, there was a king named Kittisirimegha who, in his ninth year—precisely when the number of kings in that very island reached sixty-two—in the 130th year after the Wheel of the Conqueror (Jinacakkra), in Jambudīpa, before Kaliṅga...
Prince Danta, the son-in-law of King Kuhasiva, took the daughter of the king named Hemamālā,
stole the Tooth Relic, crossed over by boat, and went to the island of Siṃhala. During the wheel of the Conqueror’s dispensation, when eight hundred and thirty years had passed,
King Jeṭṭhatissa reigned for nine years.

King Buddhadāsa ruled for twenty-nine years, King Upali for forty-two years, and King Mahānāma for twenty-two years; when all these are combined, the teaching of the Conqueror reached a duration of nine hundred and thirty-two years.

At that time, when the dispensation was two years short of reaching nine hundred and thirty years—specifically during the reign of King Mahānāma—the Elder named Buddhaghosa went to the island of Laṅkā.

It is stated that this occurred more than nine hundred and fifty-six years after [the Parinibbāna], during the time of King Amarapuramāpaka, when a letter containing a request was sent by the bhikkhus of the island of Sīhaḷa.
Staying on this point, we shall briefly relate the origin of the Elder Buddhaghosa. How so?
Who indeed would be capable of translating the scriptural teaching (pariyattisāsana), which had been rendered into the phonemes of the Sīhaḷa language, back into the phonemes of the Māgadha language?
The Great Elders, having been invited, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;

there, seeing the divine son Ghosa, they requested him together with Sakka, Lord of the Devas, and caused him to take conception in the womb of a Brahmin woman named Kesī, the wife of a Brahmin named Kesa, in the village of Ghosa near the Bodhi tree. "Eat, sirs! Drink, sirs! and so forth.
Because he was born at the time when the brahmins were making proclamations to one another, they gave him the name Ghosa.
At the age of seven, he became a master of the three Vedas.
Then, while conversing on the subject of the Vedas with a certain arahant, having brought that discussion to its conclusion, he [became] skilled...
He asked about the "Buddha-mantra" known as the *Paramatthaveda*, beginning with the words, "Dhammas that are unwholesome, Dhammas that are indeterminate," and so forth.

Having heard it, he desired to master it; he went forth into homelessness in the presence of that Arahant and recited the Three Piṭakas day after day—some sixty thousand verses—and committed them to memory.
In just one month, he became a master of the three Piṭakas.
Then, while sitting alone in private, this thought occurred to him:
"Between my own wisdom and that of my preceptor, which is superior regarding the three Piṭakas spoken by the Buddha? Having understood the reason for this, the preceptor rebuked him.
He exhorted him. Having become filled with spiritual urgency, Sīhaḷa bowed down to ask for forgiveness.
His preceptor said, "Friend, having gone to the island of Siṃhala, you must transcribe the Tipiṭaka—which is currently written in the Siṃhalese script—into the Māgadhī script;
if you do so, I shall forgive you."
Buddhaghosa, having liberated his father from the state of wrong view and having received his teacher’s words upon the crown of his head,
set out by ship for the island of Sri Lanka to transcribe the Tipiṭaka. At that time, while they were crossing the middle of the ocean for three days,
the Elder Buddhadatta, who was traveling from Sri Lanka by ship, encountered [them] on the way through the power of the deities.
Having seen one another and asked the reason, they understood. Having understood, the Elder Buddhadatta said this:
"Friends, thinking that the *Jinālaṅkāra* composed by me was of little flavor, they did not grant me the opportunity to transcribe or revise the *Tipiṭaka*.
But you, please comment upon the *Tipiṭaka. Having said this, [he spoke] to his own Sakka, the Lord of the Devas.
He gave a myrobalan fruit, an iron stylus, and a whetstone to the Elder Buddhaghosa.
While these two elders were thus conversing with one another, the ships moved away on their own.
And when the Elder Buddhaghosa reached the island of Siṃhala, he first saw the Elder Saṅghapāla and [studied] the Tipiṭaka.

Having announced his purpose, saying, "I have come to translate [the scriptures] into the Magadha dialect," he presented the verse beginning with, "And let the Sinhalese bhikkhus, being established in virtue...
He was then instructed: "Explain the meaning of this verse by illuminating the Three Piṭakas.
Starting from that very evening, he took the aforementioned verse as his primary focus.
He composed the *Visuddhimagga*. Having completed that work and brought it to fulfillment, Devānaminda, desiring to test the source of his knowledge, caused that book to disappear.
Again the Elder composed it; likewise, Devānaminda caused it to disappear.
Once more the Elder composed it. After having him compose it three times in this manner, he showed him the original manuscript as well.
Among these three [masters], there was not even a single word of difference between them; and the Elder Saṅghapāla, having propitiated him, handed down the Tipiṭaka.
Thus it is recorded in the *Visuddhimagga* that the *Visuddhimagga* was composed at the request of the Elder Saṅghapāla.
However, in the *Buddhaghosuppatti*, it is stated that it was at the request of the Elder Saṅgharāja.
"Concerning the request" is how it has come down [in the text].
This is a summary of the account of the origin of Buddhaghosa as presented according to the method found in the *Buddhaghosuppatti-kathā*.
However, in the *Cūḷavaṃsa*, it is recorded as follows: "The Elder named Buddhaghosa, near the Great Bodhi Tree, in a certain Brahmin village..."
Vijāta was a master of the three Vedas and was highly skilled in various doctrines.
Desiring to engage in the practice of questioning and answering with others, he wandered throughout the land of Jambudīpa until he reached a certain monastery.
He stayed there as a guest. In that monastery lived an elder named Revata, and [Vijāta] sat down together with that elder.
Having mastered the three Vedas, that young brahmin student questioned the Elder. For every question he asked, the Elder provided an answer;
however, when the Elder posed a question in return, the student was unable to answer it.
Then the student asked, "Venerable sir, what is the name of this mantra? When it was said, "It is called the Buddha-mantra," he became desirous of learning it.
Having gone forth in the presence of that elder, he mastered the Tipiṭaka. Before long, he became one who had reached the further shore of all three Piṭakas.
Because he possessed a voice like that of the Buddha himself, he became renowned by the name Buddhaghosa.
While sitting in the presence of the Venerable Revata, Buddhaghosa [composed] the work named *Ñāṇodaya* and the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
He composed a book [named] *Nāma-gaṇṭha*. After that, desiring to compose a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the *Paritta*, he began. At that time, the teacher said:
"But, friend, in Jambudīpa there exists only the canonical text (*pāḷi*), while the commentaries do not exist;
moreover, the traditions of the teachers have become divided. Therefore, the commentaries brought by the Elder Mahāmahinda were [preserved] during the three councils."
Being exhorted thus, "The Pāli texts exist in the island of Sīhaḷa, and the method of exposition taught by the Elder Sāriputta and others is there;
go and write them down in the Māgadha dialect," the Elder Buddhaghosa went to the island of Sīhaḷa.
Having entered the Mahāvihāra at Anurādhapura, he [studied] together with the Elder Saṅghapāla and the Sīhaḷa commentaries.
Having heard the Theravāda tradition, he announced his intention to compose a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

The Sinhalese bhikkhus, following the method previously described, recited the verses beginning with "Established in virtue" (*sīle patiṭṭhāya*). And Buddhaghosa, having condensed the Three Pitakas together with their commentaries, composed the *Visuddhimagga*.

By the same method previously described, Sakka made him disappear and had the work performed three times. The Elder Saṅghapāla, having also accomplished his purpose, handed over the Tipiṭaka [to Buddhaghosa].

Although the origin of Buddhaghosa is recorded in various ways in different books, nevertheless, the only authoritative account is that the Elder Buddhaghosa went to the Island of Siṃhala and there committed the Tipiṭaka to writing and composed the commentaries; thus [one should clear] mental defilement...
"It should not be produced. Having recorded these three [prohibitions] regarding what is unfit to be eaten (*vikaṭa*), the Elder Buddhaghosa returned to Jambudīpa.

Thus, having translated the mastery of the Pāli language, the Wheel of the Conqueror (*jinacakra*) subsequently shone exceedingly in the island of Sīhaḷa—like molten gold—by way of the succession of teachers and their disciples, both direct and indirect, amidst countless millions of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants.
Lankādīpa shines exceedingly with the Pāricchattaka tree, which is three *yojanas* in height and in full bloom, like the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;

and with the hundred-petaled lotuses and other flowers, it is like a great lotus pond. In various places—on paths, great highways, at entrances to houses, by river-crossings, in forests, on mountains, in caves, in palaces, in monasteries, in halls, and so forth—there is not a single spot where the fruits of the Path have not been attained.
Even in those places where people stand to receive alms after waiting for a short while, [the same is true].
They indeed attained the fruits of the path.
Because of the great number of individuals who were realizing the fruits of the path, one had to point with a finger and say, "This is a worldling (puthujjana), this is a worldling.
At one time in the island of Sri Lanka, there was such a thing as a "worldling monk."
There is none. For it is said in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*: "At one time, there was no such thing as a bhikkhu who was still a worldling (*puthujjana*).

It is said that because those who had attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and possessed great psychic power were constantly coming and going, the women who threshed grain could not find an opportunity to do their work due to the lack of space.
Furthermore, the novice Sumanas brought the right jawbone from the deva-world to the island of Sri Lanka, and by means of displaying its miraculous power...
Having pervaded the entire island of Laṅkā for three hundred yojanas with upward-spraying droplets, so that it became like a cetiya courtyard used by the Blessed One,

five hundred bhikkhus, including the Elder Ariṭṭha, set out toward the Great Ocean in the presence of the Elder Mahinda; yet when they saw even as much water as a coconut in the great ocean, they worshipped the entire island of Laṅkā.
First, they mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka. For these reasons, Laṅkā Island became the seat of the Victor’s Wheel and acquired the name “Varadīpa” (The Excellent Isle).
Having established the Tipiṭaka in written form on the island of Sīhaḷa itself, after that, [the work of Coranāga...]
In the time of King Nāma, although the entire island of Laṅkā was oppressed by the fear of famine, monks who were upholders of the Three Piṭakas came from Jambudīpa.
Even those monks who remained there without coming were oppressed by the fear of hunger;
they bound their stomachs with cloth and, placing their bellies upon a heap of sand, continued to uphold the Three Piṭakas.
During the reign of King Kuṭakaṇṇatissa, the fear of famine having been quelled, monks returned from Jambudīpa and,
together with the monks already established on the island of Sīhaḷa, they ensured that the Tipiṭaka was not held in opposition but was established as uniform throughout the Mahāvihāra.
Having thus established it, they preserved it well right here in the island of Sīhaḷa.
There, the Elder Buddhaghosa translated and composed the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) in the Māgadhī language.

Subsequently, for the most part, it was there that they composed sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), summaries (*anuṭīkā*), word-by-word glosses (*mūlaṭīkā*), characteristic marks (*lakkhaṇa*), and various other treatises (*ganthantara*).
Once again, the Dispensation became as manifest as the moon in the sky.

Therein, the Elder Buddhadatta composed the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*. The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla composed the commentaries on the *Itivuttaka*, the *Udāna*, the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, the *Therāpadāna*, the *Therīgāthā*, the *Vimānavatthu*, the *Petavatthu*, and the *Nettippakaraṇa*.
And that Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, because he resided at Badaratittha in the Damila kingdom near the island of Sīhaḷa, should be included as belonging to the island of Sīhaḷa itself.
The Elder named Mahānāma composed the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*. The Elder named Upasena composed the *Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, the Elder Ānanda composed the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā*; and because it is the foremost of all the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), it is well known as the *Mūlaṭīkā*.

The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla composed the *Mahāṭīkā* on the *Visuddhimagga*, the *Ṭīkā* on the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Ṭīkā* on the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Ṭīkā* on the *Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.

The Elder Sāriputta, at the request of King Parakkamabāhu, composed the *Vinaya-ṭīkā* named *Sāratthadīpanī* and the *Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā*. The Elder Kassapa, a resident of the Damila kingdom, composed the *Vinaya-ṭīkā* named *Vimativinodanī*.

The *Anuṭīkā*, however, was composed by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. It is called an *anuṭīkā* (sub-commentary) because it clarifies those points in the *Mūlaṭīkā* that were not fully explained (*anuttāna*).
Other elders composed the *Cūḷaṭīkā* of the *Visuddhimagga* and the *Makhudīpanī*.
Because these works complete the remaining meanings of the *Mūlaṭīkā* and clarify what was not fully explained, and because they were composed in conjunction with the *Mūlaṭīkā*, they are sweet.
And *Sattā* is called the *Madhudīpanī*. Furthermore, the Elder Kassapa composed the *Mohavicchedanī*, a treatise on characteristics (*lakkhaṇagrantha*).
The Elder Buddhadatta [composed] the *Ābhidhammāvatāra*, the *Rūpārūpavibhāga*, and the *Vinayavinicchaya*.
The Elder Sāriputta [composed] the *Vinayasaṅgaha*. The Elder Dhammasiri [composed] the *Khuddasikkhā*. [The Elder Buddhadatta also composed] the *Paramatthavinicchaya* and the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
The Elder Anuruddha [composed] the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*; the Elder Dhammapāla, the *Saccasaṅkhepa*; and the Elder Khema, the *Khema*.
