Because these were composed in a concise manner and are easily characterized, they are called "characteristic treatises" (*lakkhaṇa-ganthā*).
Regarding their commentaries, the Elder Navavimalabuddhi [wrote] an ancient commentary on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
The Elder Vācissara Mahāsāmi composed the ancient commentary on the *Saccasaṅkhepa*, the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*, the *Khemappakaraṇa*, and the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The Elder Mahābodhi composed the ancient commentary on the *Paramatthavinicchaya*.
The Elder Sumaṅgala Sāmi composed the new commentaries on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha* and the *Abhidhammāvatāra*. [He also composed] the new commentary on the *Saccasaṅkhepa*.
The Elder Araññavāsi [composed] the *Araññavāsī-ṭīkā*. The Elder Mahāsāmi [composed] the *Nāmarūpaparicchedābhinavaṭīkā*. A certain Elder [composed] the *Paramatthavinicchayābhinavaṭīkā*.
The Elder Revata [composed] the *Vinayavinicchayaṭīkā*. The Elder Mahāyasa [composed] the old commentary (*purāṇaṭīkā*) on the *Khuddasikkhā*.
And the Elder Saṅgharakkhita [composed] the new commentary (*abhinavaṭīkā*) on that same work.
The *Vajirabuddhi* is the *Vinayagaṇṭhipadattha* by the Elder Vajirabuddhi. The *Cūḷagaṇṭhi*, *Majjhimagaṇṭhi*, and *Mahāgaṇṭhi* were composed by Elders residing on the island of Sīhaḷa (Ceylon).

These are called *Gaṇṭhipadattha* because they comment exclusively upon points that were not clarified in the previous [commentaries], rather than providing a sequential commentary on the entire text.

The Elder Mahāmoggalāna composed the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*; the Elder Cūḷabuddha, the *Atthabyākhyāna*; the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, the *Vuttodaya*, the *Saṃbandhacintā*, and the *Subodhālaṅkāra*; and the Elder Moggalāna, the *Byākaraṇa*.
The Elders residing on the island of Sihaḷa (Sri Lanka) composed the *Mahāvaṃsa*, the *Cūḷavaṃsa*, the *Dīpavaṃsa*, the *Thūpavaṃsa*, the *Bodhivaṃsa*, and the *Dhātuvaṃsa*.
Furthermore, the Elder Dhammakitti composed the *Dāṭhādhātuvaṃsa*. These works are included here because they were composed as independent treatises outside of the canonical scriptures (*pāḷi*).
These are called "other texts.
Thus, in this manner, the eminent elders such as Buddhaghosa and others, according to their strength and power, have supported the scriptural tradition and the Dispensation;
and being thus supported by many roots, many branches, and many twigs, it has attained vastness and reached full development.
It should be understood that [the Dispensation] stands for a long time, remaining firm like a great banyan tree.
This was the establishment of the Dispensation in the Island of Sri Lanka after it had been committed to writing.
And these Great Theras, according to their capacity and according to their strength...
Having composed the commentaries and other works, they approached the jaws of death.
Just as the moon in this world,
having illuminated it and brought benefit and welfare to sentient beings, goes its way.
In this very way, the great elders,
having spoken with the radiance of their wisdom and brought about the welfare and benefit of sentient beings, pass away.
Thus ends the section on the history of the Sāsana in the *Sāsanavaṃsa*, concerning the narrative of the history of the Sāsana on the island of Siṃhala.
The Second Chapter: The Name.
3. The Exposition of the History of the Dispensation in the Land of Suvaṇṇabhūmi.

Now, according to the established table of contents, the occasion has arrived for the subject matter of the exposition of the history of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Suvaṇṇabhūmi; therefore, I shall begin the exposition of the history of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
In this context, "Suvaṇṇabhūmi" is the name of one among the three Rāmañña kingdoms. There are three Rāmañña kingdoms by way of the partial names Haṃsāvatī, Muttima, and Suvaṇṇabhūmi;
thus, the entire Rāmañña kingdom should be understood [by these names].
Furthermore, in that region, in the district of Ukkala, beginning with Tapussa and Bhallika, after the Blessed One had attained full enlightenment...
Even as seven weeks were passing, from the fifth day of the waxing moon of the month of Āsāḷha onwards,
the Dispensation was established in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
This was the first establishment of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
Long before the time of the Blessed One’s full enlightenment, during the reign of King Tissa in the city of Subhinnanagara in the province of Aparanta,
there were two sons of a certain minister named Tissa and Jaya. Having conceived a sense of spiritual urgency while still laymen,
they went to Mount Gajjagiri near the great ocean, where they shaved their hair and beards and took up residence as forest-dwelling renunciants.
Then the Nāga woman, having become intimate with the Vidyādhara, gave birth to two eggs; out of shame, she abandoned them and departed.
Then the elder, Prince Tissa, having obtained them, divided them with his younger brother and placed one near each of them.
When time had passed, two human beings were born from those eggs. When they reached the age of ten years...
The younger brother, Vijāyanadaha, having died, was reborn in the Middle Country at the city of Mithilā as a prince named Gavampati.
At the age of seven, he was presented before the Blessed Buddha, who ordained him;
and before long, he became an Arhat.
However, it is said that while the elder was still in the womb, his younger brother was born;

when he reached the age of twelve, Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, came and, having founded a city named Sudhammapura in the kingdom of Rāmañña, established him there in sovereignty under the name Sīharāja.
But at Silālona, he was known by the name Sirimāsoka. And the Elder Gavampati [established] his mother...
Desiring to see her, he began his journey from the city of Mithilā.
Then, perceiving through his divine eye that his mother had passed away, he reflected, "Where has my mother now been reborn?

Upon discerning that she had been reborn for the most part in a place inhabited by hunters and fishermen, he thought, "If I go there and do not exhort her, my mother will accumulate demerit leading to the states of misery."
Having reflected, "May I be reborn in one of the four lower realms," he requested permission from the Blessed One and traveled through the air to the kingdom of Rāmañña.
Upon arriving at Sudhammapura in the kingdom of Rāmañña,
he taught the Dhamma to the inhabitants of the realm together with his brother, Sīharāja, and established them in the five precepts.
Then King Sīha said, "Venerable sir, among people in the world, you are the most eminent person. "Great king, I am not the most eminent.
However, within the three realms of existence, I have a teacher named Gotama who is like a crown to all beings;
he is currently residing in Rājagaha in the Middle Country. "But if that is so, venerable sir, regarding your teacher..."
"Are we worthy to see him or not? he asked. The Elder Gavampati replied, "Yes, Great King, you are worthy to see the Blessed One;
I shall go after making a request," and having said this, he made the request to the Blessed One.
And the Blessed One, in the eighth year after his full enlightenment, together with many hundreds of bhikkhus, [went] to Sukhummapura in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
He came through the air. In the *Rājavaṃsa*, it is stated that he came with five hundred bhikkhus;

however, in the stone inscription, it is stated that he came with approximately twenty thousand bhikkhus. In this regard, since the Blessed One arrived only with his retinue and not alone, one should accept only this much;
therefore, one should not allow the mind to become agitated based on these various conflicting accounts.
Then, having arrived and sat down in the Jewel Pavilion, he bestowed the taste of the Deathless upon the inhabitants of the kingdom, including the king.
He established them in the three refuges and the five precepts.
Then the Blessed One gave six hair-relics to the six ascetics who had come for the purpose of seeing him, so that they might worship them. After that, for seventy-three years...
Having filled [the urn], even at the time of the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, the Elder Gavampati took thirty-three teeth from the site of the funeral pyre in accordance with the Blessed One’s resolve;
he brought them to Sudhammapura, gave them to King Sīha, and established thirty-three cetiyas there.
Thus, in the very eighth year after the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, the Elder Gavampati [established these] in Sudhammapura in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
He established the Dispensation.
This was the second establishment of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
More than two hundred and thirty-five years after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, [the Dispensation reached] the kingdom of Rāmañña known as Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
Having arrived, the two elders Soṇa Thera and Uttara Thera, together with monks eligible for formal acts performed by a quorum of five,
established the Sasana. According to the commentary, these two elders were the pupils (saddhivihārika) of the elder Mahāmoggaliputta Tissa.
The Dispensation was established for the time being through the two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, and the Elder Gavaṃpati.
However, it did not penetrate everywhere in its entirety; rather, those who were faithful and confident became devoted to the Dispensation according to their own inclinations.
Later, the Elders Soṇa and Uttara, with great effort and by the command of their teacher, for the purpose of establishing the Dispensation—

Having exerted themselves with zeal, they established [the Dispensation]. Therefore, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), this is stated both as a causal condition for what was commissioned—namely, "Go to that kingdom and establish the Sasana there"—and by way of an analysis of the command.
At that time, however, in the kingdom of Suvaṇṇabhūmi, in the city of Sudhamma, a king named Sirimāsoka reigned. And him...

The city named Sudhammapura stands upon the summit of Mount Kelāsa; it occupies the eastern half of the southern intermediate direction on the mountain peak, while its western half rests upon the surface of the earth.

Its houses are for the most part like the dwellings of sugar-bakers and barbers, and for that very reason, it is also commonly designated by the name "Goḷamittika. Furthermore, that city is situated near the great ocean.
Because she was established [in her malevolent intent], the female yakkhinī Dakā came every day to the royal palace and devoured each prince as soon as he was born.
On the very day the Elder Soṇuttara arrived, a son was born in the royal palace.
Seeing him, the female yakkhinī Dakā, thinking "I shall devour him," arrived together with five hundred yakkhinīs. Upon seeing this, the people were terrified and raised a great cry.

They roared. Then the elders, having conjured and displayed a terrifying man-lion form with a single head and two bodies joined together by way of a lion’s head, caused that yakṣiṇī and her retinue to flee.
Furthermore, the elders performed a protective recitation (*paritta*) so that the yakṣiṇī would not return; and at that assembly, for those who had come...
They preached the Brahmajāla Sutta to the people. About sixty thousand became destined for the goal as stream-enterers and the like.
Three thousand five hundred sons of noble families went forth into homelessness, while three thousand five hundred daughters of noble families did likewise.
More than one thousand five hundred princes also went forth. The remaining people established themselves in the refuges.
Thus he established the Teaching there. And it is said in the Commentary:
"Having gone to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, Soṇa and Uttara, possessed of great psychic power, having expelled the Piśācas, proclaimed the Brahmajāla Sutta."
From that time forth, they gave the names Soṇa and Uttara to the two princes.

Furthermore, for the sake of liberating the inhabitants of the remaining gates from the fear of the rākṣasa, they placed at each gate a stone image of a man-lion (narasiṃha) fashioned by the elders, having displayed it upon palm-leaf and bhujapatta banners.
And the people, having made a stone man-lion image, [placed it] at Sudhammapura...

They established it in a suitable location. It exists even to this day. Thus, when two hundred and thirty-five years had elapsed since the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, the Theras Soṇa and Uttara arrived, established the Dispensation, and rendered great assistance to it.
This was the third establishment of the Sāsana in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
Subsequently, when more than six hundred years had elapsed, the kingdom of Rāmañña— which had previously been the place of origin for the Sāsana due to the three aforementioned reasons—
was [afflicted] by the fear of murderous bandits and thieves, the fear of the Pajjara disease, and the fear of enemies of the Sāsana.
It became agitated by three fears. At that time, the Dispensation (sāsana) there was weak, just as a lotus grown in shallow water is weak.
There, even the monks were unable to fulfill the Dispensation according to their desire.
During the time of King Manohara, known as Suriyakumāra, the Dispensation was exceedingly weak. [This occurred] during the wheel of the Conqueror (jinacakkre).
When one thousand and sixty-one years had elapsed since the Kali Yuga began, and four hundred and nineteen years had passed,
King Anuruddha brought the Saṅgha of monks together with the Piṭakas to the city of Ariñjaya (Arimaddana).

Subsequently, when seven hundred and ninety-one thousand years had passed since the Wheel of the Conqueror’s teaching, the Great King Sirisaṅghabodhi Parakkamabāhu purified the Dispensation on the island of Laṅkā.
Then, more than six years later, when five hundred and thirty-two years of the Kali Age had elapsed, a thera named Uttarājīva became renowned within the Dispensation.
He was the co-resident disciple of the thera Ariyavaṃsa, who resided in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
The thera Ariyavaṃsa, in turn, was the co-resident disciple of the thera Mahākāḷa, who resided in the city of Kappuṅga. And the thera Mahākāḷa was a resident of Sudhammapura.
[He was] the co-resident disciple of the Elder Prāṇadassi. This [account], however, is told for the purpose of illustrating the lineage of the Elders Uttarājīva and Chappada.

That Elder Prāṇadassi, having attained mundane supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), would regularly and frequently go early in the morning from the city of Sudhammapura to the Great Bodhi tree in the town of Uruvelā in the kingdom of Magadha;
there he would sweep the courtyard of the Great Bodhi tree and then return.

He went for alms. This was the Elder’s regular practice. Furthermore, this matter is understood because they told the residents of Sudhammapura when they returned after going from Sudhammapura to the kingdom of Magadha and performing merchant work in the town of Uruvela, where they had seen him in that manner.
And at that time, the Elder Uttarājīva went to the island of Siṃhala together with a novice named Chappada, who was twenty years of age.
The monks residing on the island of Siṃhala said, "We belong to the lineage of the Elder Mahāmahinda;
you also belong to the lineage of the Elders Soṇa and Uttara; therefore, we are of one and the same lineage."
Having said, "Let us be fellow-disciples," they performed the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) for the novice Chappada.
Thereafter, having completed the duties such as paying homage to the *cetiyas*, the Elder Uttarājīva returned to the city of Arimaddana together with the community of monks.
Then, this thought occurred to Chappada: "If I were to go to Jambudīpa together with my teacher, [I would be] by many..."
"There might be an obstacle to my learning the scriptures due to the strength of my kinsmen; therefore, let us stay right here on the island of Siṃhala, learn the scriptures, and then return.

Then, having requested permission from his teacher, he resided right there on the island of Siṃhala. While residing on the island of Siṃhala, [he remained] until he obtained the formal authorization as a *thera*.
Having mastered the scriptures, he desired to return once more to Jambudīpa. Then this thought occurred to him:

"If I go alone, and if my teacher is not present, and if the Saṅgha of bhikkhus dwelling in Jambudīpa should not wish to perform a formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma) together with me, then in such a case I would not be able to carry out that formal act independently."
"Therefore, it would be skillful for me to go together with four elders who are bearers of the Piṭakas.

Having thought thus, he [the Elder Mahinda] set out by ship together with these four elders: the Elder Sīvali, a resident of the village of Tāmalitti; the Elder Tāmalinda, who had been the son of the King of Kamboja; the Elder Ānanda, a resident of Kiñcipuraka; and the Elder Rāhula.
He returned. Those elders were also bearers of the Piṭakas, skillful and endowed with strength; among them, the Elder Rāhula was particularly endowed with strength.
When they arrived at Kusima City, it was nearly the time for the commencement of the rains retreat;
thus, without being able to reach the presence of the teacher in the city of Ariyamaṇḍa, they spent the rains retreat right there in Kusima City.
They entered the rains retreat. The site where they resided during that retreat and the monastery wall still exist today on the southern side of Kusima City.
When the rains retreat was concluded, those five elders performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony at the Great *Pavāraṇā* and then went to the city of Arimaddana.
However, the elder Uttarājīva performed the formal acts of the Saṅgha separately from the monks residing in the city of Arimaddana.
Although elders such as Uttara and Jīvaka returned from the island of Sīhaḷa and, after residing in the city of Ariyamaṇḍala,
supported the Dispensation, they are shown here because they were born in the kingdom of Rāmañña and had previously lived there.
At that time, in the village of Padīpajeyya in the city of Dalanagara, there was a certain elderly novice named Sāriputta who was born there.
Having gone to the city of Ariyamaṇḍana and received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of the Elder Ānanda, he mastered the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
He became one who was learned (*bahussuta*), skillful, and endowed with strength. Having heard of this matter, King Caṇḍisūra, the lord of men, thought:
"If he were endowed with the major and minor limbs [of a handsome form], I would appoint him as my teacher and support him."
The king, having reflected thus, dispatched royal messengers and had him investigated.
When the royal messengers saw that his toes were severed, they reported the matter to the king.

Upon hearing this, the king concluded, "One who is so deficient in his limbs and members would not be fit to occupy the position of preceptor for ascetic practice," and therefore did not appoint him to the office of preceptor for ascetic practice. [He then performed] offerings and honors...

With great affection, he bestowed his favor upon him. At one time, having given the title "Dhammavilāsa," he dispatched him to the kingdom of Rāmañña, saying, "Purify and cleanse the Dispensation in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
Having gone to the kingdom of Rāmañña, he taught the Dhamma and Vinaya to many bhikkhus in the city of Dalla and [established] the Dispensation.
There, the people of Rāmañña refer to the disciples and grand-disciples of that Dhammavilāsa Thera as the "Sīhaḷa Bhikkhu Gaṇa.
Thus, by way of Dhammavilāsa— the disciple of Ānanda Thera from the island of Sīhaḷa—
the path by which the Sāsana came from the island of Sīhaḷa to the kingdom of Rāmañña is established.
This was the fourth establishment of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
And at that time, in the city of Muttima, the preceptors of the Queen Consort— the Elder Buddhavaṃsa and the Elder Mahānāga—
went to the island of Sīhaḷa and once again received the training from the monks who were the lineage-holders of the Mahāhāra community.
Having taken [the relics] and returned to the City of Liberation (Muttima-nagara), they performed Saṅgha-acts separately from the monks residing in the City of Liberation and upheld the Dispensation.
And because of those elders, the Dispensation once again arrived in the kingdom of Rāmañña from the island of Ceylon.
This was the fifth establishment of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
After that, the elder named Medhaṅkara, who was the teacher of the mother of King Setibhinda,
went to the city of Muttimana; having traveled to the island of Sīhaḷa and received the training once more in the presence of the forest-dwelling Mahātheras of the Sīhaḷa island,
he mastered the scriptures for the sake of the mother of King Setibhinda, [who resided] in a palace covered with gold, silver, and tin.
Having sat in a monastery that had been built for him, he supported the Sasana. He also composed a treatise titled *Lokadīpakasāra*.

Then, once again, in the city of Muttimā itself, the elder named Suvaṇṇasobhaṇa went to the island of Sīhaḷa, received the training once more from the elders who were the pillars of the Mahāvihāra community, and returned once more to the city of Muttimā.

However, that elder lived only in the forest. He was a bearer of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), possessing few desires, contented, modest, scrupulous, desirous of training, skillful, and endowed with fortitude.

In the island of Siṃhala, at the lake named Kalambu, within the water-boundary (udakukkhepasīmā), having taken the Saṅgharāja named Vanaratana—accompanied by more than five members of the community—as his preceptor, [he ordained] one named Rāhulabhadda.
Having appointed the elder who had been the preceptor of King Vijayabāhu as his *kammavācā*-preceptor, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
That elder, returning once more and residing in the city of Muttima itself, increased the community and supported the Dispensation.
It was through these two elders that the Dispensation came from the island of Ceylon to the kingdom of Rāmañña.
This is the sixth establishment of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
Subsequently, when two thousand and eighty-one years from the beginning of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, in accordance with the Dispensation, King Dhammaceti—
known by the name Siriparamamahādhammarāja— in the city of Haṃsāvatī, within the Kusima and Haṃsāvatī regions...
In the kingdom of Muttimamaṇḍala, he ruled the realm with justice and impartiality, protecting the inhabitants like his own children.
That king was proficient in the three Piṭakas, the four Vedas, and in grammar, prosody, poetics, and so forth;

he was skilled in various arts, adept in many languages, endowed with virtues such as faith and moral conduct, and possessed a countenance as white as the kumuda lily, the kunda flower, or the autumnal moonlight.
And he became exceedingly devoted to the Teaching.
At one time he reflected: "The so-called Teaching of the Blessed One is connected with the going forth and full ordination;

and the state of full ordination is connected with the perfection of the formal act consisting of the motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamation (*kammavācā*), based upon the assembly within the boundary (*sīmā*). And thus...
Having reflected upon this, and having repeatedly examined both the word and the meaning of the *Sīmāvinicchaya* and its commentary, the *Vinayasaṅgaha* and its commentary,
the *Sīmālaṅkāra*, and the *Sīmāsaṅgaha*, and having compared them with one another and weighed their preceding and succeeding parts,
he perceived that such was the intention of the Blessed One and such was the intention of the authors of these texts.
"In our kingdom of Rāmañña, although there are many boundaries such as rivers, seas, and lakes, it is difficult to determine which one is truly pure.
This being the case, it seems difficult for the boundary assembly (*sīmaparisā*) to be pure.

Thereafter, after consulting with elders who were experts and capable in the Three Piṭakas, the elders decided that the boundary assembly would be difficult to purify in accordance with the King's insight.

Then the king thought thus: "Alas! Although it is stated in the scriptures that the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One will endure for five thousand years, yet within only two thousand six hundred and forty years from his full enlightenment, a stain has appeared in the Dispensation, giving rise even to a point of doubt regarding the ritual of higher ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*). How much more so [will this be the case]?"
"The establishment of the Dispensation will last for five thousand years.
Having thus aroused a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma, he further reflected:

"Even though such impurity is seen within the Dispensation, and even though grounds for doubt are seen regarding the formal act of ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*), one like me should not remain indifferent and neutral, failing to strive for its purification."
"It would be improper for me to sit; for if that were the case, I would not be able to declare, 'I have faith and confidence in the Blessed One.
Therefore, I shall begin to make the Dispensation stainless.
Then, reflecting on how the Dispensation might now be brought forth and established firmly, he thought thus:

It is said that when two hundred and thirty-six years had passed since the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa dispatched the Elder Mahāmahinda and established the Dispensation in the island of Siṃhala.
At that time, King Devānaṃpiyatissa caused the Mahāvihāra to be built and gave it [to the Sangha]; and for two hundred and eighty-one years, the noble Dispensation remained stainless.
Having offered [the oblation], he established [the community]; the Saṅgha of monks also stood as one body by way of the group residing at Mahāvihāra.
Thereafter, it split into two factions by way of those residing at Abhayagiri and those residing at Jetavana.

When the number of years since the Wheel of the Conqueror reached one thousand seven hundred and eight, King Sirisaṅghabodhi Parakkama Bāhu [invited] the Elder Mahākassapa, who resided at Udumbaragiri, and others.
Having favored the community residing at Mahāvihāra, he purified the two aforementioned groups and rendered the Dispensation stainless.
Thereafter, during the reigns of both King Vijayabāhu and Parakkamabāhu, the Dispensation remained stainless;
for that very reason, having requested learned and capable bhikkhus, he went to the island of Siṃhala and once again received the training.
"I shall go; however, through the succession of those monks who will continue the lineage, the Dispensation shall become stainless and be established once more in our kingdom of Rāmañña.

Having reflected thus, he requested the Elder Moggalāna and the Elder Soma to go to the island of Ceylon. The Elders, considering this to be a task for the preservation of the Dispensation, gave their consent.
And the King, having prepared articles of offering and gifts for the purpose of worshipping the tooth-relic, for the purpose of honoring the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus,
and as a diplomatic gift for King Bhuvanekabāhu, appointed these two ministers— Citradūta and Rāmadūta— as leaders on two ships;
and when eight hundred and thirty-seven years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, in the month of Māgha...
On the eleventh day of the waxing moon of the month of Puṇṇami, on a Sunday, Puṇṇamitta sent the Citradūta by a single ship together with monks headed by the Elder Moggalāna.
On the eighth day of the month of Phagguṇa, he arrived at Kalambutittha on the island of Sīhaḷa.
As for the Rāmadūta, however, in that same year, on the twelfth day of the waxing moon of the month of Māgha, on a Monday, [he set out] together with...
He had them travel by means of a single boat accompanied by monks headed by the Elder Soma.
However, failing to obtain a favorable wind, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Citra, he set out for Valligāma on the island of Siṃhala.
Subsequently, those two ministers also brought on two boats the articles intended as gifts and the letters of message.
And Bhūvanekabāhu gave [the requisites] to the King and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then, in accordance with the instructions set forth in the letters sent by the King,
they established [the candidates] on the level of sāmaṇeras within the water-throw boundary (udakukkhepasīmā) at the river named Kalyāṇī,
and subsequently performed the formal act of full ordination (upasampadakamma).
Having received the full ordination, King Bhuvanekabāhu gave various kinds of suitable requisites to the monks;
and thinking that while this gift of material goods would be enjoyed only until the end of their lives, his name and seal would not decay, he [bestowed them] upon the Elder Soma—
who was like the keel of the ship that was Rāmadūta— and upon Sirisaṅghabodhi Thera.
He gave [him] a name. As for the remaining ten elders, he gave them the names Kittisirimeghasāmi,
Parakkamabāhusāmi, Buddhaghosasāmi, Sīhaḷadīpavisuddhasāmi, Guṇaratanadharasāmī, Jinālaṅkārasāmi, Ratnamālisāmi,
Saddhammatejasāmi, Dhammarāmasāmi, and Bhūvanekabāhusāmī.
He gave the name Dhammakittilokagarusāmi to the Elder Moggalāna, who served as the helmsman for the ship of Citradūta.
As for the others, he gave the names Sirivanaratanasāmi, Maṅgalattherasāmi, Kalyāṇatissasāmi, Candagirīsāmi,
Siridantadhātusāmi, Vanavāsitissasāmi, Ratanalaṅkārasāmi, and Mahādevasāmi.
He gave them the names Udumbaragiri Sāmi and Cūḷābhayatissa Sāmi. However, he did not give names to the twenty-two monks who followed later.
Instead, he gave the name Abhinava-sikkha to all of them.
After that, having performed the worship of the cetiya and other rites, and having accomplished their respective tasks, they returned once more. King Bhuvanekabāhu...
The messenger Citradūta spoke thus: "I wish to return the royal gift to King Rāmādhipati; please wait for me while I dispatch a return envoy.
Having said this, later, on the way back, the ship was driven off course in the middle of the great ocean by the fear of a violent wind.
Then, all those sent by the Sihaḷa king gathered together, boarded the ship, and set out.
After three days had passed, again, due to the fear of fierce winds, they struck against rocks in a shallow place and were unable to proceed;
thus, having lashed together a raft, they traveled on foot.
Meanwhile, the messenger of the King of Siṃhala returned, delivering a gift. And as for the monks, death overtook them even along the way.
Having taken it, he departs, thinking: "Alas, conditioned phenomena are indeed impermanent! And on this matter there are these verses:
"But while this work of theirs has been begun, yet not completed, they will not take it with them;
for Death has no regard for one's expectations."
"For he is indeed merciless; taking them by force, he departs while they weep and their kinsmen do not consent.
And at that time, King Rāmādhipati, in the western direction of the city of Haṃsāvatī, [prepared for those monks].
In a village district enjoyed by the minister named Narasūra, having repeatedly seen and scrutinized the Pāḷi, Aṭṭhakathā, Ṭīkā, and other texts,

he performed the formal acts for the removal of boundaries (*sīmasamūhana*) and the authorization of boundaries (*sīmasammuti*). In the river named Kalyāṇī, where the Blessed One had previously bathed on the island of Sihaḷa,
he established a water-boundary (*udakukkhepasīma*) there for the residents of the Mahāvihāra.
Because it was performed by monks who had received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of [other] monks, they gave it the designation "the auspicious boundary" (*kalyāṇī-sīmā*).
Thus, King Rāmādhipati, relying upon the monks who had arrived in Laṅkā, caused the Dispensation to be firmly established.
This occurred from the time of 838 years of the Kali Age until 841 years.
In the lineage of those bhikkhus, there were about eighty senior elders who were leaders of groups.
Their disciples numbered four thousand two hundred and sixteen. In this way, the Blessed One’s dispensation attained growth, increase, expansion, and abundance in the kingdom of Rāmañña.
This was the seventh establishment of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Rāmañña.

However, when King Anuruddha conquered and destroyed Sudhammapura along with its royal inhabitants, the kingdom of Rāmañña remained established, though it became devoid of a king. In the city of Muttima in the kingdom of Rāmañña...
The Soṇuttaravaṃsa was one group, the Sivalivaṃsa another, the Tāmalindavaṃsa another, the Ānandavaṃsa another, the Buddhavaṃsa another, and the Mahānāgavaṃsa another;
thus these six groups remained separate, belonging to different residences (saṃvāsa) and different sects (nikāya).
However, the Dispensation established by King Dhammacetiya remained unbroken. They were of the same residence.

There was only a single *nikāya*. By means of the liberation of Haṃsāvatī, all three Rāmañña kingdoms—counted as Sunāparanta—remained joined as one. Furthermore, they had previously been the seats from which the Maramma kings exercised their authority.
Therefore, some bhikkhus from the Maramma kingdom went to the Rāmañña kingdom and [established themselves] within the Kalyāṇī boundary.
They took up the training once again. The teaching, which had been propagated by King Dhammaceti, remained after spreading throughout and penetrating the entire kingdom of Burma (Marammaraṭṭha).
From the time the teaching was established by the elders Soṇuttara and others in the kingdom of Rāmañña until the city of Sudhammapura...

The existence of Arahants should be understood during the time of King Manohari. After that, however, it was only during the times of Kings Uttara, Jīvāriya, Vaṃsama, Mahākāla, and Prāṇadassi that those who had attained mundane jhānas and supernormal powers (abhiññā) were found.
At present, however, in all three kingdoms of Rāmañña, only the Dispensation established by King Dhammaceti remains. And herein, by way of the relationship between cause and effect:

And having weighed the lineage of the Dispensation with wisdom by way of its beginning and end, one should grasp it so that it is joined according to the traditional sequence by means of the three methods shown from the very beginning.
Furthermore, this lineage of the Dispensation should be understood as being stated only for those who are modest, gentle, and desirous of training, not for those who lack shame.
And through that lineage of elders, the Elder Medhaṅkara, a resident of the city of Muttimanagara, composed the work titled *Lokadīpakasāra*.
Furthermore, the Elder Ānanda, a resident of the city of Haṃsāvatī, composed the sub-commentary on the Abhidhamma titled *Madhusāratthadīpanī*,
and the Elder Dhammabuddha, likewise a resident of the city of Haṃsāvatī, composed the prosody commentary titled *Kavissāra*.
Indeed, the Elder Saddhammālaṅkāra, a resident of the city of Haṃsāvatī, composed the treatise named *Paṭṭhānasāradīpanī*,
and likewise another elder produced the work named *Apheggusāra*. Thus,
having become the dwelling place for many such great elders who were authors of various texts, the Dispensation (Sāsana) entered [that region] and flourished there.
Thus ends the third chapter in the History of the Dispensation, titled "The Account of the Path of the History of the Dispensation in Suvaṇṇabhūmi. 4.
The Account of the Path of the History of the Dispensation in the Yona Country.
4. Now, however, I shall relate the establishment of the Dispensation in the Yona country.

For the Blessed One, bringing welfare to those capable of being trained, considering that my Dispensation would endure for a long time in the Yona country, traveled through various regions with the community of monks and arrived at the city named Labuñña. At that time, a certain hunter [saw] a *hariphala*...
Having given it and consumed it, when the seed of the Hari tree was cast upon the earth, it did not fall but remained suspended in the air.
Seeing this, he broke into a smile. Having seen that matter, the Elder Ānanda asked him about its meaning.
He replied: "Ānanda, in the future a relic-shrine (dhātucetiya) shall be established in this place, and the Dispensation (sāsana) shall reach full growth."
Because it was the place where the Blessed One ate the *hari* fruit, the name of that kingdom became Haribhuñja.
Based on the water-strainer (*jalasuttika*) set out for the two ascetics, its name became Labhuñja in the language of the Yonakas.
At that time, there sat near a certain boundary-mark (*mātikā*) named Mapinnā a chief of the Lavakulikas.
Having handed over his seven-year-old son to the Blessed One, he had him ordained.
Through application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), the boy attained *arahantship* before long.

Because this was the place where the seven-year-old novice realized *arahantship*, it is called *Caṅgamaṅgha* in the Yona language; due to its long-standing existence, it is also known as *Jaṅgamaṅgha*.
Thus it is said. From that time forth, the Dispensation was established in the Yona country.
This was the first establishment of the Dispensation in the Yona country.
However, when two hundred and thirty-five years had elapsed since the beginning of the Dispensation, the Elder Mahārakkhita [went] to the Yona country.
Having gone, he established the Sasana in many kingdoms such as Kamboja, Khemāvara, Haribhuñja, Yuddhaya, and others.
Indeed, all those kingdoms were referred to by the commentators—who presented them collectively—by the general term *Yonakaloka*, using the common word *loka* to denote "the world" (or "region").
For it is the nature of authors to convey a different meaning through whatever means possible.
The Elder Mahārakkhita, together with five bhikkhus, traveled from Pāṭaliputta to the Yona country by way of the aerial path and converted the Yonas through the Kāḷakārāma Sutta.

When the study [of the scriptures] has disappeared, there is no such thing as realization; however,
just as when the letters have been inscribed on a stone slab for the purpose of knowing the location of treasure-pots, those treasure-pots are not said to be lost as long as the letters remain,
even so, as long as the study remains, the Dispensation is said not to have disappeared.
Just as it cannot be said that water will not remain in a large reservoir with firm embankments,
nor can it be said that while water exists, lotuses and other flowers will not bloom; even so,

when the word of the Buddha in its three baskets (Tipiṭaka)— which is like the firm embankment of a great reservoir— exists, there are sons of noble family who fulfill the practice, who are like the water.
It should not be said that it does not exist; for as long as those [teachings] exist, it should not be said that there is no penetration (paṭivedha) resembling the lotus and other flowers.
Thus, the scriptural tradition (pariyatti) alone is the absolute authority. Therefore, even if only two Pātimokkhas remain, the Dispensation (sāsana) has not yet disappeared.
However, once the scriptural tradition has disappeared, there can be no realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya), even for one who is perfectly practicing.
There is no direct realization of the Dhamma; there is only the realization of the Dhamma through what has not been lost.
Even now, our scriptural teaching (pariyatti-sāsana) is not complete, nor are the bodily relics present.
Therefore, one should send a messenger with a gift to wherever the scriptural teaching and the bodily relics exist, so that they may be brought here. This being the case, in our kingdom—
"The teaching of the Jina will endure for a long time.

"But, venerable sir, if that is so, where shall we request [the scriptures]? "Great King, in the city of Sudhamma in the kingdom of Suvaṇṇabhūmi, he had the Tipiṭaka written down and deposited there three times; furthermore, many relics of his body are located there."
The king, having replied, "So be it, venerable sir," prepared many gifts, wrote a royal letter,
and dispatched an eightfold-endowed minister as his envoy.
King Manohari, the lord of Sudhammapura, being possessed of a stingy mind, [addressed] those of wrong view such as yourselves...
It was not appropriate to send the Tipiṭaka and the bodily relics to that place; for the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Supreme One in the Three Worlds,
will be established only among those of right view, just as the fat of the king of lions, the maned lion,
belongs only in a golden vessel and not in an earthenware pot.
The messengers returned and reported the matter to King Anuruddha. Upon hearing this, King Anuruddha became enraged; he seethed like sesame seeds cast into a hot pan.

Then the king, having marshaled an army of eighty thousand ships along the river route and eight crores of sailors and warriors, together with four great military commanders and eighty thousand elephants, set out by the land route.
Having arrayed his army with three hundred and ninety thousand horses and eight hundred million warriors, he went to Sudhammapura himself to do battle.
Hearing this, King Manohari became terrified; having mobilized many of his own warriors, he sat down in Sudhammapura itself to form a counter-formation.
Then, although they exerted themselves again and again according to the applications found in the Atharvaveda, they were still unable to approach the foot of the city.
At that time, the king asked those learned in the Vedas: "Why is it that we are not able to approach the foot of the city here?
The Veda-knowers replied: "O Great King, there is likely some specific ritual procedure of the Atharvaveda [that is required]. Then the king—
Having buried the corpse in the earth and then dug it up, he threw it into the great ocean.
It is said that he had a certain man from the Hindū clan named Jeṅgu eat a worm, killed him, and having taken his limbs and members—
hands, feet, and so forth— and having cut them into pieces, he buried them in the earth around the city.
He established [the relics]. At that time, however, it was possible to approach the city.

Having entered the city, King Anuruddha captured King Manohari alive. Then, taking the Tipiṭaka—which had been enshrined and worshipped in a jewel casket according to the traditional lineage of the ancient kings of Sudhammapura—along with the bodily relics, he [presented them] to King Manohari.
Having placed them upon the backs of thirty-two elephants belonging to his own retinue, he brought them.

Upon reaching the city of Ariyamaṇḍa (Arimaddana), he placed the relics inside a casket made of jewels and set them down upon a jeweled couch in the chamber of the Glorious Bed (Sirisayana-gabbha), near the head of the bed. He also placed the Tipiṭaka in a palace made of jewels.
He dedicated [the city] for the sake of the Bhikkhu-saṅgha’s learning, memorization, and so forth.
It is said that from there, about a thousand noble ones (*ariya*) came to study the Three Piṭakas that had been brought back.
Having conquered the city of Sudhamma, he brought the Bhikkhu-saṅgha along with the Piṭaka and established the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
It is stated in stone inscriptions that 601 years of the *jinacakkavā* (the era of the Conqueror’s Wheel) and 416 years of the *kaliyuga* had elapsed.
During the time of King Anuruddha, because the three jewels were complete through the power of his merit, the village was given the name Puṇṇagāma (“Full Village”).
After a long time had passed, it was stated in the future chronicles of kings that, by way of the elision of the letter *ṇ* and the substitution of the nasal *m* for the *niggahīta*,
it came to be designated as "Pugami" in the Maramma language.
King Anuruddha himself dispatched four great warriors to the island of Siṃhala and brought back the Tipiṭaka from there as well.
The Arahant Thera compared and reconciled the Tipiṭaka brought from the island of Siṃhala with the Tipiṭaka brought from Sudhammapura;
he examined them, and they were found to be neither deficient nor redundant, like the waters of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā meeting one another.
Having augmented those Piṭakas with others and established them within the Triple-Piṭaka Repository, he...
He made offerings to them. He also established them in various locations.
King Manohari, too, he placed in the region named Mraṅkapā along with his attendants.
It is said that whenever that king spoke aloud, a radiance would flash forth from his mouth. At times—
On one occasion, she came into the presence of King Anuruddha and, out of reverence, performed acts such as prostration.
At that time, King Anuruddha experienced a thrill of horripilation and became agitated.
Therefore, in order to appease the king, she offered food to a Buddha-image at a cetiya, took it, and shared it with King Manohari; at that moment, his supernatural power vanished.

King Manohari, overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), made this aspiration: "As long as I wander through *saṃsāra* and do not reach *nibbāna*, may I never remain under the power of others.
He then sold his own mind-made jewel, which had been brought from the Sudhamma palace, to a certain merchant; with the proceeds of that sale—five measures of silver—...
By means of the *abhujita-pallaṅka* (cross-legged) posture, he had two Buddha images fashioned— one large Buddha image in the manner of the Parinibbāna,
and one [smaller]— and these exist to this day. Thus, King Anuruddha, having brought the Dispensation from Sudhammapura and from the island of Siṃhala, established it in the city of Ariñjaya.
This is the fourth establishment of the Dispensation in our realm of Maramma, in the province of Tambadīpa, in the city of Ariñjaya (Arimaddana), following King Anuruddha. The Elder Uttaraññānavīra,
having received the Dispensation from the lineage of Soṇa and Uttara, came to the city of Ariñjaya from Sudhammanagara and established the Dispensation there.
This is the fifth establishment of the Sāsana within our realm of Marammaṇḍala, in the province of Tambadīpa, in the city of Ariyaddhana, based upon the Elder Uttarājīva.

When the Elder Uttarājīva went to the island of Sīhaḷadīpa, the novice named Chappada, who had gone with him, was ordained as a monk by the Sīhaḷa monks right there on the island of Sīhaḷadīpa. Having been ordained, the novice Chappada [studied] the scriptures...
Having mastered [the teachings] and resided there for ten years, he returned to the city of Arimaddana.
He brought with him the Elder Sivali, the Elder Tāmalinda, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Rāhula.
Those elders were bearers of the Tipiṭaka, being both proficient and skillful. This matter has been explained in detail below.
Having reached the city of Arimaddanapura, they sat down separately, without performing the formal legal acts (*vinayakamma*) together with the monks residing in Arimaddana.
King Narapati placed his great trust in those elders;
he had a raft tied together on the Erāvatī River and had the full ordination ceremony (*upasampadākamma*) performed right there. After a long time had passed, that community...
Having grown, he was reborn.
King Narapati, having invited those elders together with the Saṅgha, gave a great almsgiving.
At that time, seeing a certain famous dancer at a festival—one endowed with perfect deportment and the full bloom of physical beauty—the Elder Rāhula became bound by desire for her.
Like a monkey stuck in birdlime or like an elephant stuck in the mud, he became attached to the mire of the defilements of sensual pleasures;
having desisted from the Teaching, he began to turn back toward the low life.
Overcome by the disease of death as if it were incurable, he paid no heed even when the remaining elders gave him exhortations. Then the remaining elders said this to him: "Do not you..."
They sent him, saying: "You ought not to put all of us to shame on account of this one man;
do not behave so baselessly here, but go to Mallārudīpa and act as you please. Then the Elder Rāhula boarded a boat at Kusimatittha and went to Mallārudīpa.
Upon his arrival at Mallārudīpa, King Mallāru, desiring to know the Vinaya, [sent] the *Khuddasikkhāpakaraṇa* together with its commentary.
Having learned [the craft] from him, he gave him a gem worth only a single bowl. And having obtained that, he returned to the lower life.
Regarding this, there are these verses: "A monk indeed must remain very far away from women;
for women, in this world, become enemies to monks."
Let alone those of poor wisdom, even we of old,
though possessed of great wisdom, met with destruction— Haritaca and the others.
Therefore, a wise bhikkhu should, at the very least, [keep himself aloof] from women.
"One should not place trust in the world, for passion is difficult to restrain.
Among the other elders, the elder named Chappada passed away first.
Then the three elders—Sivali, Tāmalinda, and Ānanda—after strengthening the Sasana through their mastery and retention of the scriptures and other qualities, resided in the city of Arimaddana.
Once, on one occasion, the king gave an elephant to each of those three elders.

The elders Sivali and Tāmalinda accepted them and released them into the forest. However, the elder Ānanda sent someone ahead to the city of Kiñcī, saying, "Give this to my relatives," and then went to Kusimatittha, where he boarded a boat. Having learned of that reason, the elders Sivali and Tāmalinda—
They said this: "Friend, we release elephants into the forest for their comfort, yet you are acting unrighteously.
[The other] asked: "Venerable sirs, why indeed should the gathering of kinsmen not be permitted? Is it not stated by the Blessed One that there is a gathering of kinsmen?
The elders said: "If you do not follow our word, then do as you wish; however, we shall no longer live in association with you," and they sat down separately.

From that time on, the community split into two factions. Later, when some time had passed, the Elder Tāmalinda, for the sake of favoring his disciples who were learned and possessed of proficiency, would issue verbal intimations to householders, saying, "This one is very learned," "This one has great wisdom," and so forth.
When this was done, young men of good family [entered the order] because of the ease with which they could obtain the requisites for the Dispensation.
Thinking, "They will eat what brings benefit," and having heard that reason, the Elder Sivali spoke thus:
"Why do you perform an act loathsome to the Buddha after having produced a verbal intimation? [The other replied:
"Verbal intimations were prohibited by the Blessed One for his own sake; however, I produce verbal intimations solely for the sake of others."
"It is not for my own sake, but solely for the sake of the expansion of the Teaching that I am thus manifesting vocal intimation.
The Elder Sivali, however, thinking, "You do not follow my word;
do whatever you wish, but I will no longer live in association with you," sat apart from him together with his own faction. From that time forth...
The three groups split apart.
Thus, in the city of Arimaddana, there were four groups: one lineage of the Elder Arahan, one of the Elder Sivali, one of the Elder Tāmalinda, and one of the Elder Ānanda.

Among them, the group of the Elder Arahan was designated as the "First Group" (*purimagana*) because it arrived first from Sudhammapura; the others, however, were called the "Later Groups" (*pacchāgana*) because they arrived later.
The Elder Sivali, having upheld the Dispensation in the city of Ariñjaya for as long as he lived, passed away at the time of five hundred and ninety years into the Kali age.
The Elder Ānanda, however, having upheld the Dispensation in the very same city of Ariñjaya for forty-four years, passed away at the time of five hundred and ninety-six years.
The Elder Tāmalinda also, having upheld the Dispensation for as long as he lived, passed away at the time of five hundred and ninety-eight years. "Oh, such is the nature of conditioned phenomena!"
Just as a hare, though it has retreated, remains clinging to the wheel of the navel of a sleeping python and goes toward its mouth, even so all beings,
once caught in the wheels of death, [cannot escape].
"Even after running for as long as life lasts, they have come to the mouth of Death.
Thus, in the city of Arimaddana, the teaching of the Conqueror shines like the moon in the sky, through both Arahants and ordinary disciples (puthujjana) who are authors of the scriptures.

For when King Anuruddha brought the Sasana from Sudhammapura, approximately six hundred thousand Arahants arrived; as for those who had attained the stages of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, and Non-returner, they were beyond counting.
Even during the time of the king named Chattaguhinda, eight arahants came from Mount Gandhamādana in the Himalayas to the royal palace for alms.
The king, taking their bowls and feeding them with alms-food, asked: "From where have you come now?
They replied: "From Mount Gandhamādana in the Himalayas, Great King. Thereupon, the king became exceedingly devoted.
Having made this request, saying, "Having spent the three-month rains retreat here, please accept [an invitation]," he had a monastery built and gave it to them.
For those three months as well, he invited them into his own home and fed them with alms-food.
On one occasion, having constructed for the Arahants a cave on Mount Gandhamādana like the Nandamūla Cave...
He requested, "Let me see it. Those Arahants, having miraculously fashioned a cave similar to the Nandamūla Cave, showed it to him.
The king then had a cave constructed identical to that one; because it was made in the likeness of the Nandamūla Cave, he gave it the name "Nanda.
Thus, during the time of King Chattaguhinda, from the Nandamūla Cave on Mount Gandhamādana...
Having arrived, the Arahants established the Sasana.

Indeed, this state of being an Arahant is difficult to recognize as it truly is, because for those who are not fully ordained, the manifestation of superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma) is prohibited, and even after attaining Arahatship, one may not have abandoned the residual tendencies (vāsanā). For even while being an Arahant, I thought: "I am..."

It is not permissible to speak [of one's own attainment] to those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). Even after reaching *arahatta*, some are unable to abandon their residual tendencies (*vāsana*);
the case of the Elder Pilindavaccha serves as an illustration here. Thus, it is difficult to know the state of being an *arahant* in the world.
For this very reason, a certain monk who was an attendant to the Elder Mahākassapa [spoke] to his own preceptor, the Elder Mahākassapa...
Even though he lived in the presence of the Elder Mahākassapa, he did not know his state of being an arahant. For one day,
while the Elder Mahākassapa was walking for alms from a forest dwelling to a village together with a single co-resident disciple,
that co-resident disciple, taking up his bowl and requisites on the way, followed behind him alone.
He spoke thus: "Venerable sir, in this world an Arahant is known as such; I have merely heard of him, but I have never before seen one.
Having heard that, the Elder turned back and looked around, saying: "Friend, even while taking up the requisites and following behind the Arahant, one does not know his state of being an Arahant."
In the city of Ariyamañña (Arimaddanapura) as well, there were indeed Arahants such as the elders Sīlabuddhi, Polloṅka, and Sumedha.
For when King Narapati had gone to Mount Pādapabbata by means of a tunnel and was returning, he saw a vision in his mind at a certain irrigation channel along the way;
thinking, "He wishes to have merit performed here," and reflecting that it must be Sakka who was showing him this, he resolved, "I shall have a cetiya built."
In that place, he had the inhabitants of the kingdom level the ground.
Then a certain elder named Sīlabuddhi said: "Great King, you have had this preparation of the ground carried out thinking, 'I shall perform a meritorious deed.
But for one who acts in this way, it results only in demerit, not in merit. Having said this, he caused many beings to abstain...
Thinking, "They will become weary," he did not eat the almsfood given by the king for the purpose of intimidating him with royal punishment.
And the king said, "If you should be unwilling to eat the almsfood given by me, even while living within my realm, you shall not escape from my almsfood;
[so too shall it be] from the almsfood given by the inhabitants of the kingdom."
"It belongs to me alone; surely you eat only my alms-food," he said.
The Elder Sīlabuddhi, thinking, "If I were such a person, I would go and dwell on the island of Siṃhala," lived in the forest.

Then, having learned of this matter, a certain *yakkha* who was guarding the city gate sat down in a terrifying form, standing directly in front of the king when he arrived. Even though [the king] tried to drive him away with various spells and rites, he could not be driven away.
Then the king, having summoned the interpreters of omens, asked: "For what reason is this yakkha sitting here?
They replied: "Great King, you previously spoke of the Elder Sīlabuddhi with disrespect; we have heard before that even yakkhas are exceedingly devoted to the Elder.
It is on account of that that the yakkha must be sitting here, having manifested a terrifying form out of fear."
The king also commanded his ministers, "Have the Elder brought here. But the Elder did not come; he set out, thinking, "I shall go to the island of Siṃhala itself.
When the king heard this matter, he summoned a minister named Caturaṅgapaccaya and sent him, saying, "Go and summon the Elder.
And because of his skill, Caturaṅgapaccaya [prepared] a golden [image].
Having placed an image of the Buddha on a boat, he went to the landing place of the great ocean. Then, having reached the Elder, he sent a messenger, saying:
"Now the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has arrived here;

let the Elder Sīlabuddhi come for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. The Elder also [set out] for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
He came because he was unable to refuse the words "Please come," out of reverence for the Buddha.
As it is said: "The wise man, with a mind full of faith, should here show reverence toward the Buddha, as did the elder monks of old."
Having boarded the ship, the Elder paid homage, honor, worship, and respect to the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Even as the Elder was thus performing his homage, honor, worship, and respect, the ship arrived with great speed and departed.
Then the provider of the fourfold requisites said: "Venerable sir, now [is the time] for your teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One..."
"It is fitting for you to uphold the Dispensation. Then the king, surrounded by his ministers, went out to meet him.
Taking the Elder’s hand, he brought him to the royal palace. When they reached the door, the *yakkha* sat down upon the ground and paid homage to the Elder.
Having entered the palace, the king fed the Elder with various kinds of food and spoke thus: "From this day forward, venerable sir..."

"You are my teacher; having received the Blessed One’s instruction with my head bowed in reverence, I shall follow it," he said, and gave his five sons to the Elder. Those five youths followed along with the Elder.
The Elder summoned them and went to the monastery. On the way, on a consecrated plot of ground (*kappiyabhūmi*), [he drew] five circular shapes.
Having written it down and shown it to those princes, he had them turn back. The princes, having returned, reported the matter to the king.

The king said, "He shows this for the sake of causing you to perform meritorious deeds," and so, by way of a scale, those princes made the gold equal [to the weight], and using that gold as the capital, during the lifetime of the Blessed One...
He had individual images fashioned, like the sandalwood image commissioned by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
Sakka, acting as the architect, established five *cetiyas* as the repositories for those [images].
Furthermore, in the past, the king, having gained faith, gave his royal sons to the Elder; having given the root of the Triple Gem, [he established them there].
Furthermore, it should be understood that the Elder gave this instruction with the desire to have the prince made a laborer.
And that Elder Sīlabuddhi should be regarded as belonging to the lineage of the Arahants.
During the reign of King Narapati in the city of Ariyamaṇḍala (Arimaddana), an elder named Kassapa, while wandering on a regional tour, [arrived there].
He arrived at the country named Polloṅka. Then two elderly men of Polloṅka, out of excessive devotion to the Elder, offered their two sons to serve him.
Because of the extreme faith of the people of Polloṅka, the Elder was also known by the designation "Polloṅka Thera. When—
Furthermore, when that Elder desired to go to the island of Siṃhala, Sakka, the lord of the devas,
manifested the form of a tiger and carried him on his back as far as the shore of the great ocean. Having reached the shore of the great ocean,
he boarded a ship and crossed over together with the merchants.
But having reached the middle of the great ocean, that ship did not move; it remained standing perfectly still.
Then the merchants said, "We suspect there is some ill-fated person on our ship. Having deliberated thus, they drew lots.
Even for the third time, the lot fell into the Elder’s hand due to the ripening of his past karma. This, however—
Regarding the elder’s past deed: in his seventh existence after that one, the elder was born as the son of a family in a certain village.
While playing, he let a dog down into a river and made it play in the water.
As the dog was thus playing, [the boy] himself seized it by the chest and brought it to the bank. Thus, it was through the ripening of this past deed performed previously...
The voting stick fell into the hand of that very elder.
Then the merchants threw it onto the surface of the water. Thereupon, Sakka, the lord of the devas, manifested the form of a jackal, placed [the elder] upon his back, and carried him away.
When the elder reached the island of the *yakkhas*, through the power of his loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward the blind-eyed *yakkhas*...
He caused [the king] to regain his sight. And the yakkhas, having recognized the elder’s virtue, gave him two yakkha brothers.
The elder, having gone to the island of Siṃhala, brought back the image of the Mahācetiya, the image of the Lohapāsāda, the bodily relics, and the seeds of the Great Bodhi tree, and then returned.
The Elder Sumedha dwelt in the monastery named Dinnā, located in the southeastern direction of the city called Halaṅka.
Because of the name of that site, the monastery itself came to be known simply as "Dinnā-vihāra.
That elder was also a wearer of rag-robes, modest, amiable, desirous of training, an attainer of jhāna, and indeed an Arahant.
For he went every day, day after day, to the Pādacetiya, which measured eight or nine yojanas [in circumference], and paid homage there. He also performed the duties of the cetiya courtyard.
Then, having returned, he wandered for alms in Mhattigāma. This was the fixed routine of the Elder.
There are many other instances as well, but all of them have not been related in detail here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
We shall not speak further. For if all [these accounts] were to be told, this *Sāsanavaṃsappadīpikā* would become excessively prolix.
Indeed, what is intended here is solely the compilation and bringing together of the succession of elders from the Parinibbāna of the Sammasambuddha down to the present day.
As for the aforementioned instances, they concern individuals who have recently attained supernormal powers (*abhiññā*).

These [details] were stated for the purpose of warding off the suspicion that it is not a suitable field [for the Dhamma], and to show that the city of Ariyamaṇḍala (Arimaddana) was a dwelling place for many individuals who had attained direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*). And this was said in the *Bhikkhunī-khandhaka-ṭīkā*:

“For a thousand years there were those who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), for a thousand years dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*), and for a thousand years non-returners (*anāgāmī*).”

"With once-returners for a thousand years, and with stream-enterers for a thousand years"— thus the Dhamma of penetration will endure for five thousand years. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*,

it is stated that [the Dhamma will endure] for a thousand years with those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), for a thousand years with those possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*),
for a thousand years with those possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*), and for a thousand years with dry-insight practitioners (*sukkhavipassaka*).
It is stated that [the Pātimokkha lasts] for a thousand years.

However, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya-aṭṭhakathā* and in the *Vibhaṅga-kathā*, it is said that they are able to produce the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) for exactly one thousand years after the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas;
beyond that, they can attain the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), and those unable even to do that [attain] the three [knowledges].
The true knowledges (*vijjā*) arose. As time passed, even they became unable to produce them and thus became "dry-insight" practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
By this same method, it is said that non-returners (*anāgāmin*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), and stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) [became dry-insight practitioners].
Since it has been handed down in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) through various such methods, it is impossible for noble persons (*ariya-puggala*) to exist in the world today.

It should not be said [that this is impossible]. Since the field for the Noble Ones (ariya) still exists even now, it must be understood as a settled conclusion that if one were to undertake insight (vipassanā), they would certainly be able to become an Arhat. However, it should be seen that what is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) was spoken according to the various opinions of elders who were different reciters (*nānābhāṇaka*). Nevertheless, even though the doctrine was split by such a difference of opinion, the Dispensation (*sāsana*)— [The text continues: ...remained undivided. Just as when the Elder Mahinda arrived in Laṅkā, although there were differences among the elders regarding the Vinaya, the Dispensation remained undivided; so too, although there was a difference of opinion here, the Dispensation remained undivided. Furthermore, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, having gone to the Himavant region, established a monastery at the foot of Mount Vebhāra. There, he taught the Dhamma to many people, including the King of Kāsi. Among them, there was a certain person who, having heard the Dhamma, attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). When he went back to his own country, he told his relatives about the Dhamma he had heard. They all developed faith and became lay followers. Later, when the Elder returned to Jambudīpa, he heard that his relatives had become lay followers. He thought, "I shall go there and establish them in the higher training. Having gone there, he taught the Dhamma to them. At that time, a certain person among them, having heard the Dhamma, attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). When he died, he was reborn in the Aviha heaven. The Elder, seeing him with his divine eye, thought, "This person has been reborn in the Aviha heaven. I shall go there and teach him the Dhamma. He went there and taught him the Dhamma. The deva, having heard the Dhamma, attained the fruit of arahantship. Then, the Elder thought, "This person has attained the fruit of arahantship. I shall now return to Jambudīpa. He returned to Jambudīpa. This is how the Dispensation remained undivided. Therefore, it should be understood that even if there are differences of opinion, the Dispensation remains undivided. Thus it is said: "Even if there are differences of opinion, the Dispensation remains undivided. This is the meaning. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. It indeed breaks apart; for in this matter, the non-breaking of the Dispensation alone is the authority.
Thus, in the city of Arimaddana within the realm of Maranma, the Dispensation shines forth through many hundreds of Arahants.
Furthermore, more than nine hundred and thirty years after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, in the supreme kingdom (Parammaraṭṭha), by one named Śeṇikaññikrodhi—
During the time of King Mahānāma— who attained sovereignty over the island of Siṃhala at the same time as the King—
beginning with the two elders Buddhaghosa and Buddhadatta, those great elders composed those texts. Subsequently,
for the sake of easy comprehension by means of the excellence of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, they composed commentaries (*ṭīkā*) in the city of Arimaddana.
When one thousand six hundred and ninety-seven years of the Victor’s Wheel had elapsed,
for the sake of proficiency among those who hear the grammatical systems (*saddanaya*) which are the foundation of the Three Piṭakas,

the Elder named Aggavaṃsa— after thoroughly examining the Three Piṭakas along with their commentaries like a great fish named Ānanda in the great ocean— composed the treatise *Saddanīti* in the city of Arimaddana.
Indeed, even before the departure of the Elder Uttarājīva and others for the Island of Siṃhala, there were three great elders who were experts in the scriptures:
Mahā-Aggapaṇḍita, his co-resident (saddhivihārika) the second Aggapaṇḍita, and his nephew the third Aggapaṇḍita.
Furthermore, the third Aggapaṇḍita is also designated as the "Foremost of the Lineage" (Aggavaṃsa).
At that time, there were many residents of the city of Ariyamaḍanapura who were experts in grammar, and thus their fame spread as far as the island of Laṅkā.
Consequently, those from the island of Sīhaḷa, being experts in grammar and desiring to investigate [the matter], came to the city of Ariyamaḍanapura.
Then, the monks residing in the city of Ariyamaḍanapura showed them the treatise on grammatical rules (*saddanītipakaraṇa*).
And the Sinhalese monks, having seen that [manuscript] and examined it, praised it in various ways, saying: "In the realm of sounds, this book is like a jewel;
such a book exists in the island of Sri Lanka, yet we did not know the entire analysis contained in this treatise.
Thus, the path of discourse was never interrupted until the present day.

In the city of Ariyamaḍanapura, the Elder Saddhammajotipāla, known as Chappada, having gone to the island of Siṃhala and returned, composed the *Suttaniddesa* due to his mastery of grammar (*saddanaya*).
Due to his mastery of ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*), he composed the *Saṅkhepavaṇṇanā* and the *Nāmacāradīpaka*.
Due to his mastery of the Vinaya, he composed the *Vinayagūḷhatthadīpanī* and the *Sīmālaṅkāra*. By himself...
In the collection of texts (*kathānaṃ ganthānaṃ*), he is referred to by his original name as Saddhammajotipāla.
However, because he was born in the village of Chappada in the city of Kusima, he became widely known by the name of that place, "Chappada.
Furthermore, there was also a certain elder named Chappada in the city of Kukhana; he was shameless and immoral. Some...
Yet, by the mere sign of a common name, they slander the Venerable Chappada Thera— who had reached Laṅkā, was virtuous, excellent, and desirous of training—
on account of his lack of shame and immoral conduct, just as they did the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta on account of improper conduct by the mere sign of a common name.

During the reign of the king named Aloṅgacaññi in the city of Ariyamaḍanapura itself, there were two elders, Mahāvimalabuddhi Thera and Cūḷavimalabuddhi Thera, who were experts in the scriptures (pariyatti). Among them, Mahāvimalabuddhi Thera composed the *Nyāsa* commentary on the *Kaccāyana*.
However, some say that it was Vimalabuddhi Thera, a resident of the island of Sri Lanka, who composed it. As for Cūḷavimalabuddhi Thera—
However, he composed an ancient commentary on the Vuttodaya. Saddhammajotipāla Thera composed the *Chandosāratthavikāsini*.
Vepulla Thera, however, composed the *Vacanatthajoti*. An official during the time of King Narapati composed an ancient commentary on the *Nyāsa* treatise.
For the king, upon seeing a daughter born of one of his concubines, became attached to her with a mind fixed on her like a monkey clinging to a smear of pigment;
having become so infatuated, he clung to her. Knowing this matter, the king said:
"If you desire her, compose a book that is complete in its analysis and possesses a hidden meaning; if you are able to compose such a book..."
"You shall be able [to do this]; you will obtain it. Then he composed an ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭīkā*) on the *Nyāsa*.
After that, having returned to the lower life and given his daughter in marriage, he appointed her as the minister for receiving the royal taxes, who is called *Saṃpyaṅga* in the Maramma language.
Because it was composed by him, that book is also called by his name. This is its *kārikā*:
And the Elder Kāledhammasenāpati composed a commentary on the *Chattaguhindatthera* while seated at the Nanda Monastery near the Nandaguha, which he had caused to be built.
At that time, Arahants came from the Nandamūlaguha on Mount Ganthamādana and spent the rains retreat in that monastery.
They approached him. Because he composed them in their presence, the teachers say that those texts should be understood as essential by the wise.
Furthermore, the novice named Dhammadassi composed the *Vāccavācaka*.
As for the *Saddatthabhedacinta*, it was [composed] at the mountain Khaṇittipāda, situated near the city of Arimaddana.
A thera named Saddhammasiri, residing in a nearby village, composed it.
That same thera also translated the *Brahma-jāla*—a treatise on the Vedas—into the Maramma language (Burmese).
Furthermore, the thera Saddhammakitti composed the *Ekakkharakosa*. For he [lived] in the eight hundred and eighty-seventh year of the Kaliyuga.
When that situation arose, out of fear of families who held wrong views and were characterized by cruelty, the radiance of the Sasana faded throughout the entire Tambadipa province.
Many books were also destroyed by the threat of fire.
Seeing that occurrence at that time, [the king thought]: "If the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) should perish, the Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-dhamma) will also perish."

It is stated in the *Taṭṭikā* that [the author] composed this treatise after experiencing a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking: "If the Dhamma of practice (*paṭipattidhamma*) is lost, how can there be the Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedhadhamma*)?
Sāgara Thera composed [a work] whose essence consists merely of its opening words.

When five hundred and eighty-one years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, a king named Kyaccavā—son of King Jeyyasiṅha, who had attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) upon the death of his only young son and aspired to the state of a *paccekabuddha*—reigned over the kingdom.
He also bore the title "Dhammarāja. Furthermore, regarding the three Piṭakas, he [understood] them as they truly are...
Because of his discernment, he is designated by the Marma terminology as "Kyacva.
It is said that this king, having mastered the Three Piṭakas— since there was no one capable of even engaging in a mere discussion regarding the Piṭakas,
their commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), or sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) due to their extreme profundity— would [instruct] the Saṅgha of monks for seven days each day.
He causes his son to recite the texts.
Having also caused a pond to be constructed near the mountain Khaṇittipāda, and having built a royal palace there, he sits there and causes his son to recite the texts.
Furthermore, all the duties of kings are entrusted to his son, the uparāja.

He assigned [the responsibility]. For the sake of the women of the harem who were learning the texts, he composed the treatise called *Saddabindu* in brief, as well as the treatise called *Paramatthabindu*.
Indeed, his mind delighted only in the scriptures (*pariyatti*);
he did not wish even to hear of other royal duties. King Anuruddha thought, "In the future, may I become king..."
Then, having resolved, "May these palm seeds sprout right now," he planted them. They sprouted during the time of that king;
therefore, the inhabitants of the kingdom perceived him as "King Anuruddha himself.
For they say that these three—the conventional king (sammutirāja), the Anuruddha king, and the Kaccāna king—belong to a single continuum.
Thus the king built even a single cetiya, yet it did not reach completion; it is recorded in the royal chronicles that he served only as a supervisor over the construction.

According to worldly convention, on the day bricks were prepared, on that very same day he leveled the ground, and on that very same day he caused all other work to be completed. Therefore, in the Maramman language, it is called *prassadā*.
The term *cetiya* is well known up to the present day.
That king composed a single work called the *Vibhatyattha* for the purpose of analysis.
It is said that formerly, in the city of Arimaddana, the Sasana had attained a state of extreme flourishing by way of mastery, retention, and so forth.
Indeed, in the city of Ariṭṭhapura (Arimaddanapura), a certain elderly monk who had gone forth entered the royal palace desiring to write a text with a stone-inscribing rod.
The king asked, "For what purpose have you come? He replied, "I have come desiring to write a text with a stone-inscribing rod. [The king said:
"Though you are so advanced in years, even if you were to master the texts with great effort..."
"I see no room for you to become proficient; even if a pestle were to sprout a shoot and grow, only then might you attain proficiency in the texts," he said.
After that, having gone to the monastery, he wrote every single day a portion of text the size of a single tooth-stick.
Having mastered it, he learned [the Abhidhamma] from his teacher, beginning with the *Kaccāyana-abhidhammattha-saṅgaha* treatise.
Before long, having attained proficiency in the texts, he tied a sprout of a rose-apple tree to a pestle,
hoisted it up, and entered the royal palace.

Then the king asked him, "By what means have you come? When he replied, "Great King, I have come to explain that this pestle grows by producing a sprout," the king understood, "He is saying, 'I have attained mastery in these texts.
To investigate whether this was true or false, he sent him into the presence of the Great Elders. The Great Elders also—
They asked about the hidden points (*gūḷhaṭṭhāna*). He, too, answered each question as it was asked.
Then that bhikkhu said to the great elders: "Venerable sirs, you ask me many questions; I also wish to ask you something.
Grant me the opportunity," and having thus requested, [he spoke] regarding the phrase *aññasamānacetasika*; here, concerning the word *añña*:
