Because he was seeking a limit, the king asked him to set forth the "limit-word" (*avadhipada*) after extracting it. However, because the Great Elders had not previously given it their attention, they were unable to provide the answer quickly.
When the king heard this matter, he became delighted and appointed him to the position of Preceptor (*ācariya*), with the title "Foremost of the Quarters.
Furthermore, that monk—though not an author of texts himself—acted as if he were an author of texts for those who followed.
Having rendered assistance by means of the instructions given to the people, he arose within the Dispensation.
And there are these verses on this matter: "I am old and dull-witted regarding the scriptures;
I shall not be able to master them through great exertion."
And thus one should not despise others,
nor fall into negligence;
being truly desirous of skill in the true Dhamma.
Just as a man might exert himself,
so too a bhikkhu who has gone forth in old age—
even one who is elderly and lacking wisdom— [should strive].
"She attained proficiency in the Dhamma;
may the listeners behold it.
It is said that formerly, even women in the city of Ariñjaya (Arimaddana) mastered the texts, for the most part by means of learning and memorization.
They exerted themselves in the teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*). For it is said that women, seeing one another, would ask:
"How much of the texts have you mastered? How much of the texts have you committed to memory?
It is reported that one woman asked another: "How much of the texts have you now committed to memory?"
"Do you? he asked. "But I, having now become preoccupied with the offering of *balibodha* to young children, am unable to commit much of the textual tradition (*gantha*) to memory;
however, I do manage to master at least the *kusala-ttika* (the triad of wholesome states) from the *Samantapāsādikā*," he replied.
This too is an instance of women residing in the city of Arimaddana engaging in the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
It is said that while a certain bhikkhu was wandering for alms, a young girl of twelve years asked him, "What is your name, venerable sir?
He replied, "My name is Khemā. She said, "How is it, venerable sir, that being a male, you have taken a female name?
Then, sitting inside the house, the mother heard this and said to her daughter: "You [should learn] the characteristics of the king and his retinue..."
"Do you not know? "Yes, I know; however, this word *khema* does not belong to the class of words beginning with 'king' (*rāja*).
Then the mother said, "But this word *khema* belongs to the class of words beginning with 'king' in one respect.
Herein, the daughter's intention was this: the word 'king' is never used in the nominative singular form as "the king" (*rājā*).
The word ending in *-okāra* (the vowel *o*) is seen [in compounds] excluding the scope of compounds such as *devarāja*;

however, the word *khema* appears in some instances with different forms according to gender, namely as both *khemam* and *khemā*. Therefore, it should be understood that the word *khema* does not belong to the *rājādi* group.

This, moreover, is the intention of the author: because the word *khema* possesses the gender of its referent (*abhidheyyaliṅgatta*), it is tri-gendered; yet, when it occurs within the section on technical terms (*saññāsadda*), [it is treated as a specific term].
When it is seen ending in the form "khema" by way of the singular (paccatta) case-ending, then, in one respect, the word *khema* belongs to the class beginning with *rāja*.
This is another instance:
it is said that in the city of Arimaddana, a certain householder had one son and two daughters. And at one time—
At that time, having been overcome by the heat, he sat after bathing on the upper floor of the house.
Then, a certain female slave, standing beneath the house while performing some work, looked toward the private parts of that householder.
Knowing the significance of this, the householder composed a single verse—“He looks at the branch”—and showed it to his son. Of this...
"Make it eight yojanas long. Then the son made it eight yojanas long; he looked up, gazing from branch to branch of the tree.
Afterwards, he showed it to one daughter, saying, "Make this eight yojanas long.
She too made it eight yojanas long; she, like a dog, looked up, gazing into the sky. Then afterwards, to another...
She showed it to her daughter, saying, "Make eight *yojanas* for this. She too made eight *yojanas*.
That woman looked at her own private parts; she looked while holding her face upward.
This, too, is one story.

It is said that a certain novice monk, a resident of Ratanapura, having heard that even the women in the city of Ariyamañña were highly skilled in the arts of music, went to the city of Ariyamañña, thinking, "I shall go there and find out.
Then, on the way, near the city of Ariyamañña, he saw a young woman sitting and guarding a field of *kappāsa* cotton. Then the novice [approached] her...
He went into his presence for the purpose of asking about the path. Then a young woman asked the novice, "From where have you come?
The novice said, "I am coming from Ratanapura. When she asked, "Where are you going?
he replied, "I am going to the city of Arimaddana. Then the young woman spoke thus: "Venerable sir, without having reflected upon the *Saddayogavinicchaya*..."
[The elder] explained: "In our tradition, you have indeed spoken by joining [the term] with the word *yoga*.
Is it not the case that the speech of the wise must be complete in meaning, consistent in its method of expression, and resemble the full moon?
Then the novice said: "Even those who guard their fields and lands, and even poor young women, are proficient in the methods of grammar."
"How much more so, then, for elderly women endowed with wealth? Thinking thus, she felt ashamed and turned back from that very spot to return.
This concludes the account of the establishment of the Sāsana in the city of Arimaddana, within the province of Tambadīpa in the realm of Maramma, by way of the succession of theras.
Now, I shall speak of the lineage of the Sāsana in the city of Ketumatī, within the province of Jeyyavaḍḍhana in the same realm of Maramma.
Indeed, when eight hundred and seventy-two years of the Kali Age had elapsed, a king named Mahāsiri Jeyyasūra reigned in the city of Ketumatī in the kingdom of Jeyyavaḍḍhana.
Relying upon a single highly skilled elephant named Devanāga, he expanded his conquered territory.
During the reign of that king, eight hundred and ninety-two years of the Kali Age had passed.
When the Elder named Mahāparakkama arrived by ship from the island of Sīhaḷa, he reached the city of Ketumatī.
The King, having had the Mahāvihāra constructed on the southern side of the city of Dvāravatī, granted it to him and provided a permanent endowment of alms-food.
Within that monastery, having formally established the boundary (sīmā) and having fashioned a bronze image of the Buddha equal to himself in weight, he [placed it] within that boundary.
He had it built. And that image of the Buddha became well known by the name "Sampattalaṅkādīpa.
During the time of that king, there arose a controversy concerning the training rule on fermented liquor and spirits (*surā-meraya-sikkhāpada*). How so?
From the seed onwards—that is, from the time the ingredients were prepared and placed in the vat—[the juice] of the flowers of the *tāla*, coconut, and other such trees...

Some say that based on a distorted interpretation of the intent expressed in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-Ṭīkā* and other commentaries—stating that "from the time the juice has flowed from the flower until it is fresh, it must not be drunk"—the juice of the palmyra palm, coconut, and so forth, is not permitted to be drunk from the time it has flowed until it is fresh.
Others, however, say: "The juice of the palmyra palm, coconut, and so forth, is permitted to be drunk at the time when the juice has flowed and while it is still fresh."
Regarding this, the intention of the teachers in the first position is as follows:

"Starting from the seed" means that once the ingredients have been prepared and placed in the vat, it is not to be drunk from that time onward; likewise, the flower-juice of the palmyra, coconut, and so forth, is not to be drunk until the period immediately following its fresh extraction has passed.
However, this is the intention of the teachers in the second position:
"Starting from the seed": here, once the ingredients have been prepared and placed in the jar, it is not to be drunk from that time forward.
Flower juice prepared with ingredients such as palm and coconut is not to be drunk from the time the juice has recently flowed from the flower.
Thus, regarding the juice of palms, coconuts, and so forth, it is permissible or impermissible to drink it starting from the time it has recently flowed.
Sitting in the midst of those engaged in dispute, the Elder Mahāparakkama, who had arrived in Laṅkā,
adjudicated that it was permissible to drink such [liquor] and composed a treatise titled *Surāvinicchaya*.
Thus, with the support of King Mahāsirijeyyasūra, who was building the city of Ketumatī, the Sāsana became established in Ketumatī.
This was the establishment of the Dispensation in the city of Ketumatī within the realm of Maramma itself.
Now, I shall relate the history of the Khandhapura Dispensation specifically within Tambadīpa province of the Maramma realm.
Indeed, in the sixty-fourth century of the Kali Yuga, three brothers deposed the king named Kittitara from his kingdom and ruled in the city of Khaṇḍapura.
At that time, a son of King Kittitara, having requested aid from the sovereign of the Cīna kingdom,
stood surrounding the city of Khaṇḍapura with many divisions of the army.
Then, having summoned a great elder (mahāthera) who was skilled in the three Piṭakas, they consulted him. The elder spoke thus: "This matter depends on the local populace;
it is not permissible for recluses (samaṇas) to deliberate upon it. I too am a recluse; however, you should consult with the actors.
Then, having summoned the actors, they consulted them. The actors also said: "If there is no cause [for the performance], then in that case, there will be no fruit."
"If there were no putrid matter, flies would not gather," they thought, and so they sang songs and played in the water.
Then those three brothers, having heard that, seized the king named Kittira from prison, killed him, and thinking,
"Now we shall install [another] in the kingdom," said, "Go, this is his head."
Then they showed him the head, saying, "Now he has gone to the other world. Thereupon the army of the Cīna kingdom also said, "Now there is no one of the royal lineage;
we did not come wishing to fight, but thinking, 'We will install him upon the throne.
Now that he is no more," having said this, they turned back and departed.
It should be understood that because it was stated only, "And so the elder consulted with the actors," he was not released from his status as a bhikkhu. And this has been said:
"In the first and second [cases], there is both the sequence and the command;
in the remaining ones, there is only the command. These two [factors] are not found [in those cases]."

In that city of Khandhapura, known as Arimaddanapura, many elders resided belonging to the lineage of the Arahant-group, the lineage of the Chappada-group, and the lineage of the Ānanda-group. However, there was no one among them who had composed any books.
This concludes the account of the establishment of the Dispensation in Khandhapura.
Now, within the realm of Maramma, I shall describe the history of the Dispensation specifically in Vijayapura, in the province of Tambadīpa.
Indeed, in the Kali Yuga, in the 774th year, a king named Sīhasūra founded Vijayapura.
Subsequently, after two years had passed, he obtained a single elephant that had died in the Camu River;
thus, his name became renowned as "Ekasetthin" (The Single Elephant-Owner). During the reign of that king, virtuous people [resided] in Vijayapura.

There were not many monks who were modest and virtuous. During the time of King Anuruddha, there were only many sham ascetics remaining, having hidden themselves out of fear of the king from the city of Arimaddana.

It was only after the arrival of the Elder Cūḷa-Arahanta and the Elder Dibbacakkhu that the modest and virtuous monks became powerful and increased their following. And the king [honored] the Elder Dibbacakkhu.
Having caused him to enter the inner palace, he fed him daily with alms-food.
King Anuruddha, having obtained seven relics that had been enshrined within a betel-box and worshipped there, deposited five of those relics in the Caṅkī Cetiya.
As for the remaining two relics, he assigned them for the purpose of worshipping the minister named Puñña. And he...
A minister made a deposit at the Puññacetiya in Jayyapura.
At that time, it is said, those who were merely sham ascetics attended upon householders as well as kings and royal ministers.
When six hundred and eighty-four years of the Kali age had elapsed, King Sīsasūra’s eldest son, named Ujana—
The king ruled the kingdom. In a place called Avapaṅkī, he had seven monasteries constructed out of *campaka* wood.
These monasteries were completed at a time more than two years after seven hundred years [of the era] had passed.

Among those monasteries, he gave the one named Campaka, the monastery for intensive practice (*padhānavihāra*), to Sudhamma Mahāsāmi Thera, the son of a minister. That elder, moreover, should be understood as the Arahat Thera known as Vaṃsika in the city of Ariyamaḍanapura.
Furthermore, he gave the Parivāra-vihāra named Veḷūvana to the Elder named Ñāṇadhaja, who was an expert in the Abhidhamma; that Elder, too, belonged to the lineage of the Arahant Elder [Mahinda].

He gave the Parivāra-vihāra named Jetavana to the Elder Guṇārāma, who had mastered the entire Vinaya Piṭaka by heart; that Elder, moreover, belonged to the lineage of the Elder Ānanda within the city of Ariyamaṇḍala itself.
He gave the Parivāra-vihāra named Kulavihāra to the Elder named Ādiccaraṃsi; he, too, belonged to the very same lineage as the Elder Ānanda.
He gave the dependent monastery named Suvaṇṇavihāra to the elder named Sudhammālaṅkāra; he too belonged to the lineage of the elder Ānanda.
He gave the dependent monastery named Nīcageha to the elder named Varapatta, who was a pupil of the great elder Sudhammasāmi.
He gave the dependent monastery named Dakkhiṇakoṭi to the elder named Siripuññavāsin, who was also a pupil of the great elder Sudhammasāmi.

In the vicinity of those monasteries, the king himself took hold of the Great Bodhi tree with his own hand and planted it. For the maintenance of those monasteries, he also granted many fields and lands, as well as families to serve as guardians of the monastery grounds.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the lineage of these elders originated from the monks of Sudhamma and Ārimaddana; for this very reason, the Dispensation was exceedingly pure in Vijayapura.
Their lineage of disciples also numbered many thousands.

Thus, from among those monks who were modest and virtuous, certain co-residents arose at Kīṭāgiri who were shameless and immoral, like unripe sour fruits appearing on a tree of sweet mangoes. They indeed practiced many forms of misconduct.
This, however, is the account of their original origin.
At that time, the king granted many fields and lands for the purpose of maintaining those monasteries.
Regarding those fields and lands, the Elder Sudhamma Mahāsāmi appointed certain bhikkhus as guardians for the purpose of collecting the tax-share (*balivicāra*).
He appointed them. Furthermore, he had the monks guarding [the fields] instruct the farmers according to the Dhamma, and he also had them accept a share of the field-land as the owners' portion.
At that time, the monks fell into dispute over the field-lands.
Then, having heard of that dispute, the Elder Sāsanadharo and the two Elders Parakkamato departed from there. Having departed,
The Elder Sāsanadhara sat on Mount Khaṇitti-pāda, while the two Elders Parakkama sat in the cave of Caṅgakiṅga-pabbata.
Because that was their place of residence, it became known down to the present day as "Parakkama’s Place" (Parakkamaṭṭhāna).
Those elders were designated as "the Wanderers" (Ekacārā), whereas the remaining monks were "Village-dwellers and Wanderers" (Gāmavāsī-bahucārā).
They spoke thus. From that time forth, there were separate groups according to whether they were forest-dwellers or village-dwellers.
There was also a common designation of "Saṅgha" for the monks who received the tax-grain from the fields and lands belonging to the monastery.
In the seventh century plus four years of the Kaliyuga, while King Ujana was still reigning, his younger brother, a prince named Kyecvā, took over the kingdom.
This, however, is the origin of that story: King Ujana sent you forth, saying, "Go to the village named Samuddamajjha, sit there, and partake of the sacrificial offering produced there.
That prince, however, was by nature fond of cruel deeds. Once, having gone to hunt boars and returning at night, he saw a dream.

Sakka, the lord of the gods, having arrived, said, "Obtain the virtue of the Uposatha; if you do so, before long you will obtain the white elephant," and having said this, he returned again to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
From that time forth, the prince undertook the virtue of the Uposatha. Later, even in his own hand—
He saw another dream, thinking, "I have become moist with dung. Before long, he obtained five *setibhas*.
Then a certain minister went and reported this matter to the king.
The king, with a joyful heart, praised him in the midst of his royal attendants, saying, "It seems my venerable younger brother has obtained five *setibhas*! The minister—
Again, having gone into the presence of the prince, he reported that matter to him.

The prince thought, "My brother the king is speaking words of censure never spoken before," and so, having conciliated him, he went back again and reported that matter to the king, saying, "The king speaks in just that way.
Upon hearing this, the prince became even more confident in him.
But why did King Ujana not address Prince Kittitara by the term "younger brother"?
It was because King Ekasetibhinda had brought the pregnant queen of another king and established her in the position of chief consort;
she gave birth to Ujana shortly after being installed, and thus Ujana was not the son of Ekasetibhinda, but rather Prince Kittitara himself.
He was the son of Ekasetibhindu; therefore, for that reason, he did not address him by the name "younger brother.
Having heard that the younger brother would receive the five hundred *setthis*, the king became afraid and handed over the kingdom to him.
The king departed through the western gate of the royal palace, while the younger brother entered through the eastern gate. Of the five...
However, because he acquired the title of "Setibhāna," he became widely known as Pañcasetibhinda; his original name, however, should be understood as Sīhasūra.
During the time of that king, many shameless individuals lived in monasteries on the outskirts of villages and engaged in various kinds of improper conduct.
There were also many monks who had arrived through successive lineages from Sudhammapura and Arimaddanapura.
There were those who were modest and desirous of training.
Then, while that king was partaking of his meal, a certain sham ascetic arrived carrying eight requisites and stood before the king.
When asked, "For what purpose have you come? he replied, "I have come for alms-food."
He said: Then the king, having begun with the thought, "I myself shall eat," gave him the entire meal prepared in a golden bowl because of his extreme faith. Then the king thought:
"This bhikkhu has come and stood waiting for almsfood; he is not an ordinary bhikkhu, but rather one who has attained supernormal powers (abhiññā)."
"He might be an arahant; he might have come for the sake of my merit, out of compassion for me.
Having thought thus, he commanded one of his royal officers to follow behind and observe him.
But that false ascetic, being himself devoid of shame, went out to meet his own wife and took her bowl. [She] him—
Having seen this, the king’s man went into the presence of the king and first thought thus:

"If I were to report it exactly as it happened, the king’s favor would be lost; however, by not reporting it in that way, so that the king’s favor might increase all the more, I too might receive a reward, and this sham ascetic might also be released from his offense against the king. Thus...
"I shall inform you. Having thought thus, he reported: "But after I had followed you, O Great King, and looked back, you vanished even as I was looking.
The king, becoming even more deeply inspired with faith, stretched out his hand and uttered these words three times:
"As I believe it, so it is indeed; there is no parting from me. And he gave the man the reward he was entitled to receive.
On that very day, one minister gave a horse named Velāhaka as a gift for the king.
Then the king, thinking, "This has been obtained through the power of my merit," expressed his appreciation. Having mounted that horse, he caused an elephant-rider to lead it.
Then, while the great multitude was looking on, [the elephant-rider] [removed] the turban-cloth from the head of the elephant-rider.
Having seen him, he appeared like a crane leaping into the sky.
That horse, however, traveling from Vijayapura early in the morning, reached the city within the mountains at evening time; they gave him the name Abbhaviñjabbhana-assa.
Thus these sham ascetics even raised children, let alone other forms of misconduct. For that very reason, those sham ascetics...
They entered the king’s wrestling arena and engaged in combat with the wrestlers.
Among them, however, there was a certain sham ascetic named Ovicaṅgākhuṃsaṅghaja who was exceedingly skilled and superior in the art of wrestling.
It is said that he would win every year in the king’s wrestling arena and receive fifteen or twenty horses as his prize.
In the city of Ratanapūra, there was a man of Kambuja descent who was exceptionally skilled and preeminent in the art of wrestling.
Having challenged any wrestler of equal strength from either the city of Ratanapūra or the city of Jeyyapura, he arrived in Vijayapura,
entered the wrestling pavilion near the gate of the Campaka Monastery, and declared, "I wish to perform the art of wrestling."
He informed the king. Then the king, having addressed that wrestler, said: "Now, sir, will you be able to engage in a wrestling match with this man?
"Yes, Great King; formerly, when I was young, I practiced wrestling merely for the sake of sport.
But now I am sixty-nine years old, and hereafter I shall not be able to engage in wrestling."
"I do not know whether I shall be able to do so or not; now I shall kill my opponent, that wrestler, by means of wrestling," he said.

Then, saying, "The wrestling of kings is for the sake of sport only; do not make an effort to kill him," he had them engage in a wrestling match with one another. While the king and his retinue were looking on, those two, in the manner of wrestlers—

Having danced, they approached one another. Then Saṅghaja the wrestler, making a show of striking Kamboja the wrestler with his foot, delivered a blow to the back of his head with the fist of his right hand. Thereupon Kamboja’s face was turned backward.
At that moment, the king together with his retinue thought: "Indeed, for one whose face is turned away in such a manner, death alone is better now."
"But I cannot bear to look at this," he said. Again, Saṅghadeva struck him with his left fist.
Then the face of the Kambuja wrestler twisted and returned to its original position just as before.
At that moment, the prince, together with his retinue, having witnessed that marvel, [gave] two horses and thirty measures of gold.

"And he gave a hundred kahāpaṇas. This statement is recorded because it appears in ancient manuscripts and because it serves as a source of spiritual urgency for virtuous people; for there is no other purpose than the attainment of such urgency.
In the thirteenth year after seven hundred years of the Kali Age, his son, a king named Kittitara, [reigned] in Vijayapura itself.
He ruled the kingdom. Because he was free from passion (*vītarāga*) and shared the same name [as his father], he received the name Sihasūra.
Since only four remained of the five white elephants obtained during the time of his father the king, he became famous by the name Catusetibhinda.
Thus it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā-ṭīkā*: "Catusetibhinda. During the reign of that king, there was an army consisting of the four divisions (*caturaṅgabala*).
The great minister named Nāma, who was skilled in composition, wrote a commentary on the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*. He was one who practiced the knowledge of the entire forest of grammar and lexicography.
On one occasion, after the king had caused a great monastery to be built, he raised a clamor, saying, "This monastery was built by such-and-such a king;
let only those endowed with virtue dwell in this monastery. Then, a resident of the village named Sācañña—
An elder arrived and sat down.
This, however, was the occasion for that elder:
it is said that in the village of Sācaññi, a certain householder sent his son to a monastery to learn a craft from a certain bhikkhu.
He handed [the child] over in their presence. However, when the boy was unwilling to go to the monastery, his mother threw [a branch] from a thorny bush over him to frighten him.
That youth, having gone out, did not return home but sat right there in the monastery.
Without returning to his parents, he traveled little by little further and further until, starting from the stage of a novice (sāmaṇera), he reached the stage of full ordination (upasampadā).
He went to the city of Arimaddanapura. Because of his extreme wisdom, however, the great elders welcomed him at every place he reached.
For that very reason, he became famous throughout the entire country of Burma. Then his parents remained seated, waiting for their son’s arrival.
Having heard of this matter, [the king], wishing to investigate whether he might indeed be our son, said:
The father followed him. Having reached the city of Ariyamaṇḍala (Arimaddana), he sat down after being provided with service.
That monk, having satisfied him with the very same service, taught him the texts. However, at another time, that monk spoke repeatedly, saying, "Today the soup has little salt," and so forth.
Then the father spoke thus: "My dear son, you have never before spoken such words; yet now you constantly utter such speech.
What is the reason for this? He asked. [The son replied: "In the past, it was not said because my mind was corrupted by a lack of proficiency in the scriptures; but now, that which is desired by me—"
"The goal has been reached; therefore, I spoke such words for the purpose of securing physical strength," he said.
Having heard those words, the father requested leave to go into the presence of his mother, and returning with his father to his own place, he entered Vijayapura to pay homage to the cetiya.
Then, having heard the words spoken by the king, he ascended that monastery and sat down.
When the guards saw the monk sitting in the monastery, they reported the matter to the king.
The king then dispatched his minister with a fourfold army, saying, "Go and test the power of that monk's knowledge. And the fourfold army went.
He questioned that monk about the place where the secret was hidden, and he answered every question put to him.
Then the king’s fourfold army reported the matter to the monarch. The king, being delighted in heart, gave that monastery to the monk.
As for that monk, because in his youth he had thrown his father into a thorny bush, he was known as the Elder Kaṇḍakakhīpa (Thorn-Thrower).
This was his conventional name; his original name, however, was Nāgita. Sitting in the Sota Monastery, he composed a treatise titled *Saddasāratthajālīni*.

It is said that at the time of this elder, there were about a thousand senior monks in that city who were dedicated to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*), while the number of young monks dedicated to the study of texts (*gantha*) was beyond counting.
Furthermore, he appointed his father to the position of *seṭṭhi* (chief merchant), and for that very reason, they began to refer to that village by the name Seṭṭhigāma.

As for the commentary on the *Kaccāyana*, the Elder named Mahāvijitāpī, while residing on Mount Abhayagiri in Vijayapura itself, composed it; he also composed its recitation manual (*vācaka*). The Elder Saddhammaguru, however, composed the *Saddavutti*.
Thus, through many authors of treatises in Vijayapura, the Dispensation became widespread.

When six hundred and eighty-five years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, a king named Asaṅkhayāca constructed the city of Jeyyapura and reigned there. During the time of those kings, however, there were no books composed by the Theras.
In the sixth month of the seventh hundred and twenty-sixth year of the Kali Yuga, the city of Jeyyapura was destroyed in the month of Vesākha.
In that same year, in the month of Jeṭṭha, Vijayapura was destroyed. In that same year, in the month of Phagguṇa, King Satviva—
"Having established the city named Ratanapūra, he ruled the kingdom.
This refers to the establishment of the Sāsana in Vijayapura and Jeyyapura.
Now, within the realm of Maramma, I shall relate the history of the Sāsana specifically in the city of Ratanapūra in the district of Tambanī.

Indeed, in the Kali Age, seven hundred and eighty-eight years [after the Buddha’s parinibbāna], the son of King Aḷonkaññisūra, named Ānandasūriya, formed an intimate alliance with the daughter of King Narapati and begot a son named Siddhika.
When he reached maturity, he obtained the prosperity of the kingdom. From that time until the reign of King Mrenacodi in the city of Arimaddana—
They ruled the kingdom. After that, the noble king named Sirisudhammarājādhipati reigned in the city of Ratanapūra.

During the time of that king, when seven hundred and ninety-one years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, two elders—the Elder Sirisaddhammālaṅkāra and the Elder Sīhaḷamahāsāmi—brought five relics from the island of Laṅkā.
Having brought them by boat and reached Kusima-tīrtha, they were stopped by the king named Baññārani in the kingdom of Rāmañña;
not allowing them to stay, that very king sent the Theras as far as Sirikhetta-nagara.
Knowing this matter, King Ratanapūriṇda went out to meet them with forty ships as far as Sirikhetta-nagara and brought them back. Having brought them, [he settled them] at Mahānava-gāma.
At the appropriate time, the king himself went out to meet [the relics], accompanied by his harem and ministers.

At the very moment the vessel was filled with the jewels, the great earth quaked and let out a roar. Then the king, thinking, "I shall uphold the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Supreme One of the Three Worlds," brought the bodily relics here; at this opportune moment, this great earth—

It moved and emitted a resonant echo; [the people] declared, "This is a portent foretelling that the Teaching of the Jina shall remain established for a long time in our kingdom," and thus they spontaneously composed a manual on portents.

Let alone the power of the Perfectly Enlightened One while he was still living—oh, how great is the power of his very bodily relics! Thus, the inhabitants of many kingdoms were filled with faith. And regarding this, there are these verses:
Even for the relics of the physical body there was great wonder;
what need then to speak of the Buddha, the Supreme One, while he was still living?
Having recollected this, one should arouse faith.
"May people cultivate abundance in the virtues of the Buddha and show him reverence.

Having enshrined those five relics in the city of Jeyyapura during the seventh century and ninety-two years of the Kali Yuga, he established a cetiya on level ground in the western direction from that city. And that cetiya is known as the Ratanacetiya.
He had it designated; however, because of the great abundance of elephant-figures, it became known as *Anekibhinda*.
Having caused a great monastery (*Mahāvihāra*) to be built—adorned with three inner sanctuaries (*sirigabbha*) and seven gates—he gave it to two theras from the island of Sīhaḷa.
Subsequently, the Elder Mahanta, on the summit of a mountain near his own monastery, [established] his own disciples as well.
Having had them admitted, he established the Saṅgha by formally delimiting the boundary (sīmā) together with all three elders—those who were modest, amiable, learned, and desirous of training.

Thus, through such acts as the formal delimitation of boundaries, the recitation of the scriptures, and the transmission of the lineage, he caused the Dispensation to flourish and firmly establish it in the kingdom of Maramma.
This occurred in the city of Ratanapura within the realm of Maramma, following the tradition of the island of Ceylon.
There were two conditions dependent upon which the first establishment of the Dispensation occurred.
When seven hundred and twenty-six years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, in the month of Phagguna, King Satvavara built the city of Ratanapura.
During the time of that king, in the city of Jeyyapura, a certain shameless female baker [offered] to a certain monk...
He deposited his wealth in the presence [of that monk]. Later, she asked for that wealth.
Then, that monk spoke falsely, saying, "I did not accept your wealth. Having thus created a dispute, they reported the matter to the king.
The king had him summoned and questioned the monk himself: "Venerable sir, did you [accept] the woman's wealth?"
"Did you accept it or not? "Great King, for me as a recluse, it is not proper to speak falsely;
therefore, I say, 'I did not accept it. When the king questioned him repeatedly and investigated the matter, he discovered the monk's deceitful nature and realized:
"Though he is a recluse, he has transgressed the training rule prescribed by the Blessed One and speaks a lie."
Having become angry, he himself cut down the *sīya* (palanquin) in accordance with the offense and hurled it down from the royal palace.

That incident became well known throughout the entire Aramman country. Even shameless monks did not dare to commit other evil deeds; out of fear of the king, they did not transgress the precepts (*sikkhāpada*).
When seven hundred and thirty years of the *kaliyuga* had elapsed, a king named Maṅgakricvācoṅka reigned.
Then that king, having taken an omen for the sake of the welfare of the inhabitants of the kingdom, took a palm-leaf fan and entered the royal palace.
When seven hundred and forty-five years had passed since the coronation of that king, he established a cetiya named Cañciṅkhu near a rocky mountain called Yaṅgara. It was an ancient [site]...

He broke through the river water to the *cetiya*. At that time, as the five relics together with their casket were sinking into the water, the Nāga named Erāpatha seized them, thinking, "I shall establish another *cetiya* named Cañciṅkhu.
Even while the King was still making his preparations, he entrusted the five relics along with the casket to the Elder named Daṭhānāga. And that Elder—
He gave it to the king. The king deposited two of the relics in the Muṭṭhicetiya. However, it is stated in ancient manuscripts that three were placed in the Caññiṅkhucetiya.
That king, having given the white parasol to his teacher who had instructed him during his childhood, [attained] the position of leader of the Saṅgha.
He gave the order. A certain elder named Khemācāra struck several times upon the gong that had been hung in the courtyard of the cetiya during the middle watch of the night.

Then the king, having heard it from within the royal palace itself, thought, "Perhaps some monk has passed away in the monastery according to the established rule for the third watch," and he sent a messenger, saying, "Go to the monastery and inquire."
He dispatched [a messenger]. The messenger went to the monastery and asked for the reason. The monks said this: "There is no monk among us who has passed away;
rather, we struck the drum to inform many people that Sakka, the lord of the devas, has now passed away.
Again, the king summoned the monks and asked: "But why, venerable sirs, did you..."
"Know that Sakka, the lord of the devas, has passed away. Then the bhikkhus said this:

"Even though Sakka, the lord of the devas, gave his promise at the time of the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, saying, 'I will protect the Dispensation,' he has now not performed even the slightest act of protection for us who dwell within the Dispensation. But if Sakka, the lord of the devas..."
If he were still alive, having given a firm promise in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
he would not now remain indifferent. But since no sign whatsoever of Sakka, lord of the devas, performing his duty of protection is seen now, we know that Sakka, lord of the devas, has passed away.

Having heard this, the king was inspired with faith toward the Elder Khemācāra; he had a monastery built and gave it to him. That elder belonged to the lineage of the great elders of the Sīhaḷa school residing in Sudhammapura, and he was modest and amiable.
During the time of King Adhikarāja, he had a great bridge constructed in the southern quarter of the city of Ratanapūra itself.
However, his teacher, the Saṅgharāja, did not belong to the faction of the modest ones. For that very reason, [he was excluded] from the succession of elders.
He is not to be included here.
During the time of that king, in the Kali Yuga at seven hundred and sixty-six years [elapsed], there was a ruler named Rājādhirāja, the lord of the Rāmañña kingdom;
together with six million soldiers, he traveled by way of the river on a thousand vessels.
He had arrived facing toward Ratanapura for the purpose of battle.
Then the overlord, having convened many ministers and monks, addressed them:
"Now the king of the kingdom of Rāmañña is coming here for the purpose of battle; by what means other than fighting can we cause him to turn back?"
"I shall be able. Then, all of them remained silent without saying anything at all.
Thereupon, a certain monk of thirty-one years' standing from the Jātavaṭṭa region, who had been ordained for eleven years, spoke thus:
"Let alone the King of Kings, the sovereign of the Rāmañña kingdom; even if it were throughout the whole of Jambudīpa..."
"All the kings might come, yet even by means of this very exchange of conversation, without engaging in battle, they have caused him to turn back, thinking, 'I am able.
Then the overlord king, with a joyful heart, said: 'Venerable sir, since you are able to cause the overlord king to turn back through such conversation, please do so.
Thereupon, that bhikkhu sent a letter containing a shower of loving-kindness (*mettāsandesapaṇṇa*) and requested an audience in the presence of that overlord king."

Desiring to enter [the city], the King of Kings saw the letter containing the message of loving-kindness from that bhikkhu and dispatched a messenger, saying, "Bring that bhikkhu here quickly. The messenger brought him and presented him to the king.
Then, after that bhikkhu had given the King of Kings a discourse on the Dhamma and instruction, he sent him back to his own place. And this bhikkhu was in the city of Arimaddana.
Among the four monastic orders, he belonged to the lineage of the Arahant order; he was desirous of training, modest, and amiable.
Because he was born in the place called Cāgaha in the city of Ariyamaṇḍala, he was known as the Bhikkhu Cāgahi.
When seven hundred and eighty-eight years of the Kali Age had elapsed, King Miññhaṅga Dhammarāja, at Ratanapura itself—
He attained the kingship. During the time of that king, two great theras came from the island of Siṃhala to Ratanapūra and remained there, supporting the Sasana.
At that time, when eight hundred years of the Kaliyuga were complete, in order to remove the ancient Kaliyuga and establish a new one—
The opportunity had arrived. Then the Elder Āgiri and the Elder residing at the Royal Monastery spoke thus:
"Great King, when the time for removal has arrived, it is not permissible not to remove [the robes].
Then the King spoke again: "For one who, when the time for removal has arrived, remains indifferent without removing them..."
"What is the fault? [they asked]. "If, when it is time to remove [the old king], one does not remove him but remains indifferent, suffering will come upon the inhabitants of the kingdom;
thus it is stated in the Vedas and other scriptures. Furthermore, they said that even a king who removes his own son as king might pass away within that very same year."

Then the King, knowing that living beings were obtaining happiness, realized that it was not fitting for one like himself to remain seated without removing what ought to be removed out of regard for his own fear;
reflecting that even if his work were exhausted, his own lack of virtue would spread throughout the world and remain established there,
[he acted] when eight hundred years of the Sakkarāja era had been completed, during the friendship of the Buddha Vāsychidra-muni.
Having removed [the skin], he set aside what remained of the hide. Then, having caused a great pavilion to be built and held a grand festival, he also gave a great almsgiving.
The Elder Cāgiri and the Elder residing at Rājavihāra were among the foremost of the company of Arahants in the city of Ariñjaya; they were modest, amiable, and desirous of training.
Such a statement, however, was spoken in accordance with the Dhamma because of the preparedness for the Dispensation and because of the dependence upon the inhabitants of the kingdom.
In the Kaliyuga, eight hundred and four years [after the Buddha’s passing], the great sovereign king reigned in the city of Ratanapūra.
That king caused the Thūpārāma Cetiya to be constructed. His teacher was the Elder Mahāsāmi.
That elder, having gone to the island of Siṃhala, [studied] in the presence of the Elder Sāriputta, who was the teacher of King Siṃhila.
He should be understood as belonging to the lineage of the elders who returned after receiving the training.

During the time of that king, there was a certain elder named Mahāariyavaṃsa in the city of Ratanapūra. He was proficient in the scriptures and belonged to the lineage that had come from the Chappada group in the city of Ariyamaḍana.
On one occasion, having gone to the city of Jeyyapura, he [studied] the method of phonetics (*saddanaya*) in the presence of the renowned Great Elder known as Reṅga.
Having mastered it, he sat down. It is said that this great elder usually sat with water held in his mouth, desiring not to engage in any kind of conversation with others;
for this reason, he became well known by the Marma vernacular name "Reṅgu.
It is said that Ariyavaṃsatthera thought, "I shall request an opportunity to have Reṅgu the Elder recite the texts in his presence."
Even when he approached him, he did not engage in conversation, but returned only after completing his duties for two days.
On the third day, however, having heard the sound from the beating of a piece of leather, he spat water from his mouth and asked the reason.
[The other] informed him that he had come for the purpose of learning the texts.
Then the Elder spoke thus: "Friend, day after day I recite the scriptures three times;
furthermore, during the time for the *majjhima* and *kāttika* festivals, I go to the Paññā-cetiya and perform the duty of sweeping the courtyard of the shrine.
I find no opportunity [to study], even though you have mastered many scriptures, yet having failed to receive the instructions given by your teachers, once again..."
"You are coming into my presence; therefore, having temporarily suspended your duty of sweeping the courtyard, I shall grant you the opportunity to study the texts.
Having said this, he had him learn the *Lakkhaṇa-ṭīkā* named *Abhidhammattha-vibhāvinī*. He taught him by providing instruction through various methods.
After he had been taught, on the third day, he did not go into the presence of the teacher. The Great Elder also—
Thinking, "Perhaps he might become unwell due to this cause," [the Elder] sent monks to inquire after him.
The Elder Ariyavaṃsa, thinking, "I shall go into the presence of my teacher," arrived;
however, seeing the messenger-monks on the very path, they returned with them to the presence of the Great Elder. Upon reaching the teacher's presence, the teacher—
He asked the Elder Ariyavaṃsa, "But why have you not come for the purpose of learning?
He replied, "Venerable sir, by relying on the instruction given by you, I now know all the methods.
Then the teacher said, "However, having composed a commentary on that text by means of which you have attained proficiency, provide a service [to the teaching]."
Then the Elder Ariyavaṃsa, having received his teacher’s words with his head,
composed a sub-commentary on the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī* titled the *Maṇisāramañjūsā*. On every Uposatha day, once each section of the text was completed,
he would assemble the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in the courtyard of the Puññacetiya and [present it] to the Saṅgha.
Having had it read in the middle [of the assembly], he caused it to be heard, saying: "If there is any fault, speak it.
Then, a certain bhikkhu who had come from the city of Arimaddana for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya sat down at the edge of the assembly and listened.
That bhikkhu made the sound "ee" twice; having noted that spot, he established it [as the place for the proclamation].

He also asked about his place of residence. When the Elder Ariyavaṃsa reached his own monastery and was examining that location, he observed that in one place there was the fault of tautology because a certain meaning had been stated twice;
and in another place, where it should have been expressed in the masculine gender as "imaṃ ganthaṃ," it was stated in the neuter gender as "idaṃ ganthaṃ."
Because it was so stated, the fault of contradiction with the gender is seen.
Then, having summoned that person, he said this: "Friend, I compose this book with great effort;
and at a time of seclusion, during the night alone, I spread out the manuscript and write it. Even while composing it with such great effort..."
"You are making this noise because you are dissatisfied; but having heard what kind of fault did you act in this way?
he asked. Then that bhikkhu replied: "Venerable sir, there is no place for much to be said by way of fault regarding these books composed with great effort;
this book is indeed complete both in sound and in meaning. However, in one particular place—"
Because a single point has been stated twice, the fault of "repetition" (puranuttidoso) is seen;

however, because in one instance the word *imaṃ ganthaṃ* is used in the masculine gender where it ought to be expressed in the neuter as *idaṃ ganthaṃ*, the fault of "contradiction of gender" (liṅgavirodhidoso) is seen.
Thus, having observed only these many faults, I demonstrate this manner of disapproval.

Then the Elder Ariyavaṃsa, with a joyful heart, said, "I offer this two-layered robe worn upon my own body as an offering for your wisdom," and gave it to him. Later, King Adhika, having heard of this matter, bestowed a reward upon him.

That Elder Ariyavaṃsa composed the work named *Maṇidīpa*, which includes both an exegesis (*bharaṇa*) and a purification of the Jātaka stories, in the Pāli language. Furthermore, he composed the *Atthayojanā* sub-commentary in the Maramma (Burmese) language.
On one occasion, King Adhika went to the monastery and listened to the Dhamma. When the Elder had finished teaching the Dhamma, he requested a vehicle-offering for his own comfort.
Without giving it, the king boarded a boat and departed.
On the way, a crocodile caught the boat’s rudder in its mouth and held it motionless. It was at this point that the Elder made his request.
Crying out in a loud voice, "I am giving the vehicle-offering! he made the royal guards retreat three times. Then the crocodile released the boat and departed.
At one time, the king went out to the monastery. Thereupon, a certain person tied a female elephant near the monastery and left her there.
She broke off a branch from the Bodhi tree and ate it; she then fell right there upon the ground.
Then the Elder, having performed an act of truth and cultivated the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā*), sprinkled her with the water of loving-kindness.
At that very moment, she rose up. Having witnessed this marvel, the king paid the full value for her;
then, having constructed a stone platform on the path leading from the monastery to the river crossing, he built a bridge.

The Elder Saddhammakitti, however, was a co-resident disciple (*saddhivihārika*) of the Elder Ariyavaṃsa and a resident of the Jetavana Monastery. These two elders should be understood as belonging to the lineage of the "Six-Footed Group" (*chappadagaṇavaṃsika*).

When eight hundred and forty-two years of the Kali Age had elapsed, the second sovereign king named Sirisudhammarājādhipati reigned in the city of Ratanapūra itself. And at that time, from the city within the mountains, the Mahāsīlavaṃsa...
When eight hundred and forty-five years had elapsed, the Elder Nāma composed the *Sumedhakathā* according to the rules of poetic ornamentation (*kavyālaṅkāra*),
and having also composed the work titled *Buddhālaṅkāra*, a poetic ornamentation connected with the interior of the mountain,
he took these [works] and went to the city of Ratanapūra.
Then the king had the Elder seated in the Ratanavimāna Monastery at a spot near the Thūpārāma Cetiya.
That Elder sat there after having taught the scriptures to those who were listeners. And that Elder was the eighth among the elders seated there.
And that Mahāsīlavaṃsa Elder [lived] in the eight hundred and fifteenth year of the Kali Yuga.
It is stated in ancient manuscripts that he was born and arrived at the city of Ratanapūra at the age of thirty.
Furthermore, that elder composed a commentary on the *Nettipāḷi* in the Maramma language and also [wrote] the *Pārāyanavatthu*.
In the very same city of Ratanapūra, there was a certain elder named Raṭṭhasāra, who possessed the power of supernormal knowledge equal to that of the elder Mahāsīlavaṃsa.
However, he was born in the city of Ratanapūra during the time of the eight hundred and thirty years of the Kali Yuga.

He composed the *Bhūridatta Jātaka*, the *Hatthipāla Jātaka*, and the *Saṃvara Jātaka* according to the rules of poetic ornamentation (*kabyālaṅkāra*), as well as many other types of works in that same style.
Yet, the ancients do not include those two elders who composed in poetic ornamentation within the lineage of the Elders (*theraparamparā*).

And here, although monks and those observing the Uposatha have been granted the opportunity to compose or recite works of poetic ornamentation, to discuss what is permissible and what is not, and to speak on such matters, we shall remain indifferent to them;
for since there is already an excessive amount remaining to be said regarding the history of the Dispensation (*sāsanavaṃsa*), we shall not speak of it.
However, we have already spoken in detail concerning the subject of the training rule against dancing, singing, and so forth, within the *Uposathavinicchaya*.
When eight hundred and sixty-three years of the Kaliyuga had passed, in the city of Ratanapūra itself, the noble Great Dhamma King, Lord of Kings, Sirī Tribhuvanādityanarapati, reigned.
During the time of that king, a bhikkhu named Itthāsanadhaja learned the texts from the presence of the Elder Saddhammakitti.
Then, a certain Mahāthera, having read the Sotuna [scriptures] in the city of Arimaddana, [arrived] in the city of Ratanapūra.
He had come thinking, "I shall sit down. Then, while the Elder Saddhammakitti was teaching him the texts, that great elder sat down beneath the monastery; hearing the sound, he thought:
"In his presence, standing in the position of a junior, I shall learn a little of the texts. Then that great elder [approached] the Elder Saddhammakitti.

Having entered, he requested permission to have the texts recited to him. Then, after the Elder Saddhammakitti asked how long he had been ordained, the other replied, "Venerable sir, you are senior to me.
He said, "Although I am senior to you, I shall remain in the position of a junior and learn the texts.
Thereupon, the Elder Saddhammakitti taught him the texts. Becoming deeply inspired with faith, [he continued].
However, they address that Great Elder by the name Mahāsādhujjana.
Subsequently, from the time of the 850th year of the Kali Yuga until the 880th year, the kingdom of Burma was agitated by various dangers. At that time, from the kingdom of Kamboja...
Sīha-nisvā, having come from Bhinnakuta, seized the kingdom in the city of Ratnapūra. Then he thought thus:
"The monks, being without wives and without sons, seek a retinue by raising disciples;
if the monks were to search for a retinue and assume the status of kingship, they would then be able to seize the kingdom."
"It is fitting to take the monks right now and kill them. Having thought thus,
he had many pavilions constructed in a forest field named Toṭisīla, and saying, "I shall have oxen, buffaloes, chickens, pigs,
and so forth slaughtered and feed the monks," he [summoned] all the great elders from the cities of Jayapura, Vijayapura, and Ratnapura, together with their many disciples.
Having summoned them and seated them within those pavilions, he surrounded them with elephant troops, cavalry, and other divisions, and then had them killed.
It is said that at that time, three thousand bhikkhus died. Having killed the bhikkhus, he also burnt many books with fire and caused the cetiyas to be demolished.
"Alas! What evil karma this wicked person has committed! And on this matter, there are these verses:
In this world, the Teaching stands supported by kings;
kings who hold wrong views defile the Teacher’s Teaching,
while kings with right view indeed uphold the Teaching.
This being so, it was said that he shines in the sky like the king of owls.
Then, when nine hundred and one years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, smoke issued forth from many stars in the sky.
It is stated in the Royal Genealogy (*Rājavaṃsa*) that at Caṅkīṅkhucetiya as well, streams of water issued from the eye-sockets of the Buddha’s image, just like tears from the eyes.

Then, according to what is stated in ancient manuscripts, the Elder Saddhammakitti went to the city of Ketumatī together with a company of one thousand three hundred great virtuous monks and several other elders; the Elder Raṭṭhasāra also went to the city of Sirikhetta by himself.
However, that does not accord with the statement in the *Rājavaṃsa*: "The Lord of the City of Sirikhetta, King Satvavarāja, brought him [the Elder] there."
The Elder Saddhammakitti also passed away in the city of Ketumatī. A short time after that, the Elder Mahāsādhujjana likewise passed away in that same place.
However, when one hundred and twelve years of the Kali Age had elapsed, the Elder Tisāsanadhaja went from the city of Ketumatī to the city of Haṃsāvatī during the reign of King Anekasetibhindu.
Subsequently, having reached the age of forty-three, during the reign of King Miṅghabrahmanarati, when one hundred and thirteen years of the Kali Age had passed—
Having arrived again at the city of Jettapura, he stayed for one night in a cave near the Jetavana Monastery.
He approached the presence of the Elder Jetavana, the leader of the Great Noble Lineage (Mahāariyavaṃsa).
At that time, the Elder Jetavana was ill and said, "When I have passed away, my place [shall be taken] from the city of Haṃsāvatī."
He thought, "The elder named Tisāsanadhaja has arrived; he will be capable of taking charge [of me], so I shall hand myself over to him.
At that moment, during the first watch of the night, the elder Tisāsanadhaja had a dream:
a corpse was approaching nearby. During the middle watch, however, that corpse entered the cave. During the last watch...
"A corpse's flesh is being cut with a knife. Then he related the vision of the dream to a novice who was sleeping near him.

Having related it and recited a protective charm (*paritta*), even as the novice was sitting down, the Elder of Jetavana summoned him and assigned the Jetavana Monastery to him. Thus did the Elder Tisāsanadhaja [act].
Having sat down in the Jetavana Monastery, he sat there reading the scriptures. King Brahmanarapati of Miṅgha showed him great favor.

Later, in the Kali age, when nine hundred and sixteen years had elapsed, the lord of the city of Haṃsāvatī, a king named Anekasetibhinda, having conquered the city of Ratanapūra, caused a monastery to be built and gave it to him.
Thus, the Elder Tisāsanadhaja should be regarded as the "Arahant of the Gaṇavaṃsa" in the city of Arimaddana.
His disciples numbered several hundreds and were all possessed of moral shame (*lajjī*).
Among those disciples, there were five elders: the Elder Varabāhu, the Elder Garavāsi of Bhūminikhāna, and three great elders residing in Mahāraṭṭhagāma.
"Especially those skilled in the scriptures.
The Elder Tiṣāsana-dhaja, in his old age, took up the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), entered the forest, and took up a secluded dwelling.
At that time, the Jetavana group and others were indeed lineages of those possessing the multitude of Arahants. Later on...
Among their lineages of disciples and grand-disciples, some monks,
taking up sunshades and palm-leaf fans adorned with various colors, fell into a deviation from proper conduct.
When more than one thousand years of the Kali Age had elapsed, a king named Ukkamsika, having caused a monastery to be built for the Elder Tisāsanadhaja, [bestowed it upon him].
He gave it to the elder named Mahāratanākara, who was a pupil of the elder Varabāhu.

And that elder Mahāratanākara composed a work titled *Rajindarājanāmābhidheyyādīpanī*, which he adorned with the methods of prosody, ornamentation, grammar, and logic, and presented under the name-label of His Majesty King Sirisudhammarāja, the Great Lord of the Ukkamsika kingdom.
And for the purpose of purifying that book, he entrusted it to the Mahāthera whose name was Tiropabbata.

Among the three brother-theras residing in Mahāraṭṭhagāma who were disciples of the Thera Tisāsanadhaja, the eldest, who dwelt in the Thirty Caves, sat down after having taught the scriptures. And King Satvavara [was exceedingly devoted] to that Thera...
He became filled with faith. During the time of King Ñoṅkarami, Cūḷapitā also had a monastery built and gave it to him.
During the time of King Ukkaṃsika, he also had a monastery built on the mountain named Maṅgavaṃ and gave it to him.
Among those elders residing in Mahāraṭṭhagāma, there was also the elder Majjhima, who was the elder brother of the elder Tisāsanadhaja.
He sat down in the Jetavana monastery itself, which was their place of residence, and taught the texts.
The younger elder (Kaniṭṭhatthera) likewise sat down in those very monasteries that served as their places of residence and taught the texts.

In this context, the elder named Tisāsanadhaja is of two kinds, according to whether he is conscientious (lajjī) or unconscientious (alajjī). It should be understood that the aforementioned elder is among those who are conscientious; [the other] is unconscientious.
However, this lineage of elders need not be insisted upon here.

We shall remain indifferent toward the account of the elder Tissa-dhaja, who became shameless (*alajjī*), because there is no purpose for it and because it would lead to excessive prolixity in the text.
During the time of King Yogiraṅga, the Great Elder dwelling in the Golden Cave at Jeyyapura [was] the resident of the Dakkhiṇārāma Monastery.
The Mahāthera who dwelt at Catubhūmika Vihāra and the Mahāthera who dwelt at Toṅgabhīlū Vihāra were indeed the *saddhivihārika*s (co-residents) of the Mahāthera Tissāsanadhaja.
However, out of fear of excessive length, we shall not state their lineage or the details of their textual study.
Here, the sole criterion is the recognition that these [masters] belong to the *Lajjigaṇa* tradition.

When nine hundred and sixty-one years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, on the second day of the waxing moon of the month of Phagguna, on a Sunday, King Ññogīraṅga established a second city named Ratanapūra and ruled there. He also assumed the title of Sīhasūradhammarāja.
For the sake of the Great Elder Mahāthera, a resident of the Tocabhīlu Monastery, he constructed a four-storeyed monastery.
He had [these] built. He also had the four great cetiyas of the Great Sage built. Even while the vihāra-cetiyas were still unfinished, he departed from Sīnnī city;
having settled his enmity there, upon his return, he passed away because he could not transcend the inherent nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"Alas! Such is the nature of conditioned things. And on this matter, there are these verses:—
Just as a house-sparrow toy of merchants,
having flown about in every direction, finally perches upon the top;
even so do beings in this world, in the interval between death and rebirth.
Having wandered about in various ways, they finally establish peace.

In the year nine hundred and sixty-seven of the Kali Age, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phagguna, his eldest son took possession of the kingdom belonging to his father. He also accepted the title and seal of "Mahādhammarāja."
He had the stūpas that had remained unfinished during his father’s time completed once more.

Having brought a four-storeyed monastery to completion, he summoned the Elder Mahā-Toṭibhīlu to the palace, thinking, "I shall give [this] to the Great Elder who dwells in the four-storeyed monastery," since the Elder had passed away to the other world and was no longer present.
Although the Elder was summoned two times, he did not come; on the third [time]...
On the other hand, many of his co-residents said, "Go to the inner palace and enter; for it is not possible to refuse [the food] when the king has already invited you.
Then the Elder spoke thus: "Friends, I do not wish to consume alms-food that causes oppression to the kingdom; even so..."
"If you wish to go into the presence of the king, then since that is the case, I shall now go into the presence of the king," he said, and entered the inner palace.
Having entered and conversed with the king, he objected, saying, "This monastery is unsuitable for monks who dwell in the forest.
"But, venerable sir, if that is the case, [what of] sitting in that monastery?"
"Show us an elder," [the king said]. "O Great King, there is an elder who dwells at Khaṇittipāda; he is confident in the scriptures and desires training.
It is fitting to give him [the monastery]," [he replied]. Then the king gave the monastery to him and also bestowed upon him the title "Mahāsaṅghanātha.
He settled there and taught the scriptures.
Furthermore, among the forty monasteries surrounding that monastery, a senior elder named Varābhiṣaṅghanātha, residing in one monastery in the northern intermediate direction,
composed the Maṇikuṇḍalavatthu in the Maramma language. Another elder, residing in a monastery in the western intermediate direction, composed the Sattarājadhammavatthu.
And at that time, because two bhikkhus named Bhāmaṅkya and Ācāraṅkya were skilled in worldly affairs, he built two monasteries and gave them to them.
Those two elders were experts in the Vedas, but they were dull in the study and practice of the Dhamma;
they had come from the kingdom of Rāmañña. According to the ancient tradition, they are not counted in the lineage of the elders.

When nine hundred and seventy-three years of the Kali Age had elapsed, he had four monasteries constructed in the eastern direction of the Mahāmuni Cetiya and presented them to four elders. Those elders, having sat there, upheld the Dispensation.
At that very time, there was also a certain elder named Badaravanavāsī; he too was proficient in the scriptures and well-versed in the sixfold lineage of the Vinaya.
Thus, that elder, having upheld the Dispensation according to his strength for as long as he lived, took rebirth in his second existence in the womb of a certain woman in the city of Calaṅga.
When ten months had passed and nine hundred and forty years of the Kali Yuga had arrived, he was born on a Wednesday;
and at the age of thirteen, he went forth into homelessness within the Dispensation and mastered the scriptures.
King Sirikhettanagarinda, having brought [the work] to the city of Sirikhettanagara, became renowned there by the name Sāmaṇera.

When nine hundred and fifty-four years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, at the age of fifteen, he composed the Vessantarajātaka according to the rules of poetic ornamentation (*kavyālaṅkāra*). At the age of twenty, while still in the city of Sirikhettanagara—
King Veravijaya, the lord of Sirikhettanagara, having shown favor [to the Elder], established him in the ground of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
A king named Pacchimapakkhādika brought Sirikhettanagara under his own control.
At that time, he had the Elder brought there and settled him in Ratanapuranagara. The king’s younger brother was named Sūrakitti.
Having caused a four-storied monastery to be built on the bank of the Erāvatī River, he gave it to that elder. The king also bestowed upon him the title *Tipiṭakālaṅkāra*.
When one thousand years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, having reached his sixtieth year on the full moon day of the month of Phagguna, he went to Tiriyapabbata and dwelt there in the forest.
Two thousand and two years after the king had caused that monastery to be built...
He gave it to that very elder. Furthermore, that Elder Tipiṭakālaṅkāra was a lineage-descendant of the Elder Atulavaṃsa of Pattalaṅka, who resided in the Navaṅga-kandara of Sirikhettanagara.

The fame of that elder, while dwelling in the Suvaṇṇavihāra in the Navaṅga-kandara of Sirikhettanagara, spread everywhere. [It reached] the four-storied vihāra on the banks of the Erāvatī River in Jeyyapura.
While residing at Vaṭṭakāla, he composed a commentary on the first twenty verses of the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
He also composed the *Yasavaḍḍhana-vatthu* based on the request of his younger brother, named Sūrakitti. While residing at Tiriyapabbata, he composed a sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Vinayālaṅkāra*.
During the time of King Pacchimapakkhādhirāja, [he consecrated] the Elder Mahāsaṅghanātha in the position of Saṅgharāja.
He appointed him. That Saṅgharāja was exceedingly proficient in the scriptures (pariyatti).
At that time, there was also in the city of Ratanapūra one named Ariyālaṅkāratthara; he, however, was equal in the power of his knowledge to the Elder Tipiṭakālaṅkāra, and they were of the same age.

Among them, it should be understood that the Elder Tipiṭakālaṅkāra was preeminent in his extensive learning across various texts, whereas the Elder Ariyālaṅkāra was preeminent in the analysis of verbal roots and grammatical suffixes.
Later, during the time of King Ukkamsikaraṇa, both these elders served as the king’s teachers and upheld the Dispensation. Among them, the Elder Ariyālaṅkāra, at a later stage—
After passing away, he had a monastery named Dakkhiṇavanārāma built near the Royal Jewel-Top Stūpa for that elder’s pupil, the second Ariyālaṅkāra Thera, and gave it to him.
Furthermore, King Ukkaṃsika was a great benefactor to the Dispensation; he lived during the Kalya Yuga, nine hundred and ninety-six years [after the Parinibbāna].

He attained the kingship. Having attained the kingship, however, after four years had passed—just as King Siridhammāsoka had done—he received the head-anointing consecration and also assumed the title and insignia of "Siri Sudhammarājā Mahādhipati.
On one occasion, having gone to the city of Haṃsāvatī, he sat there. Then, the inhabitants of the Rāmañña kingdom...
They spoke thus: "There are no monks from the Ramanna country who are experts in the scriptures (pariyatti) and knowledgeable in the Vedas.
Upon hearing this, the king sent a message to a senior elder residing in a four-storied monastery, saying:
"Send to my presence from the Ramanna kingdom monks who are thirty or forty years of age, experts in the scriptures, and knowledgeable in the Vedas."
Then the Elder Catubhūmikavīhāravāsin sent forth Tipiṭakālaṅkāra, Tilokālaṅkāra, and Tisāsanālaṅkāra,
together with thirty monks who were masters of the Tipiṭaka. Upon reaching the city of Haṃsāvatī,
he had a monastery built on the eastern side of the Modha Cetiya and gave it to them.

On the uposatha days, he had the residents of the Rāmañña kingdom—those proficient in the Pitakas and learned in the Vedas—gathered in the Sudhamma Hall, and caused them to engage in discussion with those three elders.
Then the bhikkhus residing in the Rāmañña kingdom spoke thus: "In the past, however, we were proficient in the Pitakas and learned in the Vedas in the Maramma kingdom."
"We think there are none," they said, "for now the inhabitants of the kingdom of Burma are exceedingly proficient in the scriptures and learned in the Vedic sciences.
Later, when nine hundred and ninety-six years of the Kali Age had elapsed, the King returned to the city of Ratanapura.
Those elders, desiring to return, went to the presence of the Great Elder named Tilokagaru—who was preeminent in the kingdom of Rāmañña—in order to pay him homage.
Then the Elder Tilokagaru, having conversed with them, spoke thus: "Among you, however, the Elder Tipiṭakālaṅkāra shall first receive a monastery for his residence.
When asked, "Why, venerable sir, did you speak thus?", he replied:
"Because even while wandering for alms, this elder will obtain bamboo, rattan, and other materials along the way, and having taken them, he will perform repairs to the monastery."
"Therefore I say this: 'In this world, monks who are habituated to repairing monasteries quickly obtain a dwelling place,' for so said the ancient elders," he said.
They too returned to the city of Ratanapūra. In accordance with the words of the Elder Tilokagaru, the Elder Tipiṭakālaṅkāra was the very first to obtain a dwelling place.
When one thousand and nine years of the Kaliyuga had passed, the king’s younger brother died.
Then the king’s son, the governor of Uccanagara, having formed an intimacy with foolish people and taking their word to heart,
entered the inner palace in haste at dawn, desiring to have his father killed.
Taking a priceless ring, the king, together with the minister named Nandajeyya and the royal warrior named Amacca, departed from the city in a certain disguise and reached the river of silver sand.
At that time, a novice monk was coming down the river in a small boat, thinking, "I shall bring alms-food from my parents' house.
Then, seeing that novice monk, the king said: "Venerable sir, please take us across to the other bank by boat."
"Bring him here," [the king said]. The novice replied, "If I were to bring you to the other shore, O lay follower, it would cause the time for the meal to pass.
Then the king consoled him, saying, "Then bring me quickly; I will give you this ring," and requested the opportunity to be brought there.
Having heard these words spoken out of compassion, the novice brought him to the other shore.
Then, having reached the Catubhūmika monastery and reported the entire matter to the Elder in that monastery, he said:
"Venerable sir, if you come to take us away, please prevent them. The Elder replied: "Great King, we are recluses;
it is not possible to prevent them in such a way. However, there is this one expedient: the Elder who dwells in the Nisinna-vihāra [is occupied] with household affairs."
"He is exceedingly clever; it is fitting to summon him and consider the matter. Then, having summoned him and informed him of the situation, the king said this:
"Venerable sir, if they should come to seize us, then by whatever means possible, please prevent them.
Then that elder spoke thus: "In that case, Great King, do not grieve over anything; do not be afraid."
Having said, "Enter the inner chamber of glory in the midst of the monastery and sit there," he had the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras who were not wandering for alms assembled.
Then, with sticks in hand, he told them individually, "Do not give even a single man the opportunity to enter the monastery," and he arrayed them like an army.
He did the same for the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras residing in the surrounding monasteries as well.
He summoned them. At that time, it is said, there were more than a thousand monks and novices who had come and assembled.

The Elder stationed them individually at the gates and doorways of the monastery and along the paths by which they had arrived, holding staffs in their hands for the purpose of guarding them, just as a carpenter stations various pigs here and there to ward off a tiger.
"He stationed [them]" means: Then, even the king's warriors were unable to seize the king;
furthermore, out of reverence for the monks and novices, they did not dare to enter by force after killing them, and because of the great number of those monks and novices.
From the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Assayuja in that very year until the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika.
The king remained hidden right there in the monastery and sat down. Then the ministers residing in the inner palace removed the son, brought the king back, and established him on the throne.

When the king had regained his kingdom and was sitting in the monastery, a certain monk learned in the Vedas and the scriptures, while announcing to the king, "Do not fear, Great King; you shall be victorious," [struck] the Caṅki cetiya.
Having had a monastery built at that uninhabited site, he gave it to him. He also bestowed upon him the name and title *Dhammananda-rājaguru*.
Furthermore, the village where he was born came to be known by the Marma vernacular as *Ye-ne-nā-se-yāṃ-va*.
And when the king regained his kingdom, in that very same year, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika—
Having invited all the great elders and ushered them into the royal palace, he fed them with alms-food. Then the king spoke thus:

"The elder who dwells in a four-storied monastery is a teacher who brings about welfare pertaining to future lives; however, the elder who dwells in a seated monastery brings about welfare pertaining to the present life.
This is stated in the *Rājāvaṃsa*. In ancient manuscripts, however, it is said that the elder who dwells in a four-storied monastery is exclusively a true ascetic (*ekantasamaṇo*).
The Teacher says: "Furthermore, it is said that the Elder who dwelt in the Nisinna-vihāra was a king because he was worthy of being a warrior and was skilled in the work of a warrior.
It is said that the king, failing to consider the welfare of the future life (*samparāyika-attha*), did not give [the gift] to the Elder of the Nisinna-vihāra at the time it was offered;
however, occasionally, failing to consider the welfare of the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika-attha*), he gave it to him separately. And here—
Since the Elder residing in Nisinnavihāra provided protection for the sake of warding off the king's fears,
and not for the purpose of harming others, and since no application of commands is observed, there is no fault of an offense.
This should be understood as being like the activity performed by the Arahant Elders for the sake of warding off the fears of King Saddhātissa.
The Elder who dwelt in the Four-Level Monastery was born in Khaṇittipāda village; he was one of the multitude of Arahant Elders at the city of Ariyamaḍana.
Having gone wherever necessary to understand the conduct of other monks as it truly was, he never shared in the four requisites with them, nor did he even drink water with them;
even when visiting various places, he would do so only by taking a piece of hide with him.

He was of a wandering disposition. King Ukkaṃsika, however, having taken the architectural form of a cetiya built by King Dvattapoṅkara in the city of Sirikhettana, constructed a cetiya named Rājamaṇicūḷa.
That cetiya measured three hundred cubits in circumference and was exactly that much in height as well. Furthermore, he had four monasteries constructed at the four corners of that cetiya.
On the eastern side was the monastery named Pubbavanārāma; on the southern side, Dakkhiṇavanārāma; on the western side, Pacchimavanārāma;
and on the northern side, Uttaravanārāma. Among those four monasteries, the one named Uttaravanārāma was destroyed after being consumed by a lightning strike. As for the remaining ones...
He gave three monasteries to three great elders who were experts in the scriptures and even provided them with their respective seals.
During the time of the last king alone, he had a monastery built on the northern side.
However, that king passed away before the parasol could even be raised over that cetiya. Regarding those four monasteries:
While the elders were seated, the Great Elder residing at Dakkhiṇavanārāmavihāra adorned the meaning of the Kaccāyana treatise with six methods of commentary and explained it in the Maramma language.
Furthermore, the Elder residing at Pacchimavanārāmavihāra composed a commentary on the Nyāsa, adorning it with six methods.
Then, when more than a thousand years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, the son of that king, the eminent lord Sirinanda Sudhammarājā, reigned.
Having demolished his father’s royal palace and having caused a monastery to be built, he gave it to the Great Elder named Tilokālaṅkāra.
And the Elder Tilokālaṅkāra was a disciple of the Elder Tipiṭakālaṅkāra, who possessed the power of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā).
He should be understood as a pupil of the Elder Ariyālaṅkāra; this matter has been shown below.
Having had the Catubhūmika-atula Vihāra constructed at Jeyyapura, he gave it to the Elder Dāṭhānāgarājaguru. And that Elder composed a commentary on the Nyāsa titled the *Niruttisāramañjūsā*.
When twelve hundred years plus [some] had elapsed in the Kaliyuga, in the month of Phagguna, the guardian deities known as Sotāpannā said, "We shall go elsewhere.
Seeing this as a dream, the people of the city gathered in great numbers and performed a worship of the deities.
However, it should be understood that there is no such thing as the physical departure of deities; rather, this was merely a foretoken.
And at that time, the warriors of King Cīna arrived and ravaged the Maramma kingdom. The dispensation became as weak as the moon obscured by a cloud.
When twenty-three hundred years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, the younger brother of that king, named King Mahāpavaradhammarājālokādhipati, ruled the realm.
And at that time, due to worldly convention, merit would become diminished.
Because it had been pointed out by those learned in the Vedas, he had a dwelling for the rainy season built merely according to worldly convention for the sake of generating fresh merit;
