having moved there on a temporary basis, he resided there. Later, after demolishing the northern house, he had a monastery built on that very same spot and gave it to a certain great elder.
Furthermore, having had a monastery built in the eastern quarter of the city,
he gave the Dakkhiṇageha to the Elder Aggaṇammālaṅkāra. That elder, in turn, translated the meaning of the Kaccāyana grammar, the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, and the Mātikā, Dhātukathā, Yamaka,
and Paṭṭhāna into the Maramma language.
And Uparājā, having caused a golden monastery to be built at the site facing the mouth of the Mahāsetu,
gave it to the Elder Jinārāma, who was a pupil of the Elder residing in the Uttarageha Monastery. At that very same spot,
having caused a monastery variegated with various jewels to be built, he gave it to the Elder Guṇagandha, who was a pupil of that same Elder.
Now, that elder was born in the village of Chinavaḍḍhana. When he reached maturity, he went to the city of Ratanapūra and mastered the scriptures.
Returning from there, he settled in the village of Badara in the town of Baduna.
Later, he lived in the village of Chinavaḍḍhana, where he dwelt while being wearied by the four requisites. And at that time, in that village, there was no liberation.
Once, a king obtained a priceless gem from the presence of a man named Nāma and cherished it exceedingly.
It became famous as the ‘Chinavaḍḍhana’ liberation-gem.

Then the Elder who dwelt at Uttaragehavihāra said: “In the village of Chinavaḍḍhana, it is not only the gem that is priceless; rather, even a single elder named Guṇagandha, who is proficient in the scriptures (pariyatti), is indeed priceless.”
Then, having heard that, the king summoned him, supported him with the four requisites, and paid him honor.
In Sahassorodhagāma there was an elder named Guṇasāra, and in Palinagāma there was an elder named Sujāta; both were indeed disciples of the elder Guṇagandha.
And at one time, the great elder residing at the Tiriyapabbata monastery [addressed] the elder Aggadhammālaṅkāra in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
He spoke thus in jest: "Friend, while we are disappearing from the world, you will become the sole elder in the world skilled in the scriptures.

Then Aggadhammālaṅkāra said: "Venerable sir, while you are disappearing from the world, among those skilled in the scriptures, there will be one person named Bhaveyyāmaka who will be skilled in the scriptures. [This is found] in the ancient manuscripts.
However, it is stated that the Venerable Ariyālaṅkāra said, "Are we not now experts in the texts? We have not yet [completed this].
That very Venerable Aggadhammālaṅkāra, when requested by the king, composed even a summary of the royal lineage (*rājavaṃsa*).
Furthermore, that Thera was the son of a minister.

And at one time, a certain high minister who had returned to the lower life took all the personal belongings he had received from the king, went to the monastery, and engaged in conversation with the Elder Aggadhammālaṅkāra.
Having conversed and shown all those belongings to the Elder, he said: "Venerable sir, if you were a householder..."
He said, "One will receive such an amount of enjoyment. The Elder also spoke thus:
"But this much enjoyment of yours does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of us monks who enter the privy after having cultivated the meditation on the foul (aśubhabhāvanā).
Although these words are not prominent in the *Sāsanavaṃsa*, they were spoken by the lions among the ancient teachers.
However, it should be kept in mind that the aforementioned statement must be remembered until the end of time; thus it was said.
Then, when thirty-four thousand years of the Kali Age had elapsed, his son, a king named Narāvara, ruled the kingdom.
He received the title and insignia of Mahāsīhasūradhammarāja. During the reign of that king—
Near the Sīhoṇa Cetiya, in the Jetavana Monastery, there was a certain young bhikkhu who, though skilled in the scriptures,
had been troubled by a childish mind during his youth. Just as one might stir up a cesspool with a stick— hidden from view by the wind and heat and appearing dry on the surface—

the continuum of his consciousness was likewise stirred up, becoming foul-smelling due to its being hidden from the wind and heat of the *pariyatti* (the study of the scriptures) and appearing dry on the surface.
Having been obscured by some object such as a form (rūpa-ārammaṇa) and becoming agitated,

he thought, "I shall return to the lower life," and after the foul odor known as the arrows of the defilements (kilesa-satti) had wafted forth, he took his lay clothes and went with his companion monks to a river crossing.
On the way, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Cetiya while still in my state as a monk," he gave the lay clothes to his companions.
Placing her hand [upon his], she entered a cave at the head of the cetiya, paid homage, and sat down.
Then a certain young woman came to the courtyard of the cetiya, sat outside the cave, sprinkled water, and made this aspiration:
"By this meritorious deed, may I be liberated from all states such as the woeful realms; and in birth after birth, may I never become the foot-follower of a man who turns back to base things."
Then, having heard that, the young bhikkhu thought: "He came here thinking, 'Now I shall return to the lower life.
May this young woman also not have to walk on foot for a man who has returned to the lower life"—thus he made a wish.
Then, thinking, "I shall now ask the reason regarding that young woman," he went outside the cave.
Having gone out, he asked her the reason for that: "But why do you make this aspiration, 'May I not be a foot-servant to a man who has returned to the lower life'?
She replied: "Venerable sir, when one says, 'May I not be a foot-servant to a man who has returned to the lower life,' it means 'May I not be a foot-servant to a foolish man.'"
There is no difference from what was stated; it is indeed of similar meaning. Is it not the case, then, that one who has returned to the lower life is simply called a fool?
However, Venerable Sir, if one who has returned to the lower life were not called a fool, who in the world would be a fool?
For a so-called bhikkhu lives happily, having enjoyed robes, almsfood, and lodgings provided by others.
If he should desire to learn the scriptures, he would obtain the opportunity to learn them exactly as he wishes;
yet, instead of being thus, if he were to be indolent, desiring only to eat, lie down, and sit, even then he would obtain the opportunity to eat and lie down exactly as he wishes.
Being such a person, he will become another's slave, [a slave] to his wife...
"Even though he did not say, 'I shall become a servant,' he would turn back toward the low life as if he had said so;
I consider him to be a fool superior even to other fools in the world.

But if it were said, 'If she were the wife of one more foolish than you, I would be more foolish still,' that young bhikkhu, having been moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), went out through the city gate."
Without his troop of monkeys, he sat meditating like a monkey in meditation.
Then his companions arrived and called out to him, "Take back your house-clothes!
At that time, the young bhikkhu said, "Come, sirs," and after explaining the whole matter to them, he added, "But now, sirs, you must return to the lower life."
"If anyone should come and strike my head with a mallet, even then I do not wish to return to the lower life;
from this moment until the end of my life, I will not even think in my mind of returning to the lower life.
Having said this, he crossed the Erāvatī River and went to Jayapura. At that time, it is said, there was a young woman named Devalābhā.
"The wise do not say she is a human woman.
Having reached Jeyyapura, however, he took up the method from the great elders who were experts in the scriptures (pariyatti) and sat in a monastery located to the south of the Puññacetiya.
After having them teach him the scriptures, he then gradually [proceeded] from those various directions.
Bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras came and learned the scriptures (pariyatti) in his presence.
However, as they could not find a dwelling place, some of the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras even sat down under the shade of their own umbrellas.
At one time, the king went out and entered the courtyard of the cetiya, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Puñña-cetiya. Then—
Seeing the bhikkhus sitting there having spread out their umbrellas, he had a monastery built together with the cave and gave it to that bhikkhu.
He also gave him the name-epithet *Tilokagaru* ("Venerable to the Three Worlds"). However, for the sake of easy pronunciation, they dropped the letter *ka* and referred to him as *Tilogaru*.
Furthermore, his pupil, a seven-year-old bhikkhu named Tejodīpa, composed a commentary on the *Paritta*.
Later, he bestowed upon him the name Tilokālaṅkāra. Thus, it should be understood that the bhikkhu named Tejodīpa composed the *Paritta-ṭīkā* during the time of King Narāvara.
Some, however, say it was during the time of King Pacchimapakkhādhirāja.
On one occasion, the Mahāthera residing at the Tiriyapabbata Monastery went to pay homage at the Foot Relic Shrine (Pādacetiya).
Upon his return, he entered the presence of the Elder Jambudhaja at Suvaṇṇaguha in Kukhananagara and engaged in conversation with him.
When those two great elders saw one another and conversed, they were exceedingly—
They rejoiced. For in this world, a fool delights greatly with a fool, and a wise man with a wise man.
Those two elders were of the same seniority. The Great Elder residing at Tiriyapabbata Vihāra returned after conversing with him.
And the Elder Jambudhaja followed along to point out the way. Then the Great Elder residing at Tiriyapabbata Vihāra—
He said to the Elder Jambudhaja: "Venerable sir, I am a favorite of the king and a royal preceptor; you yourself should go before me.
Then the Elder Jambudhaja also said to the Elder who dwelt at Tiriyapabbata Monastery: "Venerable sir, you are a favorite of the king and a royal preceptor;
in this world, one called a 'royal preceptor' stands in a position of preeminence. Therefore, you yourself [should go]."
"Go ahead of me. In this context, it should be understood that both great elders spoke thus out of mutual respect and with regard for worldly convention.
The great elder who dwelt at the Tiriyapabbata monastery also, having reached the city of Ratanapūra, went to Mount Rājavaṃsa and lived there in the forest.
Then King Ukkamsika consulted with his younger brother, named Sūrakitti:
"If you see the Elder first in the forest, you alone shall have a monastery built and give it to him;
but if I should see him first, I shall have the monastery built and give it."
Then the youngest sister, having seen him first, had a monastery named Jetavana built in a mountain cave at Tiriyapabbata and gave it to him.
And from this statement, because of the excellence of virtuous people, a sense of joy and gladness arose;
by that meritorious deed and by that joy and gladness, she attained the fortune of sovereignty over the devas seven times and the fortune of sovereignty among humans seven times.
Because it is stated [in the source] that he "obtained," this was said for the purpose of attaining a specific merit by recollecting the virtues of virtuous people.
Furthermore, the Great Elder residing at the Tiriyapabbata Monastery reported the virtues of the Elder Jambudhaja to King Ukkamsaka.
The king, being exceedingly pleased, combined the original name "Jambudhaja" with the word "Dīpa" and bestowed upon him the title and mark of "Jambudīpadhaja."

The elder named Jambudhaja was the co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika) of the elder Dhammananda; the elder Dhammananda was the co-resident pupil of the elder Jotiputta. Those elders belonged to the lineage of the company of Arahants.
Furthermore, the elder Jambudhaja composed a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya Piṭaka and its commentaries in the Maramma language.
Moreover, the elder named Maṇiratana [composed] the commentaries on the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the *Sammohavinodanī*, and the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
He translated the meaning of the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvanī* and the *Saṅkhepavaṇṇanā-Ḷīkā* into the Maramma language.

Furthermore, in Mūlāvāsagāma, a Thera residing at the Pubbārāma Monastery composed the work titled *Gūḷhatthadīpanī*, as well as the *Visuddhimagga-gaṇṭhipadattha*, in the root language (Pali), and he also translated the meaning of the *Nettipāḷi* into the Maramma language. That Thera, moreover, previously...
Having become a village dweller, he took head-wrappings and palm leaves and practiced conduct contrary to the Vinaya according to his own lineage of teachers.
Later, however, he abandoned that practice and lived in the forest. That elder, too, possessed profound wisdom and was exceedingly skillful in the methods of grammar and meaning.
Furthermore, when more than thirty-five thousand years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, a king named Siripavaramahādhammarāja reigned as the youngest [of his line].

Because he had a residence built at the Dabbimukha Jātassara lake and resided there, it became well known by the name "Dabbimukha Jātassara. Moreover, having constructed a monastery named Jeyyabhūmikitti at that lake,
He gave [the position] to the Elder Sirisaddhammapāla. He also rendered assistance to many village-dwelling and forest-dwelling bhikkhus.

For in the city of Ratanapūra, among the ten royal lineages (*ñyauṃ yāṃ*), the last five kings—without even investigating—upheld the Dispensation (*sāsana*) by mixing together those who were shameless and those who possessed shame.
At that time, the Conqueror’s Dispensation was within [the kingdom].

The moonlight was not exceedingly pure. Nevertheless, because even those possessed of a sense of shame (lajjino) were not prevented from fulfilling the Dhamma by way of preserving their own respective lineages, the lineage of the group of the conscientious (lajjīgaṇavaṃsa) did not break off.

Likewise, it should be understood that even those lacking a sense of shame (alajjino) continued to practice according to their own respective traditions of teachers (ācariyappaveṇī), and thus the lineage of the group of the unconscientious (alajjīgaṇavaṃsa) also did not break off.
During the time of that king, there was a certain elder named Devacakkobhāsa; he was an expert in the Vedic scriptures, yet dull in regard to the Piṭakas.

When thirty-eight thousand years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, from the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vesākha, in order to avert the danger arising through worldly convention, that elder Devacakkobhāsa [acted] within the Nine Caves.
In accordance with the stated method, he first had the monks from the border regions (marammika) recite the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa*.

Thereafter, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha, he had the monks residing in the kingdom of Rāmañña recite the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa* and caused a great festival to be held.
He also had the inhabitants of the kingdom perform extensive offerings and honors. To him...
It is said that during the king’s time, they prepared a manuscript by smoothing it with the resin of the *aṭṭhibhallika* tree,
writing upon it with *manosilā*, coating it with gold, and placing it in a casket. From that time until the present day,
they have performed this work of manuscript production in the Maramma kingdom.

When more than six thousand years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, on the sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Assayuja, on a Tuesday, his son reigned. He also received the title and insignia of Sirihāsīhasūrasudhammarāja.
He caused a cetiya to be built at the site of his father the king’s residence. His [other] name was Mārajeyyaratana.
This became the conventional designation. Now, during the time of that king, in a village named Tuṇṇa on the western bank of the river called Sallāvati, there was an elder named Guṇābhilaṅkāra.

When he was assigning the village duties to the novices, he had them put their upper robes over one shoulder, but he did not have them take head-coverings made of palm leaves; rather, he had them take only palm-leaf fans. One...
Having formed a group, he sat in the village of Tunnaga together with his retinue; thus he became known by the name "Tunnagaṇa.
However, that elder did not understand the intended meaning as it truly is within the texts of the Canon, the Commentaries, and the Sub-commentaries;
he merely sat there teaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka alone to his disciples.
And at that time, while the novice monks were entering the village, these four elders—the elder Buddhaṅkura and the elder Citta sitting in the city of Ketumatī;
the elder Sunanda sitting in the village of Uḷuka in the city of Dīpayaṅga;
and the elder Kalyāṇa in the village of Jeyyabahu in the city of Taluppāda—did not have them arrange their upper robes over one shoulder, nor did they have them remove the palm-leaf head-wraps.
Having had them take their seats, have them put on their robes, and have them take up palm-leaf fans, they sat down after giving instructions to the entire assembly.
Those elders, moreover, understood the intended meaning exactly as it was in the various texts of the Canon, the Commentaries, and the Sub-commentaries;
they were experts in all three Piṭakas. Thus it was during the time of King Sirimahāsīhasūrasudhamma.
The monks who wore upper robes having become divided and fallen into disarray, a group known as the Ekamsikas split off separately;
just as this [metal] here, rising from its base, becomes dissimilar and opposed.
Even while thus splitting into factions, the kings, being negligent and indifferent, sat about conducting themselves according to their own individual inclinations.
Among those two groups, the elders in the group wearing upper robes sat free from doubt and fault,
relying on statements expressed according to the explicit meaning (*nītattha*) found within the texts of the Canon, the Commentaries, the Sub-commentaries, and other treatises. However,

in the group of those with one shoulder bared, the elders [found that] their respective doctrines were not seen in the Canon, nor in the Commentaries, nor in the Sub-commentaries, nor even in other treatises.
Not understanding this matter, some said, "This alone is the truth; everything else is false," and gave counsel to their respective disciples.
Such disciples as these accepted the advice.
However, others, having realized that their own doctrines were not destined to appear in the scriptures and so forth, became troubled in mind regarding the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Without looking at the face of the Blessed One, and recollecting only the virtues of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, they realized that their own position was like a hand stretched out in mid-air—utterly without support.

Knowing this, they took as their patron even one who was not a patron, thinking, "Our doctrine is the lineage-source of the Elder Saddhammacāri, who has reached Laṅkā. They did so by means of falsehood.

They slandered the virtuous Mahāthera. Having given a bribe to an immoral lay follower named Phya—who was indifferent to matters pertaining to this life and the next and had returned to the lower life—they urged him, saying, "Compose a treatise in accordance with our own position.
Thus, they sought support, showing no fear of the suffering they would experience in the future.

At that time, a resident monk of the Nigrodhapāḷi Suvaṇṇavihāra, having formed a gathering of village-dwelling monks and acting as their leader, claimed that monks who did not wear head-cloths were inauspicious and would not remain within the Dispensation;
thus, he disrupted the lineage of forest-dwelling monks and ordained them from various places. Then, from the village of Hatthisālā...

Having thought, "While sitting in the monastery to the south of the Seṭṭhi tank in the southeast direction, we shall ordain more than fifty bhikkhus," he prepared the village-dwelling bhikkhus and departed.

Then, when the king heard of this matter, one group was the community of village-dwelling bhikkhus and the other was the community of forest-dwelling bhikkhus; they harassed the village-dwelling bhikkhus and the forest-dwelling bhikkhus.
He sent a royal decree stating that it was not possible [for all to stay together], and that each person must sit in their respective place according to their own school of thought (*vāda*).
Thereupon, the forest-dwelling monks (*araññavāsī-bhikkhu*) obtained the opportunity to dwell in comfort.

When more than one thousand seven hundred and sixty years of the *kaliyuga* had elapsed, the son of that king, named Mahāsīhasūradhammarājādhirāja, reigned. He alone is also known by the titles Sūrajjarāja and Setibhinda.

During the time of that king, a certain minister who was a leader within the royal court brought from the village of Lokanaga, a resident of Suvaṇṇayāna, a Thera named Ukkaṃsamāla; having arrived at Ratanapūra city, he had a monastery built on Suvaṇṇakukkuṭācala and established him there.
He was exceedingly proficient in the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, the Ṭīkās, and other literary works. He also composed a method of writing known as the *Vaṇṇabodhana*.
Furthermore, because his village had been granted by kings, his family was engaged in the maintenance of the Cetiya. Thus, for the sake of the king...
Having appointed him to the position of teacher, he dedicated [the robe] for the purpose of honoring him alone during the internal conflict.
Regarding this, some said that during the time of that king, when the novices were departing from the village, they should enter after putting it on;
others, however, said they should enter having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder. Thus, they quarreled with one another.

In that regard, the Elder named Ukkamsamāla, being preeminent among those who favor the wearing of the upper robe, declared that the rules for wearing the upper robe (*pārupana-vatta*) alone were recorded in various texts.
However, in the group favoring the single-shoulder style (*ekaṃsika*), the Great Elders residing at the Tiriyapabbata Monastery rejected the doctrine of wearing the upper robe,
on the grounds of demonstrating the lineage of their own teachers.
Then the king, having appointed these four elders— the elder who resided at the Phalikakhacita Monastery, the elder who resided at the Meghuñcana Monastery,
the elder Suhattha, and the elder Buddhaṅkura— to the position of adjudicators of the Vinaya, said: "Let the two factions present their respective arguments."
Furthermore, those four elders were unskilled in the texts of the Canon, the Commentaries, and the Sub-commentaries.
Indeed, they possessed no special quality other than being royal favorites for the purpose of serving as royal preceptors;
just as tigers, when seated in a difficult place concealed by trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth, are unable to seize even small and weak deer, so too were those [four] one-sided elders.
Because [the opponents] were dependent on texts that had not yet appeared during the time of the king, they were weak; nevertheless, they were unable to overcome them by means of their own arguments.

For this very reason, just as a wise warrior who, having recognized the strength of the enemy army, shows humility, makes peace, and sits down, so too the groups of robe-wearers sat down without bringing the debate to a conclusion.
When more than ninety-five thousand years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, his son named Mahārājādhipati reigned.
Later, when one hundred and thirteen thousand years had passed, the King of Rāmañña overcame him;
because he did not lead [the people] away [into exile], he became renowned as Pattahaṃsāvatī.
During the time of that king, having brought a senior elder named Ñāṇavara from the village of Jālayutta in the city of Kukhana, he appointed him to the position of preceptor.
That elder was exceedingly proficient in the texts of the Canon, the commentaries, the sub-commentaries, and other works.
For the sake of the listeners who were reciting the scriptures in the Sudhamma Hall, [he composed] the *Gaṇṭhipadattha* on the treatise *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
First he composed [the *Saddanīti*]. After that, he composed the *Gaṇṭhipadattha* and the *Surāvinicchaya* for the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
Subsequently, at the request of that king, he rendered the meaning of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* into the Maramma language.

Having adorned it with the name-seal of the king and embellished it with prosody, poetics, grammar, logic, and the methods of *daṇḍī* and *vyañjananaya*, he [composed] the *Rājādhirājanāmatthappakāsinī*.

He even composed a book. The king demolished the residence he had caused to be built in the place called Hatthisālā and, having constructed monasteries measuring one hundred [units], assigned names to all the monasteries as commemorative endowments and gave them to that very elder. By means of the names of these monasteries—
And that became the designation for the Elder as well.

At that time, during the reigns of both King Ayyaka and his father, because of a dispute between those two groups, the discussion—which had remained unresolved—was brought forward once more for the sake of settling the dispute; and in the Pārupana group, that Elder [spoke].
In the Ekaṃsika group, however, Pāsāṇatthera was the leader and conducted the battle accordingly.
Then the king placed the thera residing at the Jeyyabhūmi Suvaṇṇavihāra— who was exceedingly dear to the king— in the position of a Vinaya expert in order to adjudicate their dispute.
Although that elder was indeed somewhat knowledgeable regarding the texts, commentaries, and sub-commentaries, he remained unqualified among those expert in the higher teachings (pariyatti).
Nevertheless, because he was a favorite of the king, the king—without knowing the truth of the matter—appointed him to the position of a Vinaya-holder.
This was merely for the sake of defining the directions, such as "this is the eastern direction" and "this is the western direction," and so forth.
Just as one might place a ploughshare that has grown large at the tip of a plough in a royal palace at a place where legal disputes are to be adjudicated—

without knowing whether it is of such a kind or of such a kind— so too, because this Elder who dwells in the Jeyyabhūmi Suvaṇṇavihāra was placed in the position of a Vinaya-expert without [the King] knowing what he was like,
he [is the one who knows] the truth between these two sides in their two arguments.
It cannot be said that this was not real, for it existed even at the time he entered the gateless house.
Just as a buffalo standing nearby would perceive no difference whatsoever between the sounds of a divine musician singing celestial songs and playing a divine lute,
and those of a village boy striking a bamboo pole— so too is this.
The prosperity was to be observed. Then the king issued a royal decree stating:
"Whatever monks in my realm desire whatever [they wish], let those monks go and practice that, and then sit according to their respective duties. At that time, their dispute was not pacified.
Later, when one hundred thousand and thirteen years had passed, the city of Ratanapūra was destroyed.

Thereafter, in the second year, the King who had brought the city of Ratanaśikhara expelled the army of the King of Rāmañña from the barley fields by the power of his own merit— like driving a cātaka bird away—
and having brought the entire kingdom of Rāmañña under his own control, he reigned.
And at that time, he gladdened the hearts of all the inhabitants of the Maramma kingdom,
just as one might restore the greenness of night-lotuses withered by the sun’s heat by sprinkling them with water from Lake Anotatta; even so,
he restored the state of those householders and monks among the inhabitants of the Maramma kingdom who had fallen into suffering due to the heat of the armies of the Lord of the Rāmañña kingdom.
Having sprinkled himself with water heated by his own merit, he produced both kinds of happiness—bodily and mental.
And all the inhabitants of the Maramma kingdom addressed him as "This is our king, the Bodhisatta.
Then, on four Uposatha days during one month, having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and caused them to enter the inner palace, [he served them] with almsfood.
He provided them with food. Together with the royal concubines and ministers, he observed the Uposatha.
He caused all the royal concubines and ministers to recite the Triple Gem formula (guṇattaya-pāṭha) together with its word-by-word commentary.
Then, having brought the Elder of Beluvagāma, he established him in his own position as preceptor. Thus he was known as Mahā-Atula-Yasa Dhammarājaguru.
He also gave him a seal. From that time on, he became well known by the name Atula Thera.

At that time, Sūjāta Thera and others, who were residents of Pārupanagaṇa, Pakkhāpaliṇa, and Gāmavāsī villages, sent a message-letter to the King, stating that the novice monks should enter the village after having put on their robes, and they wrote this down as a formal instruction.

Then, even those such as the incomparable Theras, who belonged to the faction of the Ekaṃsikas, settled the legal dispute during the time of previous kings; now, having written a document stating that the matter already settled should not be raised again, they sent it to the king.

Then the king, although wishing to hear the respective arguments of both factions, said, "There is much business pertaining to the state affairs at present; let matters pertaining to the Sasana wait for now—let us attend only to what pertains to the state."
"I shall first undertake secular affairs, and afterwards I will perform duties connected with the Dispensation," he declared, and thus established his royal edict.
Later, however, the king issued this command: "Henceforth, let all the bhikkhus within my realm conduct themselves in accordance with the views of my teacher."
Then the group of monks who wore robes over one shoulder also followed the group that wore them on both shoulders, in accordance with the king’s command.

However, in the village of Sahassorodha, two great elders sat down after instructing their own assembly that they must fulfill the duty of entering the village while wearing their robes in the manner of the *pārupana* (both shoulders covered).
At that time, the king’s teacher, the elder Yasa, having heard of this matter, summoned them. They then arrived at the city.
At that time, a certain lay follower, having become full of faith, attended upon those elders with almsfood.
Then, the elder Atula brought sand from a distant place and had it scattered near the house of that lay follower.
This was a disciplinary action against those who were acting in a manner inconsistent with the Dhamma of the Vinaya; there was even a great outcry [regarding this].
He caused it to arise. Then, while they were still bringing sand, they conversed with one another:
"Venerable sirs, for us who are now acting in accordance with the Dhamma of the Vinaya, such work as this is unseemly; oh, how wonderful is this world-Dhamma!
said one elder. Then another elder spoke thus: "Friends, the world-protecting deities [are now...]"

"Having seen an illegal act (*adhammakamma*), it is not possible to remain sitting with indifference and little concern; one must think, 'Now the world-protecting deities (*lokapāla-deva*) are sitting here having become negligent.

At that very moment, a cloud suddenly arose, and lightning bolts struck simultaneously at the monastery of the Elder Atula and at the royal palace. Even though this was so, that elder did not regain his mindfulness due to his excessive pride and stubbornness."
Again, the king asked his ministers, "Do all the bhikkhus in my realm now follow the opinion of my teacher, or not?

The ministers reported to the king as follows: "Great King, there is currently a certain great elder named Munindaghosa residing in the village of Nīpa in the city of Kukhaṇa; he, by way of his own wearing of the upper robe..."
"Having exhorted the assembly and produced great merit, he sits down.

Then the king spoke thus: having summoned him and assembled the Great Elders in the Sudhamma Hall, let them instruct him by demonstrating the true nature of that Elder’s lack of knowledge regarding the Vinaya-paññatti as it really is.
Then the ministers did accordingly. And the Great Elders, having assembled in the Sudhamma Hall, summoned him.

They exhorted him. Among those great elders, one elder—looking toward the face of the protector of the earth, the King of the Saṅgha, but not looking toward the face of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—spoke thus to the Elder Munindaghosa:
"Friend, now all the bhikkhus in this land of Marammarāṭṭha [follow] the command of the protector of the earth, the King of the Saṅgha."
Having followed along, they all became one-sided; you alone, together with the assembly, sit having walked about wearing the cloth used for covering [the body].
But why do you remain thus, stubborn in pride, without abandoning such improper conduct?
Then the Elder Munindaghosa, looking directly at that elder’s face, spoke thus: "You are modest and gentle..."
"One who desires to train" means: I have heard this before; however, such a person is fit to speak such words, for such speech is appropriate for such a person.
Even if you, thinking of me as one of little merit, lacking in splendor, and without a protector, should wish to speak out of disrespect, even so, you must look upon the face of my teacher.
"Knowing the virtue of my teacher and remembering that he is his disciple, it would not be possible for him to speak such unrighteous words.
Then the Elder asked him, "But who is your teacher? Thereupon, having enlarged upon the image of the Buddha placed in the Sukhama Hall, he said, "This is my teacher.
Having said, "He is my teacher," he rose up in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks.
Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, sitting down on his heels, and raising his joined palms in salutation,
he declared: "Venerable Sir, for as long as life lasts, I shall sacrifice even my own life, but I shall never abandon the training precepts of the Blessed One,
the Supreme One in the World."
Then the king, having heard that matter, thought, "This man is arrogant and haughty; it is fitting that he be seated within my own realm, but he must be sent away to another kingdom.
By royal command, the king dispatched him to another kingdom. The king’s men summoned him and led him away to that other kingdom.
Upon reaching a place called Bahaṅga, a man who was the leader of Bahaṅga gave a bribe to the king’s men and spoke thus: "But, sirs, this is merely a border district of the Maramma kingdom."
"Leave him right here and turn back.
The king’s men, having taken the bribe, left him right there and returned.
The Elder, for his part, gave exhortation regarding the wearing of robes to the monks and novices who had come from the four quarters, and after teaching them the scriptures, he remained there.
He sat down. He also composed a word-for-word commentary (*atthayojanā*) on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* in the Maramma language.
Later, when the king heard of this matter, he said, "Now that elder has sat down right within the borders of my kingdom and performed an act we did not desire—namely, he prohibited [our work].
Summon him! The royal messengers went there and summoned him. The elder, thinking, "The king now wishes to have me executed," [reflected thus:]...
Having renounced the training and put on the clothes of a householder, he came along with them.
But having arrived at the city, he brought him into the presence of the king at the appropriate time.
Then the king said: "I have heard that you were sitting there as a monk, increasing the community; why is this?"

"But now you have become a householder. "Great King, if you had summoned me while desiring to kill me, then had you killed me while I remained without having renounced the training, it would have been a grave deed for you.
Considering this, and for the sake of ensuring that your deed was not so grave, I have come here after renouncing the training. If you [should kill] me..."
"If you wish to kill me, then kill me. The king, having placed him in prison, departed for the sake of waging war against the kingdom of Siam.
However, upon his return from the campaign, he passed away on the very road.
Now, when one hundred and twenty-two years of the Kali Age had elapsed, his eldest son, Siripavaramahādhammarāja—
He ruled by that name. Because he moved from the city of Ratanasikhā and established Jeyyapura as his second capital, he was also known by the title King Jeyyapurameka.
At that time, having brought the Elder Ñāṇa, a resident of the city within the Great Mountain, he appointed him to the position of preceptor.
That elder, possessed of profound wisdom, [taught] nine or ten [discourses] in a single day.

He was capable of reciting even a single *bhāṇavāra* by heart. At the very time of his recent full ordination (*upasampadā*), he composed in the Maramma language (Burmese) a word-by-word analysis of the texts, as well as commentaries on the *Nyāsa*, the *Yamaka*, and the *Mahāpaṭṭhāna*.
King Mahābhūmi had a monastery named Ramaṇīyavihāra built and bestowed it upon him. [This was] Ñāṇālaṅkāra Mahādhammarājaguru.
He gave him a certain mark as well.
At that time, the elders in the group of those who wore robes thought thus:
"Now our preceptor has become the king's teacher; now we shall gain a firm footing. Having thought this, [they acted] toward the novices...
At the time of entering the city, [the monks] put on their robes and entered; thus they sent a letter of communication into the presence of the king.
Then the Elder Atula sent a letter of communication into the presence of the king, stating that "this is the karma that has been pacified according to the method previously described.
For this very reason, they did not find an opportunity to show each other's replies to one another.
Thereafter, when one thousand two hundred and twenty-five years had elapsed in the Kali Age, that king named Siripavarasudhammamahārājindādhipati reigned.
Because he was the builder of the third [shrine], Ratanapūra, he was known as Ratanapūramāpaka;
and because he was the master of the elephant-king Chaddanta, he was also known by the name Setibhinda. And Caracca was a village-dweller of Candāvara.
Having summoned the Elder Nāma, he appointed him to the position of his own teacher. He had a monastery named Sūmikittiatula constructed and gave it to him.
He also bestowed upon him the title and seal of *Jambudīpa-anantadhaja-mahādhammarājaguru*.
During the time of that king, some people fell into erroneous views; the king summoned them as well and established them in right view.
He caused it to be taken up. However, during the time of that king, they did not find an opportunity to overcome the Ekaṃsika sect.
Subsequently, when one thousand three hundred and thirty-eight years had elapsed in the Kali Age, the son of that king, named Mahādhammarājādhirāja, reigned.
To the southern side of the city, he [built] a five-storied monastery.
Having had it constructed and designated by the name Jeyyabhūmivāsātula, he gave it to the elder named Mārāvaṭṭana.
He also bestowed upon him the title and seal of *Guṇamunindābhisāsanadhajamahādhammarājādhirājaguru*.
And at that time, the elder named Nandamāla was residing in a monastery in the eastern direction of the city of Calaṅga.
He taught the texts to many bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras. He frequently gave this advice: "When entering a village, sāmaṇeras must enter only after fulfilling the rule for wearing the upper robe;

however, the practice of wearing the robe over one shoulder is not found in the Canon (Pāḷi), nor in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), nor in the Sub-commentaries (Ṭīkā), nor in other texts, and it is not in accordance with the Dhamma. [This is stated] in the Canon, the Commentaries, and so forth.
Having presented his definitive judgment, he composed a single treatise.
Then, the proponents of the Ekamsika school had that treatise introduced to the presence of the king for the purpose of exposing its faults.
At that time, the king saw such a dream: Sakka, the king of the gods, having dressed himself in white garments...
Having adorned herself with white ornaments and wearing white flowers, she approached the king and spoke thus: "Great King, in the Aparanta country,
on the bank of the Nammadā River at the Pādacetiya, many blades of grass have grown up, standing joined to one another—
root to root, stem to stem, and leaf to leaf— so as to completely conceal them."
"However, those [relics] were not purified by previous kings because they did not know them as they truly are;
now, you who know them as they truly are and desire to make them perfectly pure must purify them. And in that matter, one monk will come and provide instruction.
Having seen such a dream, he summoned the Elder named Nandamāla and had him reside in a royal palace built near the city of Ratanapūra for the purpose of sporting in the water.
Then the Elder informed the King— just as the Elder Mahāmoggaliputta Tissa informed King Siridhammāsoka— that according to the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, the Ṭīkā, and other texts,
one must enter the village while wearing the robes at the time of entering. Then the King, who possessed a vast accumulation of merit from the perfections (pāramī) and great wisdom,
understood that among the Pāḷi, Aṭṭhakathā, Ṭīkā, and other texts, it is indeed the "wearing of the robes" (pārupana-vāda) [that is correct].
However, the doctrine of exclusivity (ekaṃsikavāda) is not found anywhere among them.
Having understood this, he had the two groups of elders assembled at the king’s palace and had each state his own position.
Then the Elder Ekamsika said, "Where is your doctrine of wearing the upper robe (pārupana) recorded? At that time, the Elders who supported wearing the robe...
They said that the discourse on wearing the robe appears in various texts such as the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathās, and the Ṭīkās, according to the method beginning with "I shall wear it rounded.
Thereafter, the Pārupana Theras spoke thus: "But where does your discourse on the 'one-shoulder' (ekaṃsika) appear?
Then, at that time, the Ekaṃsika Theras were like those who had entered a house without a door, [standing] on the great forest path during the night.

Being as if on the verge of departing, they were unable to say anything at all. Since it is said that "the mouth exists for the purpose of speaking and for the purpose of eating," even though they spoke this or that, they were unable to please the king.
And the king, owing to his proficiency in the Vinaya derived from his reliance on the Elder, [realized] that such indeed is how it appears in the Pāḷi, and in the Aṭṭhakathās and other texts.

Having said, "It is exactly like this," he asked: "Your categorical doctrine is not seen in the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathās, or other commentaries; even though it is so, why did they perform such a practice?
Then those Ekamsika Theras, being unable to say anything—like thieves caught with the stolen goods in a four-cubit room, or like crows driven away by people—[fell silent].
Having looked in all directions, they said, "Our conduct has never before been seen in the Pāḷi or other texts; nevertheless, we have practiced solely according to the tradition of our teachers.
Having thus suffered defeat, they entered the ranks of those who wear the upper robe.
And the king issued a royal decree that from now on, monks should cause the novices to be instructed only in the practice of wearing the upper robe.
He established [them]. From that time forth, the theras of the Ekamsika faction were unable even to raise their heads from their couches at the time of sunrise.

Having caused to be built to the east of the Mahācetiya at Sōkāsarabhū a four-storied monastery adorned with two palaces and named Bhūmikittivirāma, he gave it to the thera Nandamāla, who was the preceptor of the Great King Dhammarāja, whose secret name was Narinda.
He also gave him the name Alaṅchi. That elder, moreover, should be understood as Chappadavaṃsi.
At the very time of his full ordination, he composed a word-for-word commentary (*atthayojanā*) on the *Vinayavinicchaya*, the *Suttasaṅgaha*, and the *Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā* in the Maramma language;
he also composed a work titled the *Sāsanasuddhidīpikā*.

Thereafter, when one thousand four hundred and forty-three years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phagguna, the middle son of King Ratana-sikhāmāpaka reigned.
At that time, the king thought thus: "The dispute arising from the practice of wearing robes in a single shoulder (ekamsika-pārupana) could not be settled during the time of previous kings;
even during the time of the great sovereign King Siripavara-Sudhamma, having assembled [the people] in the royal palace..."
Because he spoke in the presence of the king, and because he had not been granted the opportunity to speak freely—having failed to obtain the chance to speak as he wished—he was defeated;

thus there might have been an occasion for him to cast a pretext. However, in my time, instead of doing such a thing, I shall send messengers to the monasteries of those various elders and have them state their respective doctrines; for if that were the case, [there would be no such pretext].
"The elders will speak freely," he thought. Having thus reflected, he made the minister Antoyudhanāyaka his chief agent;
going to each of those elders in turn, he had him announce: "Speak freely according to your own respective doctrines. Then the elders, like courtesans who have been given exclusive rights, [spoke].
"The words spoken by us are not found in the Pāḷi or other texts; nevertheless, we have acted solely according to the tradition of our teachers," they replied.

And when the Great King had thus received the elders' consent, he felt there was nothing further to be done; now, as for the training rules concerning the complete roundness and the proper covering [of robes]...
He sent royal edicts here and there, stating: "Let the novices enter the village without causing disturbance.

Later, however, having brought from Sahassorodhagāma a monk named Ñāṇa—who was seven years senior by the number of rains since his full ordination—and having had the monastery named Antoyudhavihāra built, he gave it to him;
[Ñāṇa] was known as the Great Dhamma Preceptor of the King, the Banner of the Ñāṇābhisāsa lineage.
He also gave him a name-ornament. Then, when requested by the king, he purified the *Rājābhisheka* manual and composed its commentary in the Maramma language.

Later, while the Blessed One was still living, he arrived there, tamed four *yakṣas*, accepted the meat-rice offered by them, went to a region near the mountain, ate it, and after surveying that place, manifested a smile.
Then the Elder Ānanda asked for the reason. He replied: "Ānanda, in the future there will be a great city in this place, and these four yakkhas will become kings in that city.
In accordance with that very prophecy, when one hundred thousand and four hundred and forty-four years of the Kali Age had elapsed, [the city arose].
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, on a Tuesday in conjunction with the lunar mansion Uttaraphagguṇī, he founded the capital city named Amarapura.
He also received the title and insignia: *Siri-Paravijayānantayaśas-tribhuvanādityādhipati-paṇḍita-mahādhammarājādhirāja*.
He gave to the Elder Guṇābhilaṅkāra Saddhammamahādhammarājādhirājaguru—the one known as "Me O Sayāḍo"—the monastery named Jeyyabhūmi-vihārakitti, which had been caused to be built by the Chief Queen.

He gave to the Elder Guṇamunindādhipati Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru—the one known as "Māṃ Le Sayāḍo"—the monastery named Vihāraramaṇīyavirāma, which had been caused to be built by the Princess who was the Bhojaka of Kannīnagara.
He bestowed upon the Elder Tipiṭaka Saddhammasāmī Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru—the one known as “Soṃ Ṭhā Sayāḍo”—the monastery named Maṅgalāvirāma, which had been built by Queen Uparaññā.

He bestowed upon the Elder Ñāṇajambudīpa Anantadhaja Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru—the one known as “Meṃ Jvā Sayāḍo”—the monastery named Maṅgalāvāsātula, which had been built by the Queen who resided in the middle house.
Furthermore, he appointed these four great elders to the position of Saṅgharāja.
He gave to the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Kavinda, who was known as “Ñyoṃ Kāṃ Sayāḍo,” the monastery named Maṅgalabhūmikitti, which had been built by the queen residing in Uttarageha.
He gave to the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Kavinda, who was known as “Sve Ṭoṃ Sayāḍo,” the monastery named Atulabhūmivāsa, which had been built by the prince who was the governor of Sirikhettanagara.
He gave the monastery caused to be built by one of his ministers to the Elder Ñāṇālaṅkārasaddhammadhajamahādhammarājaguru, who is called “Seṃ Ṭe Sayāḍo.
He gave the monastery caused to be built by the minister Vāmabalanāyaka to the Elder Paramasirivaṃsadhajamahādhammarājaguru, who is called “Me Ṭhī Sayāḍo.”
He gave a monastery, constructed by a minister who was a judge of the Dhamma, to the Elder who was the preceptor of the Great Dhammarājādhirāja Kavinda Sāradhaja, who is called “Lokāmhāṃ Keṃ Sayāḍo.
Thus, having bestowed the monastery along with the names and insignia of many great Elders who were experts in the scriptures, he showed his favor.
However, because it would be too much to mention the names of all the Elders individually, they have been omitted.
"This narrative, *Sāsanavaṃsappadīpikā*, will become excessively prolix; therefore, disregarding it here, I shall speak only what ought to be said.
Later on, four great elders (mahātheras), due to the weakness of the king, will be able to purify the Dispensation according to their wish."
Having reflected thus, he further appointed eight elders, together with these four great elders, to the position of leaders of the Saṅgha in order to purify the Dispensation.

They were as follows: the Elder Kavindābhisaḍḍhamma-pavara-mahādhammarājaguru, the Elder Tipiṭakālaṅkāra-dhaja-mahādhammarājaguru, the Elder Cakkindābhidhaja-mahādhammarājaguru, and the Elder Paramasirivaṃsa-dhaja-mahādhammarājaguru.

[They were] the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Janindābhivara, the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Mahāñāṇābhidhaja, the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Ñāṇālaṅkārasaddhammadhaja, and the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Ñāṇābhisāsanadhaja. Then, although he was an Arahant, [he thought:
"It is not permissible to live without a preceptor and teacher, as one would be deficient in the factor of being released from formal dependence (nissaya)."
Having understood this, he had the elders who were capable of providing guidance fulfill the requirements for granting *nissaya* and the requirements for lifting that *nissaya*;
then, having obtained *nissaya* from those who were dependent [upon him], he had them sit down.

Subsequently, when more than five hundred years of the Kali Age had passed—specifically upon the arrival of the year one thousand—he [appointed] the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru, the banner of the Abhisāsanadhaja, as his preceptor alone.
He appointed one [monk] to the position of Saṅgharāja. From that time forth, he alone became the leader of the Saṅgha and purified the Dispensation.

Subsequently, when more than one hundred and fifty-five years had passed, in the month of Phagguna, in the Asokārāma—which was surrounded by two brick walls and consisted of five stories—located to the south of the Mahāmuni Cetiya...
Having caused the construction of an exceedingly vast monastery named Ratanabhūmikitti, he presented it to the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Ñāṇābhisāsanadhajathera.
He further bestowed upon him the title-ornament of Ñāṇābhivaṃsadhammasenāpatimahādhammarājādhirājaguru.
Subsequently, he granted that same elder many other monasteries, such as Jayabhūmivihāra, Kittimaṅgalavirāma, and others.

In those monasteries, he sat by turn and taught the scriptures (pariyatti). He also committed both the Vibhaṅgas to memory. He constantly undertook the practice of eating at a single sitting (ekāsanika) and living as a forest-dweller (dhujaṅga).

That elder, having reached five years of seniority since his full ordination (upasampadā), even before becoming the Sangharāja, composed a new commentary on the Nettippakaraṇa known as the *Peṭakālaṅkāra*. At the age of eight, he became the Sangharāja. [He was] the Sangharāja.
Having offered [this], he composed the *Dīghanikāya-ṭīkā* named *Sādhujjanavilāsinī*. He also composed the treatise named *Ariyavaṃsālaṅkāra*.

At the request of King Mahādhammarāja, he composed the *Atthayojanā* on the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, the *Catusāmaṇeravatthu*, the *Rājovādavatthu*, the *Tigumbhathomana*, the *Chaddantanāgarājuppattikathā*, and the *Rājādhirājavilāsinī*.
He also composed works such as the *Nāmagrantha*.
However, when one thousand six hundred and sixty-two years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed,
there were six novices from the island of Sri Lanka named Ampa Gahapati, Mahādampa, Kocchagodha, Brāhmaṇavatta, Bhogahavatta, and Vāturagamma.
The ten dhātu-dhamma-plates were brought for the sake of the royal seal and arrived at the capital city named Amarapura together with a lay devotee (upāsaka). Then,
by Saṅgharaja, the Preceptor (upajjhāya) and Great Dhamma-King of the Lord of the Dhamma-Senāpati Ñāṇābhivaṃsa...

He had the ordination ceremony performed at the Hatthirajjasuvaṇṇaguha boundary by such royal preceptors as the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Kavindābhisaddhammadhara, the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Janindābhijaha,
and the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru Munindaghosa; and he [admitted] the lay follower into the state of a novice.
He established [the community], and thereafter he caused numerous monks who arrived on many occasions to receive the training once again,
had the novice monks undergo the ceremony of full ordination (*upasampadā*), and had the lay devotees undergo the ceremony of going forth (*pabbajjā*). Later,
when the Kali Age had reached one thousand four hundred and forty-six years, during the reign of his father, the King...
The Elder named Atula, formerly a teacher, sent a letter to the King, insisting that when novices go out into the village,
they must enter only after having arranged their upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over one shoulder and fastened the waist-band (urabandhanavattha),
because it is stated in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* that "having made the robe-fabric into an upper saṅghāṭi, the waist-band cloth is to be fastened."
Then the king, having heard that, had the great theras assembled in the Sudhamma Hall and engaged them in discussion with the Thera Atula.

Thereupon, the Thera Atula, having arranged a piece of cloth for his robe as an upper *saṅghāṭi* and showing the text found in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* stating that the waist-binding cloth (*urabandhanavattha*) must be tied, [spoke] at the time when the novices were entering the village.
"Having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder and fastened the waist-cloth, one should enter," he said.
Then the great elders asked him: "Is such an intention seen elsewhere, or not? Then the Elder Atula replied:
"But such an intention is not seen elsewhere. [The others said: "Let it be so; by whom was this text [composed]?"
"Where? [It was] in the village of Pokkanta, in the southern region of Anurādhapura on the island of Siṃhala, by the Arahant Thera Moggallāna.
How is this matter to be known? Because it is recorded in the *Piṭakattaya-lakkhaṇa* treatise. And from where was this *Piṭakattaya-lakkhaṇa* treatise obtained?
It is said that because it was brought from the island of Siṃhala by the Thera Buddhaghosa, it was obtained from there.
"This book was composed by the Elder Buddhaghosa for the purpose of identifying which of the books he himself brought from the island of Sri Lanka were written by which Elder;
now this book is found in our hands. "If this book is now found in your hands, show it to us. "Look, friends!"
"This is our manuscript," he showed. Then, when the Great Elders, headed by the Saṅgharāja, had examined that manuscript, it was found to state:
"The *Vinayagaṇṭhipada* was composed by the Elder Moggalāna during the time of King Parakkamabāhu in the island of Sīhaḷa;
[it does not state] that the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* was [composed] in the village of Pokkanta, in the southern region of Anurādhapura, in the island of Sīhaḷa."
"The Arahant Elder Moggallāna did it.
Then the elders said: "But why do you speak falsely, making as if what has not been included in the texts characterizing the Three Piṭakas were actually included?
Does not the training rule against lying exist even for you, the Ekasīka bhikkhus?"
Then, because he was unable to say anything further, the Elder Atula stood trembling like a deer caught in a hunter’s snare;
seized by his own act of falsehood, the elder was captured along with the lie itself.
This is the story told for the purpose of illustrating this point.
It is said that in this kingdom, a certain inhabitant of the countryside came to the great royal capital city named Amarapura on some business.
Having arrived, at the time of his return, his provisions for the journey were exhausted along the way.
Then it occurred to him: "Now my provisions for the journey are exhausted; it is said that in this kingdom..."
In the village of Sahassorodha, there was a great merchant named Laddhavara who was exceedingly famous throughout the entire earth.

"I shall deceive them by saying, 'He is my kinsman. If this is done, the people of that village will provide me with abundant gains to establish a friendship with that great merchant; thus, I shall have no difficulty regarding provisions for the journey. Thinking thus, he—
Having reflected thus, he searched for the houses of those of great wealth in every village he encountered along the way;
entering into the presence of those wealthy people, he engaged them in conversation.
Then those villagers asked him: "From where have you come? Where are you going? Whose relative are you, or who are you?"
"I have come from the capital city of Amarapūra; I am going to the village of Sahassorodha.
I am the son-in-law of a great merchant named Laddhavara in Sahassorodha, and my name is Dhanavaddhaka," he said.
Then the villagers of that village, wishing to establish a friendship with the great merchant Laddhavara, fed him with various kinds of food.
They also showed him hospitality with many other kinds of gifts.
Following this same method, he traveled along the road, deceiving the various villages he reached by speaking of his own virtues. Later, however, he arrived at the village of Sahassorodha.
He had never before been to the village of Sahassorodha, nor had the Great Merchant, who had received the boon, ever seen him.
As soon as he arrived at the village of Sahassorodha, without even asking what the name of that village was,
he searched for a large house belonging to someone of great wealth. Finding the vast residence of a merchant who had received a boon,
he entered the presence of that boon-recipient merchant and engaged in conversation with him.
Then the great merchant asked him: "From where have you come? Where will you go? Whose relative are you?
Who are you? He replied: "I have come from the great capital city of Amarapura, Master; I am going to the village of Sahassorodha.
I am the son-in-law of the great merchant named Laddhavara in the village of Sahassorodha, and my name is Dhanavaddhaka."
Then the great merchant, looking straight at his face, thought: "This young man is indeed from Sahassorodhagāma;
I too am a great merchant who has received a boon. I have daughters, but they are already married and now live with their respective husbands.
You have never been seen by me before—for what reason [have you come]?"
"From where have you come to become my son-in-law? she asked.
Then, like a deer being pursued by men, he made his entire body tremble; not knowing what words to speak and finding no foothold for himself, he thought:
"If this is the case, from where have I come, where shall I go, and to whom [do I belong]?"
"Kinsman, who indeed am I? Now I know not; I am utterly bewildered in every direction. Forgive my offense!
From this moment until the end of my life, I shall not deceive you; I am unable to deceive you. Now I am exceedingly afraid;
do not inflict any punishment upon me. Having spoken thus, he rose up in haste and fled.
Thus, having become sullen and having uttered whatever came to his lips in lamentation, the Elder Atula sat down in the midst of the Saṅgha.
This was the first defeat of the Elder Atula.
Thereafter, as if treading further upon a man who had stumbled and fallen into the mud, the great elders...

They asked thus: "Venerable sir, is this *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* of yours the same *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* shown according to the authority of the three great Vinaya commentaries (*vinayamahāṭīkā*), or is it another?
[The response was: "This is indeed the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* shown according to the authority of the three great Vinaya commentaries.
If that is so, why is it that it is stated only in your *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* [and not in others], as it is found in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*?
For it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā*: "Likewise, it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā*";
thus, after those [earlier] great commentaries on the Vinaya, three great commentaries on the Vinaya are presented as supporting evidence.
However, by asking in this way, he [the opponent] refers only to the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*, which was previously shown by me as the supporting evidence among the three great commentaries on the Vinaya.
"This statement is indeed true," he said again and again so that his mouth would not remain empty.
And this is the narrative for the purpose of clarifying this meaning:
It is said that a certain man, together with a companion, took service under a king for the sake of supporting a wife and children.
He went to battle to engage in warfare. Then, having fought against the enemy army and having overcome them, all the men fled to their respective positions facing away from him.
Thereupon, that man also fled toward his own position along with his companion.
Having fled a short distance, on the way he was struck by a staff hurled by the enemy troops.
Having become unconscious, that man was unable to go with him, nor even able to sit down.
Then it occurred to his companion: "Now this man is exceedingly gravely ill and close to death;
if I were to attend upon him and sit right here, my enemies will come and seize me. Thinking thus...
Having reflected thus, he took the coins, clothing, and other belongings belonging to the sick man, and having left them right there, he departed.
When he reached the vicinity of his own place, this thought occurred to him:
"If I were to say, 'I am coming after leaving it on the way,' his relatives will cast blame upon me; now that he has died, I am all alone."
"I shall say, 'I am coming. But when he reached his own place, his wife came to him and asked, "Where has my husband gone? Why have you come alone, leaving him behind?
[He replied,] "Noble lady, your husband was struck by the weapon of another and has passed away; these are your husband's belongings."
Having said this, and having given her coins, cloth, and other items, he comforted her, saying: "Do not grieve, do not lament;
now, after providing the funeral meal, simply distribute the portion of merit. Then she took those things, wept, provided the funeral meal, and distributed the portion of merit.
Later, when some time had passed, he recovered from his illness and was returning to his own home. His wife—

She did not believe him. He said, "I have not died; he merely left me while I was ill and took my possessions and departed. If you do not believe me, I shall hide myself within the inner chamber and remain there; summon him and ask.
Then she summoned him and, sitting outside the chamber, asked, "Master, is it true or false that your husband has died? "It is indeed true," he replied, "that your husband has died."
Then that man, having gone out from the womb and extended his finger, said:
"Now, sirs, I am not dying even in the slightest degree; why then do you say of me, who am not dying at all, 'He is dead'?
Then, because no reason could be given for what was being said, he extended his finger merely to fill the void of the mouth and looked straight ahead.
"Now, although you are capable of coming here, you are as good as dead; the words 'you are dead' which I have spoken are indeed true, for I do not say anything false," he said.
Although he spoke thus again and again, because [the opponent] was still living and present before his very eyes, no one believed his words; he simply met with defeat.
Thus, although the Elder Atula spoke for the sake of emptiness of the mouth, no one believed him;
he met with defeat alone. This was the second defeat of the Elder Atula.
Furthermore, just as a hunter, upon seeing an elephant, pierces it with a single arrow and [sees] it falling...
Furthermore, an elephant is pierced with spears several times for the purpose of training it;

in the same way, the Great Theras who uphold the *pārupana* (the tradition of wearing robes) have said this in order not to abandon a debate that has already been defeated in a single instance, so as to bring about its defeat through several further rounds:
"In your own *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*, [you state] that for novices, the robes must be perfectly circular and well-concealed, and so forth."

Having previously stated that one must enter only after breaking the *vatta* (formal observances), it was further said that one should fold the robe-cloth into a layer and fasten the waist-band like a collar;
why, however, was this stated without reconciling it with what preceded?
It is because, in your own system, there is an absence of the canonical texts, commentaries, sub-commentaries, and other treatises that serve as your refuge.

Having said, "You say that the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* is our refuge, yet fear arises from that very *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* which is your refuge," they seized those who spoke contrary to the Dhamma along with their supporters, just as one would seize a thief caught together with his place of concealment.
This is the narrative for the purpose of explaining this matter:
It is said that in the past, not far from Bārāṇasī, there lived on the bank of a river in a village a dancing-master named Pāṭali.
On a festival day, having taken his wife with him, he entered Bārāṇasī and, after dancing, playing the lute, and singing, [obtained] wealth.
Having obtained a great quantity of liquor and food at the conclusion of the festival, he set out for his own village;
upon reaching the riverbank, seeing the fresh water approaching, he sat down to eat his meal and drink his liquor.
Becoming intoxicated and unaware of his own strength, he tied a large lute around his neck and thought, "I shall go down into the river."
Taking his wife by the hand, he descended into the river. Water entered through the holes of his lute.
Then she caused him to sink into the water. But his wife, perceiving that he was sinking, let go of him, and having crossed over, stood on the riverbank.
Naṭapāṭali rose up once and sank down once; having entered the water, his belly became bloated.
It happened thus. Then his wife thought: "My husband will die now;
having requested a single song, I shall sustain my life by singing it in the midst of the assembly. Having thought this, she said, "Husband, you are submerging yourself in the water;
give me one song, for with that I shall sustain my life."
“The learned one, skilled in speech—the Gaṅgā carries away the *pāṭali* tree!
O venerable sir, as it is being swept away, give me a single verse.
Then he said to her, “O lady Pāṭali, how can I give you my song? Now the water, which has become a refuge for the great multitude, is killing me!”
"With that which they sprinkle the suffering one, with that which they sprinkle the afflicted one—
in the midst of that I shall die, for there is fear born from taking refuge. Then, the Elder Atula,
having developed fear regarding his own refuge based on the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*, not knowing what to say, stood with his head bowed, defeated.
This was the third defeat of the Elder Aytula.

Then the King, having heard the words of those two factions, [concluded] that because the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* was confused by the fault of internal contradictions between earlier and later passages, because it did not enter into the Suttas or the Suttānuloma and so forth, and because it lacked purity of scripture (*āgama*), [it was invalid]. Over a hundred years ago...

Realizing that the Teaching would now become pure after understanding its instability—due to its extreme weakness, like a house that has stood for a long time—he was filled with joy and issued a command:
"Let all the bhikkhus within my realm be of one voice regarding the wearing of the robes.
From that time until the present day, throughout the entire land of Burma, [the practice] has been carried out by way of the wearing of the robes.
"They become litigants. This is the summary here;

for if the debate between those two parties, consisting of their mutual exchange of words and counter-words, were to be stated in detail, it would not reach a conclusion even after five or six hundred turns.
However, since this *Sāsanavaṃsappaṭipakā* would become excessively prolix if everything were recounted without exception,
I shall therefore show here only what is intended and remain indifferent to the rest.
As for the Saṅgharāja Mahāthera, the preceptor of the Great Dhamma King Ādhirāja Ñāṇābhivaṃsa-Dhammasenāpati in the island of Sīhaḷa:
The teacher who was the foremost and most beneficial among the monks of the Amarapura Nikāya was [Sudhammasīha].

The Amarapura Nikāya originated from that elder. Then, when one thousand eight hundred and eighty-one years of the Kaliyuga had elapsed, the king’s grandson named Siri Tribhuvanāditya Pavarapaṇḍita Mahādhammarājādhirāja reigned.
Having moved from Amarapura, he established Ratanapūra as his fourth capital.

During that king’s reign, he appointed the elder named Sīlācāra— a forest-dwelling monk residing in the village of Sajīva and a disciple of the venerable Guṇamunindādhipati Mahādhammarājādhirāja— as the leader of the forest-dwelling bhikkhus.
Having had a monastery built in the place called Rājāgāra, he gave it to him.
When one thousand six hundred and eighty-one years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed,

he brought the Elder named Paññāsīha from Calañga and established him in the Ratanabhūmikittivihāra at the Asokārāma; he also bestowed upon him the title Munindābhisiri-Saddhammadhaja-Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru.
When one hundred and forty-four years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, he bestowed upon him the title *Munindābhivaṃsadhammasenāpati-Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru*,
granted him the monastery named Mahājeyyabhūmivihārarammaṇīya,
and installed that very great elder in the position of Saṅgharāja.
And on one occasion, the king questioned the great elders: "Are the so-called four tusks included among the forty teeth, or are they distinct from the forty teeth?
Then some elders said, "The so-called four tusks are included among the forty teeth.
But others said, "The so-called four tusks are distinct from the forty teeth. Then the king...
"Bring the text," he said. Then the elders who were experts in the scriptures brought the text, [saying]:
"While others have thirty-two teeth even when their dentition is complete, this one will have forty.
Regarding "teeth": for one with a complete set of teeth, there are thirty-two bone-teeth. These, by way of color, are white; by way of shape, they are of various shapes.
For in their case, first, in the middle of the lower row of teeth, there are four teeth shaped like gourd seeds placed in succession upon a lump of clay;
on both sides of these, there is one tooth each with a single root and a single point, shaped like a jasmine bud;
beyond that, there is one tooth each with two roots and two points, shaped like the linchpin of a chariot; and then there are two teeth each with three roots.
There are three triads; then two sets of four-rooted tetrad-questions each. The same method applies to the upper row of teeth as well.

It is said that because his upper lip was small, it appeared as if it had been sliced off horizontally and half-removed; furthermore, he could not cover four of his teeth and two of his fangs, and for that reason people called him Oṭṭhaddha (Small-Lipped).
In this context, "his" refers to the royal prince named Licchavi; "because his upper lip was small" refers to the upper lip.
"Because it is small. "It appears as if half has been removed" means that it looks as though the upper half of the upper lip has been taken away.
"It does not cover" means that it does not conceal even the upper half of the upper lip.
For this reason—because it does not cover the four teeth and the two fangs—they call that Licchavi prince "Oṭṭhaddha" (Half-Lip).
Thus, when the Theras brought forward and demonstrated the texts containing these internal arguments, everyone established themselves in that doctrine.

And at one time, the king asked his minister, the counselor: "Do the fields, lands, and so forth given by former kings to a monastery or a cetiya remain established as given during the time of later kings, or not?
Then the counselor-minister spoke thus: "They plant private seeds upon land belonging to the Saṅgha."
Regarding the statement that "they should be used after giving a portion," since it is stated in the Vinaya Piṭaka and its commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "having divided [the field] into ten parts,
one part must be given to the owners of the ground," fields, lands, and so forth that were previously granted by one king remain,
during the time of a subsequent king, exactly as they were granted. For in this context, it is said "of land belonging to the Saṅgha."

Just as in the case of the boundary for gains (*lābhasīmā*), because it was given together with the land without offering a separate oblation (*bali*), it is understood that there exists land belonging to the Saṅgha by way of tradition.
And here, when the recipients have passed away, the Saṅgha of the four quarters and the future Saṅgha are the owners; it belongs to them and must be administered by them.
Even a monastery given for the purpose of lighting lamps at a cetiya or for its maintenance must be tended;

or, even without receiving wages, one should have it tended. Furthermore, since it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that when repairing a damaged parasol or railing at a cetiya, or when performing work such as plastering, one should have it done using funds set aside for the cetiya, [this applies] by the previous kings.
It should be understood that the fields, lands, and so forth given to the Cetiya remained as the property of the Cetiya even during the time of later kings.
Furthermore, he asked again: "Starting from the time of which king, and at what period, were the fields, lands, and so forth given to the monastery or the Cetiya?"
Then the minister spoke thus: "It should be understood that these were given even in former aeons, in the time of former kings.

For this very reason, when our Bodhisatta was the wheel-turning monarch Sujāta, he gave the seven treasures, along with the four great continents and two thousand small islands, to the Blessed One named Sujāta; and so did the inhabitants of the realm."
It is recorded in the texts that he also had the park-keepers perform their duties; therefore, it should be understood that from long ago, fields, lands, and so forth, were granted by previous kings.
Furthermore, in the royal chronicles, more than a hundred years after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, in the city of Sirikhettanagara, a certain cake-seller...
A field measuring five *karīsa* was given to a single elder; King Dvattapoṅka plundered and seized it.
Then, although the hand-bells and drums were struck, they made no sound. Even the king’s spear-wheel did not go to the place where it had been sent, just as before.
Having understood the reason for this, [he gave] to the baker exactly what had been given.
"He entrusted it to the Elder.
Then, when one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, his younger brother, Siripavarādityalokāpeta Vijayamahādhammarājādhirāja, reigned;
that king, having moved from Ratanapura, [established himself] in Amarapura.

He built a second [monastery]. In the very year that this king ascended the throne, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha, in the city of Ratanapūra, within the Piṭakasālā named Māravijayaratanasudhammā, he had the royal edict read aloud in the midst of the assembly of the Elder named Sūriyavaṃsa and handed over the sovereignty of the Saṅgha. [The title: *Sūriyavaṃsābhisiripavarālaṅkāradhammasenāpatimahādhammarājādhirājaguru*.
He also gave him an ornament.

That elder, however, was born through rebirth in the village of Vālukavāpi on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Migasira, when one hundred and twenty-five years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed,
at the time of the recitation of the Suttas, having reached seventy-seven years of age.

When the era of the Saṅgha-kingdom had arrived, he became a disciple of the Elder Mahādhammarājaguru, the Ornament of the Tipiṭaka, who had attained the sovereignty of the Saṅgha, possessed tranquil faculties, was a Dhamma of patience, was desirous of training, and dwelt in the mastery of the scriptures. He, however,
fell under the power of death during the very reign of that king, when more than fifteen hundred and two years of the Kali Age had elapsed.
Then the king performed the cremation rites for the body with many thousands of palaces and unprecedented, marvelous deeds.

Then, when one hundred and six hundred years of the Kali Age had elapsed, he appointed the Elder named Ñeyyadhamma, a pupil of that Great Elder, once again to the position of Saṅgharāja. First, the *Ñeyyadhammālaṅkāradhamma*.

He bestowed upon him the title "Preceptor of the Great Dhamma-Rājādhirāja, Generalissimo. Subsequently, he bestowed a second title upon him: "Preceptor of the Great Dhamma-Rājādhirāja, Generalissimo, the Illustrious Ornament of the Noble Lineage of Abhivamsa, Knower of All Knowable Phenomena.
That Elder, moreover, was conceived in the village of Devasūra during the one hundred and sixty-first year of the Kali Yuga.

Having been born, when one hundred and ninety-eight years and one thousand [years] had passed, he reached the ground of full ordination on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha.
During the reign of that king, when one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine years of the Kali Yuga had arrived, from the island of Sīhaḷa...
The elder named Paññātissa, together with the bhikkhu named Sunanda, the novice named Indasāra, one lay follower, and one young boy, arrived at the city named Amarapura.
Then the Sangharāja favored them with material requisites and with the favor of the Dhamma. Later on, during the Kali age, when two years had passed...
When two thousand years had elapsed, the Elder Paññātissa passed away because he was overcome by old age and sickness, and because the inherent nature of conditioned phenomena cannot be transcended.
