His reflection, "I shall take up the training again," failed to reach its conclusion and perished.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"What was unthinkable comes to pass, and even what was planned perishes;
for wealth is not brought about by thought alone, whether for a woman or a man.

In this world, however, a wise person who desires to perform meritorious deeds should act with haste. For who indeed can know whether death will occur today, tomorrow, or the day after? Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Hasten toward the good; restrain the mind from evil.
For while one is performing merit, the mind delights in evil.
Then the Great King performed the rites for cremating his body with many musical performances and festivities. After that—
He gave the training again to the bhikkhu named Sunanda,
established the novice in the stage of full ordination, and the boy in the stage of a novice.
Then, O Great King, when two hundred and three years of the Kali Age had elapsed, in the month of Māgha, together with many...

Having supported all those various works by means of provisions, and having brought them to completion, he entrusted the entire burden of affairs to a certain minister who was the chief official of Kusima City,
handing over all his duties to him, and then dispatched [the manuscript] to the island of Sīhaḷa. Furthermore,
the Great Elder Saṅgharāja [did so] for the sake of the long endurance of the Dispensation and for the sake of easy awakening for those who hear it.

Having purified the text by comparing it with various manuscripts, he composed a word-for-word commentary (*atthayojanā*) in the Maramma language for the *Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Saddhammapajjotikā*.
By means of teaching the recitation of the scriptures to many disciples, he rendered assistance to the Conqueror’s Dispensation.
Later, when two thousand and eight years of the Kali age had elapsed, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Migasira...
His son, named Sīrīpavarādityavijayānantayasamahādhammarājādhirāja, reigned. At that time,
he appointed the Elder Paññājotābhidhajamahādhammarājādhirājaguru— the disciple of the Mahāthera Sūriyavaṃsābhisiripavarālaṅkāradhammasenāpatimahādhammarājādhirājaguru— to the position of Saṅgharāja.

He too was virtuous, proficient in the scriptures, desirous of training, modest, and amiable. He composed a word-for-word commentary (*atthayojanā*) on the Pāli text of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* and its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) in the Maramma language (Burmese).

During the reign of that king, the Elder Mahādhammarājādhirāja-guru, the illustrious ornament of the lineage of the Abhivaṃsa kings and a preeminent commander of the Dhamma, composed a word-for-word commentary in the Maramma language on the *Saddhammavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

The Elder Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru, whose name was Maṇijotasaddhammālaṅkāra, composed a word-for-word commentary (*atthayojanā*) on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya Pāḷi* and its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) in the Maramma language.
The Elder Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru, whose name was Medhābhivaṃsasaddhammadhaja, composed a word-for-word commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya Pāḷi* and its commentary in the Maramma language.
[This was done] for the Elder Ñeyyadhammābhivaṃsasiripavarālaṅkāradhammasenāpati, the Great King of Dharma...

Having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), when I was five years old and named Paññāsāmi, I composed a commentary on the word-meanings and difficult points (*gaṇṭhipadatthavaṇṇanā*) of the treatise called *Saddatthabhedacintā* in the Maramma language.

At the age of ten, however, I composed a word-by-word explanation (*atthayojanā*) of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* in the Maramma language; and having compared its text with many other books, I purified it.
In a later period, when two thousand one hundred and fourteen years of the Sakkarāj era had arrived, this righteous king of ours—

by the power of merit accumulated over many hundreds of births— attained the excellence of sovereignty as if urged on by the world-protectors of the deva realm for the sake of upholding the teaching of the Conqueror.
[This was] for the Dhamma-king who desired to uphold the teaching of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
His heart’s desire reached its fulfillment. Like water that has found an opening and overflows its banks, his faith surged like a great flood and remained steadfast.

Having passed four years, in the month of Vesākha, surrounded by many royal regalia such as the five insignia of royalty, he performed the consecration ceremony together with his chief queen upon the auspicious throne of Udumbara.
Thus it was said in the account of the origin of the Naga king:
"This king is indeed one of great merit; even when he arrived as a mere wood-gatherer, having attained prosperity under King Sakkara, he remained devoted to giving."
Then, after more than four years had passed,
having attained the status of a *sekha* together with his chief queen upon the great terrace,
he illuminated the Wheel of the Conqueror, just as Mahāsoka and others did.
Having restrained those who are shameless and having encouraged those who possess a sense of shame,
one should apply oneself to generosity, virtue, and mental cultivation throughout the kingdom,
just as King Nimi and others did.
At that time, because he performed an act of restraint against those shameless individuals as if casting them into the Avīci hell,
they had no opportunity and hid themselves, just as the *kosiyas* do at the time of sunrise. Therefore,
we said this in the narrative of the origin of the Naga king.
At that time, however, the Victor’s Wheel becomes as manifest as the moon in the sky;
those lacking shame hide away, just as owls do at the rising of the dawn.
And because the one possessed of shame performs the work of upholding—like one casting those who ought to be upheld up even to the peak of existence—[the Sangha flourishes].

Therefore, having gained that opportunity, they stand with their heads raised and free from fear, just as the beings of the first eon did when they had obtained the light of the moon and sun. Thus we said:
"At that time too, the Wheel of the Victor was as manifest in the sky as the sun."
"Even those who possess a sense of shame arise [to act], like those who have caught hold of a branch.

Desiring to ensure that the Buddha’s word—consisting of the Three Piṭakas and the ninefold division—would endure for a long time, he had it purified by the Great Theras who were experts in the recitation of the scriptures;
then, having provided wages for the scribes, he [established] the rules for throat-born and head-born sounds, as well as the rules for the lax and the tight articulations.
Having investigated again and again, and having entered the inner palace without violating even the slightest boundary line, he had [the texts] written down in books made of gold and iron.
Having selected monks endowed with the power of wisdom, he caused them to memorize and recite the Vinaya Piṭaka individually according to their respective abilities. Starting with the Chief Queen...

Having assembled the entire harem, many royal servants, ministers, and other citizens, he had them each memorize the Suttanta Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka separately, having analyzed them according to individual suttas, matrices (mātikā), word-commentaries (bhājanīya), and the sections on consciousness (cittavāra), as far as their respective capacities allowed;
he also caused them to recite them fluently. And he himself daily [recited] various suttas, such as the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta.

He performed his daily recitation (*sajjhāya*). For the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the Victor’s Dispensation throughout the entire realm, he granted freedom from fear to all beings—whether dwelling on land or moving through water—within an area measuring five hundred *dhanus* surrounding the hermitage of the forest-dwelling monks.
Furthermore, he released the elders and sub-elders, who were experts in the scriptures (*pariyatti*), from all royal duties for the sake of their parents and other relatives.
Having caused the *balikamma* (sacrificial offerings) to be released, he allowed them to dwell at their ease.

In a single day, he established a thousand noble youths on the grounds for going forth and full ordination, thereby upholding the Dispensation (*sāsana*). He also performed many other meritorious deeds.

Having performed them, he aspired only to the cessation of the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*), not to the cycle itself (*vaṭṭa*). And as for the other women of the harem and so forth, whatever you [may think]—
Having performed meritorious deeds, one should attain only the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*); do not revolve in the cycle of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*)—thus he exhorted him constantly.

He constantly exhorted him with discourses on the Dhamma connected to the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) and so forth. He himself also applied himself constantly to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
However, because of his duties as a ruler and lord of the realm, which were numerous by their very nature, he did not find an opportunity [to practice] at all times.

In order to devote himself to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), even while in such a state, he continues to practice that very meditation subject even at times when he must attend to the impurities of the body;

he does not waste his time in vain. For in the world, people bring back from the charnel ground even those things considered inauspicious, such as human skulls and bones, or have objects like tooth-sticks made resembling them, and keep them near themselves.
He discerns the merit consisting of the meditation on the skeleton and so forth.
At that time, however, he [discerns] our preeminent teacher— one learned in the scriptures, endowed with swift and rapid knowledge regarding the movement of the limbs and so forth,
whose discourse on the teaching of the diverse Dhamma was a place of refuge for all the bhikkhus in the land of Maramma, and who was a reverer of the elders.

Having attained the pinnacle of physical beauty, being a speaker of what is appropriate, and possessing the supreme knowledge that faces toward the knowable phenomena (ñeyyadhamma), he was the one whose crest-jewel is the glory of the Dhamma;

thus, having received the third title, "Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru," he established himself in the position of leadership over the Saṅgha of monks and all the inhabitants of the kingdom, just as the Great King Aśoka established the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa. Therefore, we have said:
In the narrative of the emergence of the Naga King,
he then established that Elder— who was the leader of the community of monks and had received the title of "Ñeyya" and others— as the preeminent one, saying, "Excellent!"
And at that time, when the year 1219 of the glorious reign of our righteous great king had arrived,
near the mountain named Mantalākhyāta, there was a place endowed with the characteristics of a beautiful site— like a bathing ghat for the birds that are the eyes of many people—
surrounded by all the ornaments of the city, causing the eyes of men to wander in longing, and filled with various jewels.

He had built a great royal residence named Ratanapuṇṇa, which served as a marketplace for various merchants from Vairajja, just as Rājagaha was for Mandhātā and Kusāvatī for Sudassana. Therefore, we said in the account of the origin of the Nāga king:
"Then, when the time for the wood-sacrifice arrived, and that mountain called Mantalākhya..."
Near her, he had a city built named Erāvatī,
endowed with the characteristics of a beautiful site and called Ratanapuṇṇa;
it was as delightful and beautiful as Rājagaha, the capital of King Mandhātā.
Just as the thousand-rayed sun, the maker of day, rises from the mountain of sunrise, bringing joy and gladness and providing benefit to beings in the world who long for light;
even so does this righteous king bring about joy and gladness and provide benefit to the monks and laypeople of the Maramma country who are modest, amiable, and desirous of training.
He arises in this kingdom of Burma.
And by relying upon this righteous king (dhammika-rāja), the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One shines exceedingly brightly in the kingdom of Burma; it attains growth, increase, and expansion.
For this teaching indeed stands supported by the king. Thus, this very righteous king is a benefactor of the Teaching.
Those who practice the Dhamma and esteem the Dhamma, as well as all the inhabitants of the realm who rely upon a righteous king, are indeed benefactors of the Dispensation;
they themselves practice the Dhamma, esteem the Dhamma, and follow the king. For this very reason, it is said in the Mahābodhijātaka and other texts:
"Just as when bulls are racing, if the leader goes straight..."
All the cows go straight when the leader has gone straight.
Even so among humans, if he who is regarded as the best practices the Dhamma,
how much more will the rest of the people do so.
"The king who is righteous sleeps happily throughout the entire kingdom.
Specifically, however, the chief queen of our king is the daughter of the chief queen of the Great Dhamma King who was building the second Amarapura;
she is endowed with virtues such as honesty, gentleness, and purity, is of right conduct, and devoted to her husband. Although she has attained the preeminent rank among all women...

Together with [the others], having not become intoxicated by the wine of the sensual qualities (*kāmaguṇa*), she was constantly diligent in meritorious deeds through the power of heedfulness (*appamāda*).
She constantly engaged in the study and mastery of the scriptures and became one who had reached the further shore of the Vedas.

Extremely devoted to the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, she and the other women of the harem likewise stood upon the instruction of the Great King of Dharma and practiced the Dharma. The Dispensation...

They indeed gained confidence. The viceroy as well—the biological son of the Great Dhamma King—without ever opposing the will of the Great Dhamma King, brought about the welfare and benefit of all the householders and monks residing in the entire kingdom, just like the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch who is endowed with strength and speed, exceedingly brave, and diligent in exertion.
There were also other ministers numbering in the many thousands.
Appointed to various positions obtained from the Great King of Dhamma, they carry out their respective duties and delight in meritorious deeds.
All the inhabitants of the kingdom likewise fix their minds solely upon generosity, virtue, and mental cultivation.
And the bhikkhus, headed by the Sangharāja and other elders, novices, and those of middle standing, apply themselves to the task of textual study and the practice of insight meditation.
Thus, even if one were to speak with great enthusiasm of the virtues of a single virtuous person, it would be difficult indeed to reach the end;

how then could any individual possibly reach the end of describing the virtues of the Blessed One, the Supreme One of the Three Worlds, which proceed from the power of his many thousands of *pāramīs*? Such is the case for the Great King of Dhamma as well.

If the virtues of the Chief Queen, the viceroy, and the others were to be recounted in detail, even after reaching several hundred *bhāṇavāra* sections of this *Sāsanavaṃsappadīpikā*, no end would be in sight; furthermore, it would become excessively prolix.
Therefore, this has been told in brief for the purpose of rejoicing in the great merit of virtuous people.
Indeed, this should be rejoiced in by virtuous people who hear it: "In such a time, in such a kingdom,
a king named so-and-so, having upheld the Dispensation, attained growth, increase, and abundance,
just as a tree attains growth, increase, and abundance depending upon the earth and water."

During the reign of this king, the Sangharāja Mahāthera named Siridhajadhammasenāpati Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru, who possessed the supreme renown for the knowledge of the Abhimuni (the Buddha) regarding the Dhamma to be known, composed the treatise titled *Surājamaggadīpanī* at the request of the king.
Having taught the meaning of the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* to his disciples, he had the method for the application of that meaning recorded in books according to the order in which it was taught.
The Great Elder named Medhābhivaṃsa-saddhammadhaja-mahādhammarājādhirāja-guru composed a commentary on the method of the meaning of the Jātaka-pāḷi in the Maramma language. I,
who am the same person as the one who received from the King the title and honorific name "Paññāsāmisiri-kavi-dhajamahādhammarājādhirāja-guru," being requested by the King and the Queen Consort,
[composed] this work titled *Sīlakathā* (Discourse on Virtue) and *Upāyakathā* (Discourse on Skillful Means).

I also composed the *Akāsiṃ* treatise. At the request of a distinguished lay disciple (*upāsaka*) who was a teacher to the king, I likewise composed the treatise named *Akkharavisodhanī* and the treatise named *Āpattivinicchaya*.
Similarly, urged by Saṅgharañña, I [composed] the *Nāgarājuppattikathā*, the *Vohāratthabheda*, and the *Vivādavinicchaya*.

I composed it. Likewise, at the request of the village headman of Pañcajambugāma, the minister Lekhakāmaccā, and two other ministers who were petitioners, I, that very same person, composed the treatise named *Rājasevakadīpanī*.

Likewise, at the request of the great minister Mahāamacca, the village headman of Dīghanāvānagara, I, that very same person, composed the treatise named *Nirayakathādīpaka*. Likewise, by one named Silāleḍḍuka...
At the request of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), I myself composed the treatise named *Uposathavinicchaya*.
Likewise, at the request of many students, I myself composed a commentary on the *Saddanīti* in the Pāli language.
And at one time, when two hundred and twenty-one years of the Kali Age had elapsed, this thought occurred to the King:

Nowadays, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, many instances are seen of the four requisites being acquired by certain bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras through improper actions such as corrupting families;
some shameless individuals even accept things that ought to be relinquished, such as gold and silver;
some consume betel at the wrong time without having obtained the requisite materials; and some, having made a store, smoke tobacco.
While they were not ill, they entered villages wearing sandals, carried umbrellas,

and engaged in other practices inconsistent with the Vinaya; therefore, now, having had the monks and novices make a formal promise in the presence of the Buddha, with the Buddha as their witness, saying,
"We shall not engage in these improper conducts," [the purpose is] to have them observe the training rules of the Blessed One.
"It is appropriate; and this being so, monks and novices will think:

'We have made this promise in the very presence of the Buddha, and if we should undergo any change after having made that promise, some fear might arise for us in this very life, right here before our eyes.
Considering this immediate fear, they will observe the training rules."
Having reflected thus, he thought again: "I do not know whether it is appropriate or not to have the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras give their consent in this manner;
now I shall assemble the great elders, such as the Saṅgharāja, and ask them.
Then, having assembled all the great elders in the Saṅgharāja’s monastery, he said, "Ask about this matter."
He commanded his ministers. Then the ministers, having assembled the great elders, questioned them:

"Venerable sirs, having now observed the conduct of the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras in the Dispensation that is contrary to the Vinaya, the King, in the presence of the Buddha, having made the Buddha his witness, caused them to give a promise that they would not engage in such misconduct; [now, regarding] the training rules of the Blessed One..."
[The King] wished to have [the Saṅgha] protected, and considered whether it was appropriate to have it done in such a manner.
Then, the great elders headed by the Sangharāja spoke thus: "Since he acts in this way because he desires the purity of the Dispensation, therefore it is appropriate to have it done in such a manner.
However, a few elders, including the venerable Mahādhammarājaguru—the wise Abhidhajamunindaghosa—spoke as follows:

— Now, as for those called "bhikkhus," because they possess only a small measure of the powers of faith and so forth, they incur offenses—whether conscious or unconscious—that are termed the "Blessed One’s commands.
Having then remedied these through the very rites of confession and rehabilitation permitted by the Blessed One, they purify their virtue and maintain a state of conscientiousness and amiability;
yet this is never done without having first incurred an offense. Therefore, [the practice] was prohibited by the Blessed One.
To make a formal promise in the presence of the Buddha, thinking, "I shall intentionally transgress [the training]," is an extremely grave matter.

Even if one were to make such a promise previously and later deceive it, since it is stated that for one who deceives a promise, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for one with a pure mind and a *pācittiya* offense at the very moment of making the promise for the other, therefore... [taṃ taṃ]
If one were to incur an offense simultaneously with the act of deceiving by denying it, then there would be an abundance of offenses merely from making such a formal admission; rather,
just as one who seeks to cure a disease but consumes unwholesome medicine finds that the disease not only fails to subside but actually worsens,
so too one who desires not to incur an offense [but does so] in the presence of the Buddha...
He makes a formal admission, and thus he would indeed become one who is abundant in offenses; moreover,
how much more so will monks who perceive no danger be able to transgress the training rules even after making such admissions hundreds of times in the presence of hundreds of Buddhas?
Then the Sangharāja Mahāthera exhorted me—his own disciple named Paññāsāmisirikavidhajamahādhammarājādhirājaguru—to give a reply to that Thera’s words.
Thereupon, I spoke thus: "Two persons are incapable of intentionally committing an offense:
a monk and a nun who are noble persons (ariya-puggala). Two persons are capable of intentionally committing every offense: a monk and a nun."

Regarding the term *puthujjana*: since it is stated in the *Parivāra-pāḷi*, one should consider that it is not appropriate for ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) to give their consent in the same manner as noble persons (*ariya-puggala*).

If one were to think that obtaining the consent of ordinary monk-puthujjanas is too burdensome, [one must remember] that from the very beginning, all monks—both noble and ordinary—[must perform] the four [procedures] in the ordination hall (*upasampadā-māḷaka*).
Regarding the four things not to be done that were declared as such:

"Whatever monk, even down to a blade of grass or a stick, takes what has not been given—whether it be a foot-measure, a foot-measure's worth, or more than a foot-measure—in a manner constituting theft, he is no longer a recluse, no longer a son of the Sakyan. Even down to an ant, whatever monk intentionally...
"Whoever deprives a human being of life—even down to causing an abortion—is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyans. And:

"Whoever, being a monk with evil desires and overcome by longing, claims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state—even saying 'I delight in empty huts'—is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyans.
Thus [it was said] to those newly ordained monks who were being exhorted by their preceptors and teachers.

"Yes, Venerable Sir," is merely a statement of acknowledgment. Even for novices, at the very moment of their going forth, the first acknowledgment has already been made in the presence of the preceptor by saying, "I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life," and so forth.
Likewise, when monks have committed various offenses and are performing the restoration through confession, they say, "Very well, Venerable Sir, we shall exercise restraint."

The promise has indeed been made repeatedly. Even by novice monks (*sāmaṇera*), at the time of receiving the training in the presence of their preceptors (*upajjhāya*) and teachers (*ācariya*), the promise has indeed been made repeatedly in such phrases as, "I undertake the training rule regarding the taking of life," and so forth.
Yet, to speak words such as "I am afraid of this very thing" without being afraid of those promises appears as something truly extraordinary.
For by this admission, no distinction is seen between those various admissions.

This, however, is the definitive meaning here: the offense of *dukkaṭa* for making a promise refers to when, in Sāvatthī, King Pasenadi of Kosala requested, "Please enter the rains retreat in this monastery," and [the monk], having promised "Very well" out of a desire for abundant gains, [failed to do so].

This was laid down concerning the bhikkhu named Upananda, on account of his breach of a promise, after he had entered the rains residence in another monastery along the way. And in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, in the explanation of the Khandhaka on Entering the Rains Residence, regarding the phrase "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for a promise," it says:
"It is not only [the case] when one says, 'Stay here for these three months for the rains.'"
There is an offense for making such a promise as: "Accept almsfood from me for these three months; we both shall observe the rains retreat together;
we shall have [the Uposatha] recited by one another. In each such instance of promising, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
This occurs specifically when one was initially pure in mind but later deceives; however, if one was already impure in mind at the time of the initial promise, it is likewise an offense.
It is stated as a *pācittiya*.
Thus, for monks who, having made a mutual agreement with donors, commit deception, a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated only for the purpose of dividing the property intended for others;
it is not [an offense] when one acts of one's own accord according to one's own desire, thinking, "I myself shall eat."
Having said, "I will speak," and so forth, but failing to act in accordance with what was stated constitutes deception.

However, if a monk or a novice first gives his consent by saying, "Yes, Venerable Sir," and so on, and subsequently, due to some business, incurs various offenses, he would incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) simultaneously with the deception of his promise; such being the case, in each respective instance...
If one were to prescribe two offenses for each training rule, even though they have not been so prescribed, then by that very fact, what is called the offense of *paṭissava-dukkata*—
which consists in making a promise after taking another's consent in their presence and then deceiving them at the very point of that agreement—

must be understood as having been prescribed for that purpose. Now, the King, desiring the purity of the Dispensation, was thus causing the monks and novices to restrain themselves in virtue through this means.

Thinking, "May they undertake restraint without disregarding the fear of both the present life and the future world," and having caused them to make a formal promise in the presence of the Buddha, no fault whatsoever is seen. Furthermore,
so that the monks and novices might maintain even greater purity of virtue by restraining themselves according to the precepts, the king [addressed] all the monks and novices before the Buddha.
Having made him give his promise in person, he caused him to guard his virtue.
Thus, during the time of this king, even those who were previously shameless became for the most part possessed of shame, disregarding fear.
Ninety years after two thousand three hundred years had passed since the final nibbāna of the Blessed Buddha...
In that year, for the sake of the monks' easy passage while they were performing work from the village boundary outward on the riverbank as far as the limit of the water-sprinkling (*udakukkhepa*),
laypeople constructed a bridge by connecting the water-sprinkling boundary to the village boundary.
There, the elder named Cariya— preceptor to the Great Dhammarāja Ñāṇālaṅkārasumana— performed several years' worth of formal acts of the Vinaya, such as full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The Elder Dhīrānanda, however, did not wish to perform the work there, thinking that it would involve the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*).
From that point on, those who approved of the views of the Great Dhamma-Rāja-Guru Gaṇācariya Ñāṇālaṅkāra-Sumanas became his partisans;
likewise, those who approved of the views of the Elder Dhīrānanda became his partisans.
Thus it was on the island of Laṅkā that the monks belonging to the Amarapura Nikāya remained, having split into two factions. Then, from the side of the Dhīrānanda faction,
the monk [Dhīrānanda] sent the monks Dhammakkhandha and Vanaratana— pupils of the Sīlakkhandha Thera who belonged to his own faction—
to our city of Ratanapoṇṇa in Jambudīpa, in order to receive instruction from the great Saṅgharāja Thera.

For the purpose of receiving [the relics]. And when one thousand two hundred and eighteen years of the Kali Age had elapsed, they departed from the island of Siṃhala on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika;
arriving at the city of Ratanapūra on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phagguna, when one thousand two hundred and nineteen years had elapsed.
Then the Dhamma King, having had a four-storeyed monastery built in the Saṅgharāja’s monastery, had them reside there.

He also provided for them with the four requisites. And the Saṅgharāja, having heard the words of those two factions and having compared them with many texts, adjudicated the dispute. For in such a situation, there is the fault of confusion.
Having made his presence known, he also gave them a letter of introduction.
King Mahādhammarāja had them receive their training once again in the presence of the Sangharāja;
having provided them with the necessary items, such as books of the Tipiṭaka, he dispatched them by ship on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of the first Āsāḷha month in that very same year.
After that, from the faction of the Great Dhamma King, the Preceptor of the Gaṇa, Ñāṇālaṅkārasumanamāhādhammarājaguru,
they sent monks who were disciples of Paññāmolitthera of that same faction— namely, the bhikkhu Vimalajotidhammananda—
along with a novice named Ariyālaṅkāra and four lay devotees (upāsakas). And when two thousand two hundred and twenty years of the Kali Yuga had arrived...
The fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika arrived.

At that time, the King likewise had a monastery built right within the precincts of the Sangharāja’s own monastery and settled them there. He also provided for their maintenance with the four requisites.
The Sangharāja, in turn, gave his formal judgment according to the method previously described. Thus did the Dhammarāja act.
Having had those monks again receive the training in the presence of the Saṅgharāja, and having ordained them as *sāmaṇeras*,
he provided them with support through the four requisites and sent them forth.
Subsequently, when two hundred and twenty-two years of the Kali Yuga had elapsed, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha...
From the island of Siṃhala itself, two bhikkhus, three sāmaṇeras, and four upāsakas brought a casket made of silver and gold containing relics of the Cetiya made of silver and gold,
a Buddha image made of ivory, leaves from the Mahābodhi tree, bark from the Mahābodhi tree, soil from the site where the Mahābodhi was established,
leaves from the Southern Branch of the Bodhi tree in Siṃhala, and the ground where [the Buddha] remained with unblinking eyes for the second week.
Taking them as a gift of the Dhamma, they arrived at the great royal capital city named Ratanapūra.
The Dhamma King, having provided for them with the four requisites, had them dwell in the monastery of the Saṅgha King.

Furthermore, he caused the bhikkhus to receive the training again; he caused the sāmaṇeras to undergo the ceremony of full ordination (upasampadā), and he caused those who were householders to undergo the ceremony of going forth (pabbajjā).

Thus, it should be understood that from the time of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna until the present day, the establishment of the Sāsana in the kingdom of Maramma has proceeded through a succession of elders (theras).

In this way, within the realm of Maramma, there were five groups (gaṇas) in the city of Ariṃaddana: the group of Arahant Theras, the group of Uttarājīva Theras and Chappada Theras, the group of Sivali Theras, the group of Ānanda Theras, and the group of Tāmalinda Theras.
Now, starting from these five groups in the city of Ariṃaddana, [the lineage continued] through a succession of elders in Vijayapura, Jeyyapura, and Ratnapura.
I shall demonstrate how the teaching arrived in due succession. For in the city of Sirikhettanagara, a king named So-yāṃ-noṃ,
having made Saddhammaṭṭhiti Thera— the pupil of Sāradassī Thera of the Parakkama dynasty—
his own teacher, honored him.
In the eighth century and four years of the Kali Yuga, having come from the city of Sirikhettanagara, he reigned over Ratanapūra.
Then, he caused his son, the prince named Anekibha, to rule over the city of Sirikhettanagara under the title Mahārāja.
To the southern direction was the city of ‘Kū vṭhe ṭa-yo mo’, and to the western direction was ‘Pho... [text truncated].

He dedicated [the merit], saying: "May my son’s authority prevail over the householders seated between the place named Khoṃ in the northern direction, the city of Ma Loṃ, and the place named Koṃ Khoṃ in the eastern direction;
may my teacher, the Elder Saddhammatthiti, have authority over the monks."
That Elder Saddhammaṭṭhiti had two disciples, namely the Elders Ariyavaṃsa and Mahāsāmi.
Among them, the Elder Mahāsāmi, thinking, "I shall bring forth the lineage of the Dispensation according to the method previously described," went to the island of Sīhaḷa;
from Sīhaḷa, he brought back with him five monks and the Elder named Saddhammacāri for the purpose of re-establishing the new ordination.
Having taken [the relics], he sat in the city of Sirikhetta, causing the dispensation of the Sinhalese island to flourish.

A disciple of that Mahāsāri Thera named the Thera Atulavaṃsa wandered through the four quarters, mastered the scriptures, and sat in the very city of Sirikhetta near Tambulabhuñjamātā, upholding the dispensation. A disciple of that Thera Atulavaṃsa...
The elder named Ratanaraṃsi, having attained mastery in the scriptures (*pariyatti-veśāradya*), established himself in the city of Sirikhetta to uphold the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

And the elder named Abhisaṅketa, a pupil of that elder Ratanaraṃsi and the teacher of King Sātthavaddha, having attained mastery in the scriptures, likewise established himself in the city of Sirikhetta to uphold the Dispensation.
He, moreover, had a disciple, the elder named Munindaghosa. When nine hundred and seventy years of the Kali Age had elapsed,
King Pacchimapakkhādhi, having conquered the city of Sirikhettanagara,
brought that elder Munindaghosa along with his minister named Nandayodha and established him in Ratanapura.
It is said that the King of the Western Faction spoke thus: "Having obtained the city of Sirikhettanagara, I shall obtain only one monk and only one layman.

That elder was named Munindaghosa by his novice name; at the time of his full ordination, he was named Upāli after his maternal uncle, the elder; and by his bestowed name, he was known as Tipiṭakālaṅkāra. [He resided] at the Tiriyapabbata Monastery.
However, because he resided at Vāsattā, the elder was known by the name of that place as Tiriyapabbata Thera.

It is said that after first sitting in a four-storied monastery on the bank of the Erāvatī River, he later lived for sixty years during the time of the thousand-year Kaliyuga and sat in the Tiriyapabbata Monastery. During his time as a novice, due to the fear of the Jaluma plague...
Having departed from Ratanapura and reached the city of Ketumatī, I studied the texts in the presence of the Elder Dhammarājaguru,
who was a disciple of the Elder Tisāsanadhaja. Because of my great proficiency in the Pāḷi, the commentaries, and the sub-commentaries,
and because I had already composed the Vessantara Jātaka in the style of poetic ornamentation even while still young, I became exceedingly well-known.
There was. Furthermore, that elder’s disciple, Mahātissatthera, a resident of Uccanagara, lived in forest retreats in the Saṅgira country, taught the scriptures, and upheld the Dispensation.
His disciple was Candatthera, a village-dweller from Reminagāma. His disciple was Guṇasiritthera, a resident of that same village. His disciple...

The resident of that village was named Kalyāṇadhajathara. That elder, having taught the scriptures in Padumanagara, Sahassorodha, Bodhodadhi, and Adhigāma, sat [there]. His disciples were Indobhāsa, Kalyāṇacakkavimalācāra, and Thera from Bodhodhigāma;
Guṇasāra, Candasāra, and Thera from Sahassorodhagāma; Varaesi Thera from Vaṃtumagāma; and [others] in Kanninagara.

The elder Guṇasiri, a resident of Jararājagāma, and these other elders, having again received the training and mastered the scriptures in the presence of the elder Kalyāṇadhaja, became proficient. A disciple of that very same elder Kalyāṇadhaja,
a bearer of the Dhamma, was dwelling in the village of Samiva in the Saṅgira country.
The elder Nāma, while residing in the village of Kusumamūla in Padumanagara during his old age, taught the texts and upheld the Dispensation.
Among them, the elder Guṇasiri, during the time of King Amarapuramāpaka, received the title *Guṇābhilaṅkārasaddhammamahārājādhirājaguru* and resided at the Kittivihāra in Jayabhūmi.
The disciple of that elder was the great elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsadhammasenāpatimahādhammarājāguru.
During the time of that very king, he became the Saṅgharāja. That elder was the founder of the Amarapura Nikāya in the island of Sīhaḷa.

He was the disciple of the elder Guṇābhilaṅkāra Saddhammamahādhammarājādhirāja; his disciple was the elder named Tipiṭakālaṅkāra Mahādhammarājaguru; and his disciple was Sūriyavaṃsābhisiri Pavarālaṅkāra Dhammasenāpati Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru.
The Elder Nāma was the Sangharāja during the reign of King Amarapuradutiyamāpaka.
His disciple, the Great Elder Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru— known as Ñeyyadhammābhivaṃsa, Munivarañāṇakitti, Siripavarālaṅkāra,
and Dhammasenāpati— was the Sangharāja during the reigns of both King Amarapuradutiyamāpaka and King Ratanapuṇṇamāpaka.
He, moreover, was a disciple of the Elder Saṅgharāja Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru,
and also a disciple of the Elder Varaesī.
This has been the account of the succession of our teachers, the Elders, beginning from the time the Venerable Saddhammacārī Mahāsāmittha arrived last of all from the island of Sīhaḷa.
This other lineage of elders should also be known. A monk named Saddhammakitti, belonging to the lineage of the elder Chappada, came to Jeyyapura and sat at a place on the ground in Catudīpa.
Having mastered the scriptures (pariyatti) in the presence of the elder Mahāariyavaṃsa, he subsequently moved to the Jetavana monastery, where he sat and [studied] the scriptures.
Having recited it, he upheld the dispensation.
That disciple of the Elder Saddhammakitti was named Tissāsanadhaja. His disciple was named Dhammarājaguru.
His disciple was named Munindaghosa. His disciple was named Mahātissa. His disciple was Candapañña.
His disciple was named Guṇasiri. His disciple was named Ñāṇadhaja. His disciple was named Dhammadhara. His disciple was named Indobhāsa.

From that point onward, the lineage of the Dispensation should be understood by way of the elders Kalyāṇacakkavimalācāra, Guṇasāra, Candasāra, Varaesī, Guṇasiri, Ñāṇābhivaṃsa, and Ñeyyadhammābhivaṃsa.
This is the account showing the succession of elders beginning from the Elder Saddhammakitti, who was a pupil of the Elder Chappada of Paṭṭalaṅka.
This was the establishment of the Dispensation in the city of Ratanapuṇṇa.
Thus, taking the entire Marma-raṭṭha country by way of its constituent part known as Aparanta-raṭṭha, the lineage of the Dispensation—

It must be shown. For even the Blessed One, having resided at the Candana Monastery in Aparanta, traveled by means of his psychic power to various regions in the Tambadipa kingdom and indeed taught the Dhamma to sentient beings there as well.
Thus ends the section on the history of the Dispensation in Aparanta within the Sasanavamsa.
The Sixth Chapter:
The Path of the Narrative on the History of the Saṅgha in the Kingdoms of Kaśmīra and Gandhāra.
Now, having reached the appropriate occasion, I shall explain the path of the narrative on the history of the Saṅgha in the kingdoms of Kaśmīra and Gandhāra, according to the aforementioned outline.
At the conclusion of the Third Council, the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa dispatched the Elder Majjhantika to the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra, saying:
"Go to that kingdom and establish the Dispensation there. Now, the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra is situated near the kingdom of Cīna;
for this very reason, even today, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra and the inhabitants of the kingdom of Cīna [are closely related].

From the time the Nāga king named Aravāḷa appeared until the present day, people have fashioned him in the form of a Nāga, honoring, worshipping, and revering him; indeed, they mostly fashion even their clothing, vessels, and other items in the likeness of a Nāga.
And that Elder Majjhantika, being the fifth together with four bhikkhus, [departed] from Pāṭaliputta...
Having ascended into the air, he descended upon the Aravāḷa Lake in the Himavat mountains.

Now at that time, in the kingdom of Kasmīra-Gandhāra during the harvest season, a Nāga king named Aravāḷa, having settled at the Aravāḷa Lake, caused a rain called the "Karakavassa" to fall, and after having the crops gathered, he brought them to the great ocean. And there, at the Aravāḷa Lake—
Having descended, he walked back and forth, stood, sat down, and even lay down upon the surface of the Aravāḷa lake.
When the young nāgas saw him, they reported it to the nāga king: "Great King, a certain man wearing tattered, torn garments and clad in saffron robes is defiling our water.
At that time, however, the Elder showed himself only to the nāgas.
At that very moment, the Naga king, overcome by anger, emerged and, seeing the Elder and unable to endure his disparagement, manifested many terrifying portents in the sky.

Furious winds blew from every direction, trees were torn apart, mountain peaks fell, clouds thundered, flashes of lightning burst forth, and thunderbolts crashed; the firmament seemed as if it were rent asunder.
Water poured forth; terrifying forms of *nāga* youths gathered together; he himself smoked and blazed; he discharged showers of weapons;
and with harsh words such as, "Who is this shaven-headed one wearing tattered robes?", he intimidated the Elder.
Then he commanded his *nāga* forces: "Come, seize him! Strike him! Drive him out! This ascetic!"
The Elder, having warded off all that terror by the power of his own psychic potency, said to the Naga king:
"Even if the entire world, including the devas, were to come and try to frighten me,
they would not be able to produce in me any fear or dread."
Even if you, O Great Naga, were to lift up the entire earth, together with its oceans and mountains, and hurl it upon me,
you would not be able to produce in me any fear or terror.
"On the contrary, O Lord of Snakes, there will only be distress for you.
When this was said, the Naga king, his power destroyed and his efforts rendered fruitless, became pained and dejected.
The Elder, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma appropriate to that moment, [proceeded].
Having gladdened them, he established them, together with eighty-four thousand nāgas, in the three refuges and the five precepts.
Many other inhabitants of the Himalayas—yakkhas, gandhabbas, and kumbhaṇḍas—also heard the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma and were established in the refuges and the precepts.
The yakkha Pañcaka, together with his wife the yakkhinī, [did the same].
And with five hundred sons, he was established in the first fruit [of the path]. Then the Venerable Majjhimatthera, addressing all the nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, spoke thus:
"Do not now give rise to anger as you did before;
do not destroy the crops, for living beings desire happiness."
"Practice loving-kindness toward all beings; let humans dwell in happiness.
"Very well, Venerable Sir," they replied to the Elder's words and practiced exactly as instructed.
On that very day, it was the time for the Naga king’s worship. Then the Naga king [prepared] his own jeweled throne...
Having had it brought, he prepared it for the Elder. The Elder sat down cross-legged upon the couch.
The Naga king also stood nearby, fanning the Elder. At that moment, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra arrived;

seeing the Elder, they thought, "The Elder possesses even greater supernormal power than our own Naga king," and having paid homage to the Elder, they sat down. The Elder [then taught them] the *Āśīviṣopama-sūtra* (The Simile of the Venomous Snake).
He preached. At the conclusion of the discourse, there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty thousand beings, and one hundred thousand families went forth into homelessness.
From that time onwards, as far as Jeta’s Grove, Kasmīra-Gandhāra was indeed illuminated by the saffron robes and fanned by the breeze of the seers.
Having gone to Kasmīra-Gandhāra at that time, the seer Majjhantika—
"Having appeased the wicked elephant, you released many from their bonds.

Now, however, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra, the radiance of the Dispensation is no longer perceived, as if the sun had set; therefore, there is no need for a detailed account regarding the re-establishment of the Dispensation there.
Thus ends the section on the history of the Dispensation in the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra within the *Sāsanavaṃsa*.
The Seventh Chapter.
8. The Exposition of the History of the Saṅgha in the Mahiṃsaka Province.
Now, the opportunity has arrived to speak on the path of the history of the Saṅgha in the Mahiṃsaka Province according to the aforementioned outline; therefore, I shall explain it.
At the conclusion of the Third Council, the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa sent the Elder Mahāreva to the Mahimsaka region, saying: "Go to that kingdom and establish the Dispensation there.

Thinking that a group of five monks was sufficient for the formal act of ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) in frontier districts, he went to the Mahimsaka region accompanied by four others, making five in all.
Having reached the Mahimsaka region, the Elder [preached] the *Devadūta-sutta*.
He preached the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, forty thousand beings attained the eye of Dhamma.
Forty thousand beings likewise went forth into homelessness.
Having gone to the kingdom of Mahimsa, Mahareva, possessed of great psychic power...
"Having summoned the divine messengers, you released many from their bonds.
But now, there, the opportunity for the Dispensation appears weak, like the sun obscured by clouds.
Thus ends the section on the history of the Dispensation in the Mahimsaka kingdom within the *Sāsanavaṃsa*.
The eighth chapter, titled "Nāma," is concluded.
9. The Path of the Narrative on the History of the Sāsana in the Great Kingdom (Mahāraṭṭha).
From here onwards, I shall relate the path of the narrative on the history of the Sāsana in the Great Kingdom according to the aforementioned outline.
At the conclusion of the Third Council, the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa dispatched the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita to the Mahāraṭṭha country, saying: "Go to that country and establish the Sasana there.
The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, accompanied by four others as his retinue, went to the Mahāraṭṭha country;
there, by recounting the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka, he inspired faith in the people of Mahāraṭṭha and established eighty-four thousand living beings in the fruits of the Path. Thirteen thousand...
They went forth. Thus did that seer establish the Dispensation there.
Having gone to Mahāraṭṭha, the great Dhammarakkhita, by recounting a Jātaka, inspired confidence in the great multitude.
It is said that in those days, people there for the most part performed wrong deeds such as fire-sacrifices and the like.
For that very reason, the Elder taught the story of the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka.
From then on, the people there very much desired to hear the Jātaka stories for the most part. And the monks, for the most part, [taught] the Jātaka stories to the householders.
They transmit [the text]. Specifically, however, those people listen to the *Vassantara-jātaka-kathā* after honoring it with many things that ought to be given.

And because that place called Mahāraṭṭha is situated near the Syāma kingdom, for that very reason both the monks and the householders residing in the Syāma kingdom mostly desire to hear it. The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, too, [was requested] by the inhabitants of Mahāraṭṭha...
Together with [the king], he taught the Dhamma to all the inhabitants of the Aparaṇṇavāsa country and made them drink the nectar of immortality,
just as the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita had gone to Aparanta and [taught] all the inhabitants of the Aparaṇṇa country.
Furthermore, whatever was stated in the *Yonakaraṭṭhasāsanavaṃsakathā* should also be understood here.
Because he remained identical to them. For instance, the Elder Nāgasena, after residing in the Yona country, established the Dispensation in Sīma and other regions as well.

Furthermore, the Elder Mahādhammagambhīra and the Elder Mahāmedhaṅkara, together with many bhikkhus who were residents of the Yona country, went to the island of Ceylon; returning from there, they [established it] in the city of Sogata in the Sīma country.
Having reached that place and sat there, he took up the Sasana; afterwards, sitting in the city of Laṅkāpura, he took up the Sasana.
Thus, it should be understood that once the Sasana was established in the Yona kingdom, it was likewise established in Sīhaḷa and other regions.
Ninety years after more than two hundred and two thousand years had passed since the Parinibbāna of the Blessed Buddha—
The lineage established by the Theras Upāli and others, who arrived in the island of Laṅkā at the command of the Great King Dharmika,
the Lord of the Sarāma dynasty, after receiving a message and gifts sent by that very Great King Kittisirirājasīha in his third regnal year since he had attained sovereignty over the Siṃhala Island,
is well known as the Upāli-vamśa (the Lineage of Upāli). And that—
"By way of the two types of residents: those dwelling in the Pubbārāma monastery and those dwelling in the Abhayagiri monastery.
Thus it should be understood that the Dispensation remains firm in the great cities, districts, and provinces.
Thus ends the section titled "The Account of the History of the Dispensation in the Great Provinces" in the *Sāsanavaṃsa*.
The Ninth Chapter.
10. The Path of the Narrative on the History of the Sāsana in the Country of Cīna. 10.
Hereafter, I shall explain the path of the narrative on the history of the Sāsana in the country of Cīna according to the established outline.
At the conclusion of the Third Council, the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa dispatched the Elder Majjhima to the kingdom of Cīna, saying: "Go to that kingdom and establish the Sasana there.

The Elder Majjhima, together with the Elder Aḷakarevata of the Kassapa clan, the Elder Dundubhiya, and the Elder Mahārevata, went to the five kingdoms of Cīna in the Himalayan region and [began] the discourse on the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.
Having inspired confidence in the country, he caused eighty million beings to attain the jewels of the paths and fruits. Those five elders likewise inspired confidence in five kingdoms;
in each one’s presence, about a thousand people went forth into the homeless life.
In this way, they established the Dispensation there.
"Having gone, the Elder Majjhima gladdened the Himālaya, proclaiming the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma to the host of *yakkhas*.
It is said that there, people for the most part performed worship to the *yakkhas* who were intent on the perfection of generosity. For that very reason...
Those five elders, having made the army of yakkhas manifest, taught them the Dhamma.
As for the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra, it was sometimes under the conquest of the lord of the Cīna kingdom and sometimes independent;
however, it should be understood that at that time, it was indeed independent.
However, in the kingdom of Cīna, the Blessed One’s dispensation remained weak indeed; it did not remain firm.
For that very reason, at present, the dispensation is perceived there only as a mere shadow in some places, standing like a cloud scattered by the force of the wind.
Thus ends the section titled "The Account of the History of the Dispensation in the Kingdom of Cīna" within the *Sāsanavaṃsa*.
The Tenth Chapter.
Thus, the entire course of the narrative on the lineage of the Dispensation is concluded.
And up to this point—
By the venerable Bhikkhu Citrañāṇa, known by the name Saraṇaṅkara,
who desires the endurance of the True Dhamma;
and from afar, by Sumaṅgala Joti from the island.
At the request of one of pure virtue, a bhikkhu from another country and region, and by others as well, I— named Paññasāmi—
have well composed this book, which is a lamp for the lineage of the Dispensation.
When two thousand and twenty-three years had passed,
on the full moon day of the month of Migasira, it reached its absolute conclusion.
If anyone perceives any fault here, O wise ones, [let it be pointed out].
May they forgive that for the sake of purity; may they accept what is logical.
